Nature did not wish to show herself entirely naked to be looked upon before our eyes, but she wishes to hide herself under various forms and species, lest her venerable <term>arcana</term> <note>original: "arcana"; hidden mysteries or secret knowledge.</note> fall into contempt if the common people were to divulge and speak of the inseparable nature of things. The great parent, the most beautiful of things, did not wish to be prostituted everywhere and indifferently like a public <term>harlot</term> <note>original: "meretrix"; the author uses this blunt metaphor to argue that sacred knowledge must be protected from common or vulgar use.</note>.

The text uses classical metaphors like Proteus and the Minotaur to describe the difficulty of reaching true Wisdom.</summary>

Therefore, if this work contains so many figures of the labyrinth, enigmas, and mythical coverings, let no one wonder; for gems <gloss>and pearls</gloss> are not sought in the deep sea or on <unclear>inaccessible</unclear> rocks and mountains [without great effort]. It was permitted to no one to <unclear>divulge</unclear> the mysteries of the divine teachings to the profane <unclear>masses</unclear> <note>original: "vulgisque profanis"; a standard Latin phrase used in esoteric writing to describe those who have not been initiated into the "higher" truths.</note>.

How long a voyage did <term>Jason</term> <note>In Greek mythology, the hero who led the Argonauts; in alchemical traditions, Jason’s quest is often interpreted as the difficult search for the Philosopher's Stone.</note> undertake, and with what equal labors was the acquisition of the Golden Fleece? What do the fire of the bulls, the <unclear>taming</unclear> of the <unclear>dragon</unclear> with horrible <unclear>scales</unclear> in battle, and the help of <term>Medea</term> <note>A sorceress who aided Jason; she often represents the "secret" or "auxiliary" chemical processes required to complete the Great Work.</note> indicate <unclear>to us</unclear> other than experience, investigation, laborious inquiry, and the wisdom and prudence <unclear>of things</unclear>?

Nature placed a watchful dragon to guard the golden fleece, which is to say, the secrets of knowledge; hence, even here, this Dragon is nothing other than the <term>ethereal spirit</term> <note>original: "spiritus æthereus"; a vital, universal substance or "breath" that alchemists believed was the life-force of all matter.</note> abundantly generated and <unclear>created together with</unclear> [nature], the <unclear>mystery</unclear> of the <unclear>Philosophers</unclear>.

--- Page 7 ---
<meta>This page continues the author's philosophical and technical justification for alchemy. Having previously established the "arcana" or secrets of nature through the metaphor of the Golden Fleece, the author now transitions into the specific possibility of the artificial transmutation of metals, specifically the creation of gold.</meta>

# That Gold Can Be Made by Art.

...either they entrust the things themselves to nature, and among them many are found which resist those efforts. If these things can indeed, in a wonderful manner, sometimes be made by art—things which possess the same nature as that which is produced by nature itself, and are even little distant from one another in the categories of matter—let us use the example of that Gold which is the subject at hand. For why should it be necessary to instill some form denied by nature, through the benefit of place and time?

<margin>The matter from which it is made</margin>
For how easily we might consider that the very [way] of nature’s working is changed in different parts. For although it is through heat, one may observe that gold might be judged differently by others—some striving with purer [substances] and vitriol <note>original: "atramento"; literally "ink" or "black substance." In alchemical texts, this frequently refers to vitriol (metallic sulfates), used as a reagent.</note> through alchemical powers, and others passing into a single nature. Or perhaps from a certain mixture of water, which <term>Theophrastus</term> <note>Likely referring to Paracelsus (Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim, 1493–1541), a seminal figure in the transition from alchemy to modern chemistry and medicine.</note> cited but did not fully explain here, all of which are received from quicksilver and sulfur.

<margin>An opinion <unclear>by which</unclear></margin>
Democritus, recently [called] the father of this spark, with whom [something] is mixed—I do not mean the same thing which <term>Albertus</term> <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a medieval scholar whose writings on the "minerals" were foundational to later alchemical theory.</note> attacks, for that which comes from <term>Democritus</term> <note>In this context, the author refers to "Pseudo-Democritus," the name given to the unknown author of the oldest surviving Greek alchemical texts.</note> is different, since antiquity also noted fixed things through [substances] worn down by water, from which he himself took the work of generating even for gold. For there was that note whose <term>Quicksilver</term> <note>original: "Argentum vivi"; literally "living silver," the common name for mercury, viewed by alchemists as the "soul" of all metals.</note> and [the fire of] <term>Vulcan</term> <note>The Roman god of fire; alchemists used his name to symbolize the transformative heat of the laboratory furnace.</note> existed at that time, but it was a metal resolved into water.

<summary>This page argues that alchemy ("art") can replicate and assist the natural process of forming gold by using materials that are naturally related. It cites authorities like Paracelsus, Albertus Magnus, and Democritus to validate the theory that metals can be reduced to a liquid state and then refined.</summary>
<keywords>alchemy, transmutation, gold, mercury, sulfur, Paracelsus, Albertus Magnus, Pseudo-Democritus, metallurgy</keywords>

--- Page 8 ---
<meta>This page continues the author’s investigation into the artificial creation of gold. Following the discussion of Paracelsus and the role of mercury and sulfur, the text now focuses on the "First Matter" and the relationship between the sun's light and the physical properties of gold.</meta>

<unclear>it was the 3rd in the field it favors</unclear>

...which can be called the <term>first matter</term> <note>original: "prima materia"; the fundamental, primordial substance from which all physical matter was thought to be born in alchemical theory.</note> of metals. I say it arises from those things without other kinds of things which are contained by nature in the most proximal way. Does gold not seem to use those same things? Does it not work in this way? Or does it perhaps imitate color as much as it was able? Because it must respond to nature, it would consider such a thing to be by no means necessary.

For we perceive the reality of gold from the brightness of the sun. Is there not likewise a color for the whole universal water of things that would penetrate at the greatest depth? And in that same part, this indeed could not be achieved through any other constitution, except that it be skillfully produced in the level plains by the <term>effluvia</term> <note>original: "effluvis"; these were thought to be invisible vapors or "exhalations" that rose from the center of the earth to form minerals and metals.</note> within those slopes. Thus, without channels <note>original: "fretibus"; literally straits or narrow passages, here referring to the veins or conduits within the earth.</note>, there is no fire by which even a small vapor is excited to appear here and to the "columns" of gold; which fire not only reveals many mild things, but they are seen mostly in the midday light and in clear weather, so that you may see it yourself.

<margin><unclear>symbol</unclear></margin>
Moreover, those who honestly hold the common matter of metals to have their own "mother" <note>An alchemical reference to the "matrix" or specific environment in the earth where a metal grows.</note>, from which the primary forms can be created—whether they would do so only in the simplicity of this matter is probable among these kinds, or even in such a diverse condition so rightly...

<summary>The author argues that gold is formed by natural "effluvia" and internal fire within the earth, sharing a spiritual and physical essence with sunlight. He posits that metals possess a "mother" or primary matter from which their forms are derived.</summary>
<keywords>first matter, alchemy, gold, solar light, effluvia, metallic generation, mother of metals</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of gold's nature, moving from its physical appearance and "first matter" to the specific alchemical methods of "propagating" or multiplying it using the Elixir and the traditions of Arabic alchemy.</meta>

<margin>seed of gold</margin>

->Therefore, concerning gold, when it is introduced at some time for the propagation of its own kind through the subtlety of the art <note>original: "subtilitatem artis"; in this context, "art" refers to alchemy, and "subtlety" refers to the highly refined chemical processes used to manipulate matter.</note>, to which are sometimes mixed the new first principles <note>original: "primordia"; the most basic building blocks or "seeds" of a substance.</note> of that same gold; and in this manner, they drive metals and stones to be changed, and they are said to consist of the "first" [principles]. In these things, those who have derived the name <term>Elixir</term> <note>original: "Elixir"; from the Arabic *al-iksīr*, referring to a powder or potion used to transform base metals into gold.</note> from the <term>Philosophers</term> of the Arabs <note>A reference to the foundational role of Islamic scholars like Jabir ibn Hayyan (Geber) in the development of Western alchemy.</note> from a small amount of gold-matter place much trust. <unclear>They have</unclear> <unclear>called</unclear> another [substance] the <term>medicine</term> <note>original: "medicinam"; alchemists often described the transformation of metals as "healing" them, treating the Philosopher's Stone as a universal cure for both metals and the human body.</note>.<-

<summary>This page describes the alchemical theory of "propagating" gold by introducing its "seeds" or "first principles" into other materials. It credits Arabic philosophers for the concept of the Elixir and the "medicine" used in the transmutation of metals.</summary>
<keywords>gold propagation, Elixir, Arabic Philosophers, alchemy, transmutation, seed of gold, universal medicine</keywords>

# Fixation of mercury <note>original symbol: ☿; "fixation" refers to the process of making a volatile substance stable under heat.</note>

Make a strong water <note>original: "acqua forte"; usually refers to nitric acid or a similar corrosive solvent</note> of saltpeter <term>saltpeter: potassium nitrate, a key ingredient in explosives and acids</term> and realgar <term>realgar: an arsenic sulfide mineral known for its bright red-orange color</term>, and with this, let one [part] be calcined. Then, make an amalgam of Silver <note>original: "Luna," the alchemical name for silver</note> with quicksilver <note>mercury</note>.
<note>The following four lines are heavily struck through in the original manuscript</note>
Upon one pound of mercury, and then let it be
placed above it in a small vessel <note>original: "testino"; likely a small crucible or cupel</note> made of two plates with
a leg and with the <unclear>servants</unclear> <note>original: "fante"; this may refer to a specific part of the apparatus or "sprays" of water</note> of water.
By chance, the mercury "dies" <note>loses its liquid/volatile form</note>.
Let the water be passed over the "milk of gold" <note>original: "latte di ☉"; likely a colloidal suspension or a specific chemical state of gold</note> three
times. The gold is refreshed in its body,
and when put to the fire, the mercury remains as a hard
portion of gold.

But before amalgamating a lime <note>original: "calce"; a powder produced by heating a mineral or metal until it oxidizes</note>, let
particulars be made according to the requirement of the strong water, such
that it nourishes the "unique blackness" <note>original: "nigra unica"; likely a reference to the *nigredo*, the initial blackening stage of the alchemical Great Work</note>.

---

Take care that the glass does not crack, nor the alum of
copper scale [or] bole—which is called "red"—for this
keeps the plates red-hot. And if there is one pound of saltpeter, they
have two ounces of bole <note>original: "bolo"; a medicinal or alchemical clay, often "Armenian bole," used to seal vessels or resist heat</note>.

<note>Additional illegible and heavily struck-through lines follow at the bottom of the page.</note>

<summary>A technical alchemical recipe describing the "fixation" of mercury into gold using saltpeter, realgar, and silver amalgam. The text includes specific warnings about heat management and the use of "bole" to protect glassware from cracking during high-temperature reactions.</summary>

<meta>Continuity: This page follows the previous instructions for the fixation of mercury, shifting from a method using "strong water" (acids) to a metallurgical approach involving alloying with lead, tin, and silver to solidify the liquid metal.</meta>

# Purification of Venus <note>original: "Purga di Venere"; "Venus" is the alchemical name for copper.</note>

Place copper in sheets and make layers upon layers <note>original abbreviation: "s. s. s.," standing for the Latin *stratum super stratum*</note> with powder of cornice <note>original: "cornice"; likely a mineral flux or abrasive used to clean or color the metal during heating</note> and make layers of cementation <note>a process where a metal is surrounded by powdered minerals and heated without melting</note> for twelve hours, which should be placed for a night in the copper-fire. Melt the sheets, and the metal will be white; and for whoever repeats the same process a second time, it will be white and most beautiful.

---

->Solidification and Fixation of Mercury <note>original symbol: ☿</note><-

Take a round earthenware vessel and place at the bottom lead and tin, equal parts of each <note>original: "**ana**"; a medical and alchemical term meaning "in equal quantities"</note>. Then make layers upon layers with mercury; that is, first beat [the lead and tin] firmly into thin little sheets, then make layers with said sheets and mercury. That is: place one sheet, then more mercury, then another [sheet], and mercury on top of that, and then more mercury. Melt a quantity of silver in the middle <note>in a separate crucible</note> equal to the weight of the sheets, and then pour it over said sheets. Let everything cool, and it will all be a <term>brittle: easily broken or crumbled; here referring to a solid alloy that can be pulverized for further treatment</term> mass. Grind it into powder and put it inside a ball <note>likely a cloth or leather bag, or a spherical vessel</note>. Place it to soak for three days in blacksmith's water <note>original: "acqua de ferrai"; the water used by smiths to quench hot iron, which alchemists believed absorbed the "virtue" or strength of the iron</note>; the longer it stays there, the better it will be. Melt it and make objects from it, even if they are made more brittle.

<summary>This page provides two metallurgical recipes: one for whitening copper (Venus) using a cementation process, and another for "fixing" mercury into a solid state by alloying it with lead, tin, and silver.</summary>
<keywords>alchemy, copper, mercury, fixation, silver, tin, lead, cementation, blacksmith's water, metallurgy</keywords>

# Distilling Vinegar .

In a large retort <term>retort (a glass vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distillation)</term> place 4 jugs <note>original: boccali</note> of very high-quality vinegar.
And bury it in sifted and packed ash, but let the ash be 
one finger thick beneath the base <note>original: culo, literally "bottom"</note> of the retort.
And place the receiver <note>the vessel that collects the distilled liquid</note> so that it is likewise buried 
in the ash, well-sealed so that it does not vent <note>original: spiri, literally "breathe"</note>.
Then place charcoal in the furnace, and when it is <gloss>lit</gloss> lit,
and the furnace is full of coals, seal the said furnace well,
so that it cannot vent except through a small 
hole <note>original: bucio, a dialect variant of buco</note>, so that the charcoal inside will last the 
whole day, and when it is finished, add more. Then remove
the receiver when the first quarter part has come out,
which is the phlegm <term>phlegm (the watery, tasteless part of a distillate that lacks the active spirit)</term>; replace it and seal it well, and
let it distill so that in four days it will be finished.
If you wish to make it stronger, pour it back over the dregs <note>original: feccie</note>, and 
rectify <term>rectify (to purify or concentrate a substance through repeated distillation)</term> it four times.
When the dregs have finished distilling, the oil 
comes out, which you can then collect separately.

<note>The vocabulary below lists the primary technical terms used in this recipe.</note>
vinegar, retort, ash, receiver, furnace, charcoal, phlegm, to distill, dregs, oil, rectification

<summary>This page provides a detailed technical recipe for distilling and rectifying vinegar using a retort buried in ash. It explains how to separate the 'phlegm' from the spirit and how to extract a final oil from the dregs.</summary>
<keywords>distillation, vinegar, alchemical apparatus, retort, furnace, rectification, phlegm, early modern chemistry</keywords>

## On Emblems.

The specific nature of <term>Emblems</term> <note>original: "Imprese"; a Renaissance art form combining an image and a motto to represent a personal aim or philosophy</note> is to contain great meaning within a few things. They are similar to those <note>crossed out: that were</note> Egyptian <term>hieroglyphs</term>, which contained great mysteries within various figures.

The people of China have in their language infinite letters and <unclear>dots</unclear> <note>original: "punti"; likely referring to the specific strokes or tonal marks of Chinese characters</note>, and in their <note>crossed out: letters</note> characters they hold great meaning; for when they wish at times to declare something, they draw a letter, and with that they express their concept.

But the Egyptians, in their hieroglyphs, contained the meanings of great things: of praise or of blame, or of religion and Empire, and similar matters. Great things, and the precepts of prudence...

**Vocabulary:** Emblems, hieroglyphs, hieroglyphs (alternate spelling), Egyptians, China, letters/characters, blame, prudence.

--- Page 20 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion on the use of symbolism and secrecy in the transmission of knowledge, following the previous page's introduction of Egyptian hieroglyphs and Chinese characters as precursors to the "Impresa" (emblem).</meta>

...human wisdom, and moral philosophy in particular. It was hidden by poets within fables, by philosophers in the obscurity of concepts, and by the Egyptians within their figures <note>referring to hieroglyphs</note>. Similarly, the sacred scriptures of God themselves contain many likenesses, metaphors, and parables. Therein are the seed, the fathers of the family, the thorns, the stones, the vineyards, the flowers, the lilies, and similar things; conveyed through figures and similitudes.

In this way, too, the <term>chemical philosophers</term> <note>original: "filosofi chimici"; referring to alchemists</note> hide great <term>magisteries</term> <note>original: "magisteri"; the secret processes or "masterworks" of alchemical transformation</note> under the signs of the eagle, the dragons, metal plates, and <term>Virgin’s milk</term> <note>original: "latte di Vergine"; a symbolic alchemical term for a specific solvent or purified substance</note>; using one thing to represent another: marriage, death, resurrection, spirit, soul, and similar matters.

And this was done so that noble things would not be communicated to—and thus debased by—all the fools, for they would have been despised and mocked. Philosophy would have been called madness, and the common people would not have put virtue and justice into practice.

<meta>This page continues the exploration of ancient symbolic systems, moving from a general discussion of secrecy and Egyptian/Chinese origins to specific interpretations of hieroglyphs and their influence on Hebrew scripture.</meta>

The purpose of hieroglyphs was to represent the concept of the Author through the nature of the thing depicted.

It is proven that the Ethiopians also possessed hieroglyphs, but there is no record that the knowledge of the sciences and philosophy existed among the Ethiopians as it did among the Egyptians.

The Hebrews as well included great meanings within their letters, as the Sacred Writers say; and in that long interaction <note>original: "commercio"; referring to social and cultural exchange</note> they had with the Egyptians until the time of Pharaoh, they learned many things from the said letters, as is seen at the beginning of Genesis where they hint at the true use of the aforementioned hieroglyphs.

The **Sparrowhawk** <note>original: "Sparvier"; a bird of prey often used in Egyptian art to represent the soul or the sun god Horus</note> signifies celerity, because among birds it is found to be most lively.

The **Eye** signifies justice, because they say that the jawbone of <unclear>that one</unclear> near the right arm encourages justice <note>This likely refers to a specific iconographic arrangement of the Eye of Horus or a particular Egyptian statue pose</note>.

The **Heart** between the right and left shoulder signifies speech.

The **Cynocephalus** <note>original: "Cinocefalo"; a dog-headed baboon, an animal sacred to Thoth, the Egyptian god of wisdom and the moon</note>, because it is a devotee of the moon, signifies prayer and veneration.

The **Laurel leaf** signifies the renewal of the trifles <note>original: "ruscelle"; likely referring to small branches or worldly "frills"</note> and pomps of the world, because in spring they fall, and in autumn they are renewed.

**Mud** signifies a corporeal <note>physical or bodily</note> thing.

The **Chick** signifies the matter of the body and the soul.

**Ship** A long ship with oars used by Cupid. At its highest point, it signifies happiness, as the ship is the collector of prosperous fortune.

**Eagle** The eagle signifies magnanimity and privilege, depicted with a thunderbolt between its feet.

**Dolphin** The dolphin denotes the tranquility of the sea, being the symbol of Neptune, god of the sea and of all waters. For this reason, Cupid was depicted atop a dolphin with ropes in hand, signifying that love is the lord of both the land and the sea.

**Hands** Two joined hands were a symbol of faith <note>Meaning loyalty or trust</note>, as seen on medals with this inscription: *Faith of the armies* <note>original Latin: "Fides exercituum"</note> and *of the human gods* <note>original Latin: "et dei humani"</note>. <meta>This page continues the catalog of symbolic meanings from the previous discussion on plant life and crowns, shifting the focus toward animal insignias of nations, the symbols of historical figures, and a detailed exploration of color theory in Renaissance iconography.</meta>

Many men, cities, provinces, and Kingdoms use various figures and signs as their insignias. Some imagined the gods transforming into thunderbolts; the Persians used the rooster; Venice, a lion; the Romans, the eagle; and countless others have adopted and carry various figures, such as Octavian <note>The Emperor Augustus</note> using the Sphinx, Pompey using the Lion with a sword, the Spaniards using the stork, and many others. This Sun and the East are symbols of divine majesty.

<margin>Colors.</margin>
Colors also have their own symbols, such that White is the symbol of Clemency, and Vermillion <note>A brilliant red pigment</note> is the symbol of rigor <note>Meaning severity or strict justice</note>. Black signifies firmness and constancy; yellow signifies weeping and sorrow.

<margin>White</margin>
White was also a symbol of God, of the Beginning, and of the Infinite, as well as of regeneration; it was esteemed by all peoples as being pleasing to God. It was also a symbol of splendor <note>original: "lautezza," referring to refined luxury or abundance</note> and manumission <note>The formal act of freeing a slave</note>.

<margin>
Pale
Ash-gray
</margin>
Pale: The paleness of lovers signifies hope. Ash-gray <note>original: "Berretino" or "ferretino," referring to a dull, undyed wool color</note> signifies lowliness of spirit and deception <note>original: "simulatione"</note>. From this comes the proverb: *a gray garment cheats the people* <note>original Italian: "di ueste berretin gaba la gente"</note>. Held by the Greeks as an unlucky and unhappy color, it was hated. Black was, among men, an indication of infamous and wicked character, but generally it is a symbol of sorrow and firmness.

--- Page 33 ---
<meta>This page continues the classification of emblems (Imprese) begun on page 8. Having previously discussed the "soul" (words only) and "body" (figures only), the author now explains the ideal composition where both elements are interdependent.</meta>

...material and perceptible nature are of three [kinds of] Bodies. The first is of figures and words joined together, and this is most proper to the **Emblem** <term>Impresa: a Renaissance device combining a visual image (the "body") with a short motto (the "soul") to express a personal philosophy or intent</term>, in which the words and the figures are artfully coupled together.

Thus, five parts are required for an Emblem:
The 1st: the **Concept** <term>Concetto: the underlying idea, theme, or intention of the creator</term>, or intention of the author.
The 2nd: the words of the motto.
The 3rd: the proportion [correspondence] between the words and the figures.
The 4th: the specific property of the figure—that is, the nature of that animal, plant, or other thing that it represents.
The 5th and last: the beauty of the <unclear>painting</unclear>.

And all the parts of the Emblem must serve the Concept, and this must be only one. The words of the Emblem must be quite brief, as long as they are enigmatic <note>original: "oscure" (obscure); in Renaissance emblem theory, the meaning was intended to be a witty puzzle for the learned, not immediately obvious to a casual observer</note>, and composed in such a way that they cannot stand, nor signify the author's Concept, without the figure to which they are joined. And when the motto signifies the meaning completely by itself without the help of the figure, then it is imperfect, because the figure becomes borrowed <note>original: "d'accatto," meaning the image is superfluous or merely an "extra" rather than an essential part of the meaning</note> and unbecoming.

Nor should the figure alone explain the author’s Concept without the words, because then it would be a **hieroglyphic** <note>The author distinguishes the "Impresa" from the "hieroglyph," which he defines here as a purely visual symbol that carries its own complete meaning without text</note>, which signifies by itself, and the words would be placed there superfluously, and would be nothing other than an <unclear>effect</unclear>.

...which demonstrate only the nature of that thing which it shows and represents, as is appropriate. And [Paolo] Giovio <note>Paolo Giovio (1483–1552) was an Italian physician and historian whose treatise on emblems became the standard reference for the genre</note> himself, the first writer on this subject, teaches us this, as seen in the silkworm <note>original: "Verme" (worm); specifically the silkworm used by the general Bartolomeo d'Alviano to symbolize rebirth or industry</note> and the wing of Alviano, and in the lizard in the fire of the Duke of Urbino <note>Federico da Montefeltro, Duke of Urbino, used a "stellion" (a type of lizard) in the flames to symbolize endurance or a heart that cannot be consumed by the fire of passion</note>.

<margin>According to the</margin> law, the entanglement and confused multitude of figures is not permitted, and furthermore: one cannot make a perfect or praiseworthy emblem [this way]. Because the more beautiful the unity of a multitude is, the more complete and beautiful are those **Emblems** <term>Impresa: a symbolic device consisting of an image and a motto</term> composed of a single body [image], from which, when joined to the words, there results a single, indivisible **Concept** <term>Concetto: the underlying idea or intended meaning of the emblem</term> worthy of the author. It is the error of those who, in their emblems, do not allow for a single stance <note>original: "stanza," likely referring to a singular, unified composition or "station"</note>.

The figures must have their own proper meaning preceding from the nature of that body represented, and thus distinct from the meaning that is derived from the joining of the figure with the words. Therefore, those emblems cannot be <unclear>praised</unclear> whose figures have <unclear>meanings</unclear> <unclear>that</unclear> can hardly be <unclear>understood</unclear> by even the most <unclear>learned</unclear> men.

The bodies of emblems must be noble and illustrious, and not ridiculous.

Finally: proportion is necessary, which is a certain harmony or measure of that which is sought in <unclear>designing</unclear>.

Attention should be given to the words and the figure. In this, one must consider the definition of the *impresa* <term>Impresa: a symbolic device or emblem consisting of an image (the "body") and a motto (the "soul")</term>, which is an operation of the intellect, intended to show something through brief words or useful and necessary figures, as are the general ones.

<gloss>The Academicians</gloss>
Stranio, an academician of the Trusted <note>The *Accademia degli Affidati* (The Academy of the Trustworthy) was a prominent literary and cultural group in 16th-century Pavia, Italy</note>, used a shield where nothing was painted, with the motto **It is not a mortal thing that I desire** <note>original Latin: "Non est mortale quod opto"</note>. That is to say, on the shield of my desires, nothing mortal is painted; therefore, nothing I desire is mortal.

An eagle that was looking at the rising <gloss>age</gloss> <note>the scribe crossed out "the sun" and replaced it with "age"</note> with the motto **Toward the light of midday** <note>original Latin: "ad Diem meridie"</note>. It is intended to signify that when his age was more vigorous, he would have better shown his worth.

A Hercules upon the mountain with the motto **He went forth for a few; rest preserves** <note>original Latin: "prodiit paucos, seruat quies"</note>. That is to say, if Hercules is seen, no labor is felt, just as I am able to possess perfect tranquility.

A chameleon in motion—or perhaps because it does not live on our air. That is to say, if the chameleon feeds on air, why can I not feed on our **intellect**?

The Marquis of Vasto <note>Alfonso d'Avalos (1502–1546), a prominent Spanish-Italian general and diplomat</note> used the Temple of Ephesus <note>The Temple of Artemis at Ephesus was burned down by Herostratus, who sought fame through an act of destruction</note> while it was burning, with the motto **This path is from others** <note>original Latin: "Hoc uia ex aliis"</note>. That is to say, we seek fame by a path contrary to that of the one who lit this fire—that is, through the path of ruin.

One may consult the *Commentaries on Emblems* by Luca <gloss>Contile</gloss> <note>Luca Contile (1505–1574) was a diplomat and author whose work "Ragionamento... sopra le imprese" (1574) provided an exhaustive study of the rules and examples of emblems</note>.

## Consultations on many discourses regarding emblems, and other authors

From whose authority we learn how excellent those emblems are that not only contain ancient symbols and meanings but also derive their "spirit" from the words. They even hold within them the meanings left to us by philosophers and poets in their fables <note>In this context, "fables" refers to classical myths or allegorical stories</note>, and they explain more elegantly the intention that one wishes to convey.

I have chosen to add some emblems <term>Impresa: a symbolic device or emblem consisting of an image (the "body") and a motto (the "soul")</term> that I created on various occasions for different friends or for other reasons. I have also included some explanations regarding the fables of **Ovid** and their likenesses; however, these cannot truly be counted as emblems, though they share a certain resemblance.

> *Whoever loves outward beauty and chases empty shadows—while the former perishes by fire, and while the latter holds you, you perish.* <note>original Latin: "Quisquis amat formam simulachraque inania captas / Dum perit ille igni dum tenet illa peris." A swan with one foot in the water and the other on the sand, with the motto *As long as I sing* <note>original Italian: "Pur che io canti"</note>.

To show that peace had been acquired through war. <note>The olive branch represents peace, while the sword represents the military struggle required to achieve it.</note>

### An outstretched moon
> It fails as it draws near. <note>original Latin: "Propius desuit." This likely refers to the moon's light being eclipsed or rendered invisible as it approaches the sun, a common metaphor for a mortal's proximity to the divine or a subject's proximity to a great ruler.</note>

### A ball in the hand
> For those who seek. <note>original Italian: "Cercanti." This may refer to the "ball of fortune" or a game of skill, suggesting that rewards come to those who actively pursue them.</note>

### In coral
> As it first emerges. <note>original Latin: "Ut primus emergit." According to ancient natural history, coral was thought to be a soft plant underwater that hardened into stone the moment it touched the air. This symbolizes a character or idea that gains its true strength upon being revealed.</note>

### A rose in the open
> Sun rising in the east. <note>original Italian: "Oriente sole." This image depicts the rose blooming at the first light of day, symbolizing hope, beauty, or the awakening of the soul.</note>

### A maned lion
> Rough and bristling. <note>original Latin: "Squalidus et horrido." In Renaissance heraldry, these terms describe the rugged, untamed, and fearsome nature of the lion, intended to inspire respect rather than suggest filth.</note>

### A bow with an arrow
> At the opportune moment. <note>original Italian: "opportuno." This emblem emphasizes the importance of timing and the precision required to strike when the moment is right.</note>

### A hammer over a red-hot iron
> Care. <note>original Italian: "Sollicitudine." This goes beyond "worry" to mean diligent effort and persistent labor. It suggests that one must work on one's character or projects while the "iron is hot" and opportunity is present.</note>

### A large bell
> To be heard better. <note>original Spanish: "Para se oir mejor." A bell’s purpose is public proclamation; this emblem suggests that some messages or virtues require a loud and clear voice to be effective.</note>

### A sword crowned with laurel
> You have a leader. <note>original Italian: "Hai duce." The sword represents military power, while the laurel represents victory and wisdom. Together, they signify a ruler who leads with both strength and honor.</note>

## Projection of the Moon <note>Silver</note> upon Venus <note>Copper</note>
->A fixed substance, 12 parts.<-

<margin>White</margin>
**R** <note>Recipe/Take</note> one ounce of <term>cupelled Moon|Luna di cupella: Silver that has been purified through cupellation, a refining process where ores are treated under high heat to separate noble metals from base metals like lead.</term>, two ounces of common mercury, and three ounces of white arsenic. Dissolve each body separately on its own in a vessel with common <term>aqua fortis|acqua forte: Literally "strong water," this is nitric acid, a powerful corrosive used by alchemists to dissolve metals.</term>. Afterward, combine all the liquids together. Distill using a <term>retort|storta: A glass bulb with a long neck curved downward, used for distilling liquids.</term> and a glass <term>alembic|ambico: A distilling apparatus consisting of two vessels connected by a tube.</term> six times, always returning the distilled liquid over the residue, distilling over a slow fire. 

Then take the matter that remains, which will be dry and weigh about eight ounces. Take also three ounces of common <term>sublimate|sublimato: Usually refers to mercuric chloride, a poisonous white crystalline compound.</term> and three ounces of <term>sal ammoniac|sale armonico: Ammonium chloride, a salt used in alchemy to help dissolve or sublimate metals.</term>. Combine everything together and place it inside a vessel to <term>sublime|sublimare: To heat a solid substance until it turns into a vapor and then becomes solid again upon cooling, a method used to purify chemicals.</term> seven times inside a strong flask <note>original: "garaffa"</note>. Apply fire in four degrees <note>a standard alchemical practice of increasing heat intensity from a gentle warmth to a roaring furnace</note>, beginning from the first up to the fourth. At each sublimation, break the vessel and place the matter in another, first grinding the material; at each grinding, soak the matter with two ounces of that distilled aqua fortis that you saved from earlier.

After the sixth sublimation, a shiny, gray-white stone will remain at the bottom of the flask. Grind this upon a marble slab and place it in the night air <note>original: "al sereno"</note> or in the dampness of a cellar until it all dissolves <note>a process called deliquescence, where a salt absorbs enough moisture from the air to turn into a liquid</note>. Then filter it and afterward congeal it over a slow fire. One ounce of this substance will convert twelve ounces of purified copper into fine silver.

->From the manuscript <note>original Latin: "ex manuscripto"</note><-

# Tinctures <del>for the metals</del>

# fixation of <term>mercury|☿</term>

If one ounce of <term>cupelled silver|☽ di cupella: silver refined in a shallow porous bowl called a cupel</term>, and three ounces of 
common <term>strong water|acqua forte: nitric acid, used to dissolve metals</term>, 
let the said <term>silver|☽</term> be consumed by the fine water, and 
afterward put it in a <term>small retort|stortina: a glass vessel with a long downward-pointing neck used for distillation</term> and 
boil the strong water, but let it not escape 
outside; rather, let enough remain so that the <term>silver|☽</term> does 
not remain as a <term>lime|calce: a powdery metallic precipitate or oxide</term> but in the water, 
which you will find weighs two ounces more than the said <term>silver|☽</term>.

Into the water that remains, which contains the <term>silver|☽</term>, pour 
a glass of fresh water from a spring 
or a well, and into that water throw four ounces 
of <term>Spanish mercury|☿ di spagna</term>, and let it sit 
for 24 hours. You will find in the said water 
the <term>mercury|☿</term> <unclear>smoke</unclear> congealed like a hedgehog <note>original: "ricio" (riccio). This likely refers to a crystalline, spiky growth known as a "silver tree" or "Diana's Tree."</note>.

Pour off the water into another vessel, and you will find 
the mercury like a paste; put it for one night 
in the open air <note>original: "al sereno," referring to the cool night air, believed to have specific cooling or celestial properties</note>, and it will become hard and brittle.

Into the water that you have poured off, throw in a 
small piece of copper in a thin sheet, so that upon it 
will fall all the lime of the silver in one 
night or day.

The said lime could also be made to fall with a handful 
of salt, but with salt, the silver returns into 
a body <note>re-solidifies into its metallic form</note>, and therefore it is better to make it fall with the copper, 
so that the <unclear>residue</unclear> remains apart.

And then wash the said lime with a piece of soap, 
and with <unclear>salt and saltpeter</unclear>.

## Dissolving Gold

If gold is dissolved using <term>aqua regia|acqua regia: literally 'royal water,' a powerful mixture of nitric and hydrochloric acids capable of dissolving gold</term> that contains <term>sal ammoniac|sale armoniaco: ammonium chloride, a salt used in alchemy to turn nitric acid into aqua regia</term>, this substance is an "enemy" to mercury and will never combine with it. Therefore, instead of adding the aforementioned sal ammoniac to the <term>strong water|acqua forte: nitric acid</term>, take an ounce of ordinary strong water and add a little common salt <note>original: "sale ordinario," likely sodium chloride</note>. This will dissolve into the liquid within the strong water; the solution made in this way will still be able to dissolve gold as if it were aqua regia, though not quite as effectively.

It is a great secret to reintroduce gold into mercury. This is first accomplished by thoroughly working the gold in a <term>porphyry mortar|mortaro di porfido: a vessel made of very hard, reddish-purple volcanic stone used for fine grinding</term> for three consecutive days with a pestle made of the same stone. The gold should be reduced to thin leaves beforehand, and it should be of the purity found in <term>Zecchini|Venetian ducats: high-quality gold coins renowned for their consistency</term>.

<summary>This page describes a method for dissolving gold using a modified version of aqua regia made with common salt instead of sal ammoniac to ensure compatibility with mercury. It also provides instructions for grinding gold leaf into mercury using a porphyry mortar.</summary>
<keywords>gold, aqua regia, sal ammoniac, mercury, nitric acid, common salt, porphyry mortar, Zecchini, alchemy, metallurgy</keywords>

## The Hardening of Mercury <note>original: "☿". The symbol for the planet and element Mercury, named after the Roman messenger god.</note>

Take **mercury**, **verdigris** <term>verdigris: a green pigment (copper acetate) formed by the action of acetic acid on copper plates; widely used in alchemy for its copper content</term>, and **salt** in equal parts; boil it until it forms a <unclear>film</unclear> <gloss>its own</gloss> in an iron pan with **iron-water** <note>original: "acqua ferrata". This refers to the water used by blacksmiths to quench hot iron, which becomes saturated with iron oxides and was believed to have specific chemical virtues.</note> that the blacksmiths use. Tend to it until it can be strained through **leather**, and wash it well of its dregs with clear water. Then, place it out in the night air for one night, and it will become hard and brittle. 

Put it in a **crucible**, melt it, and you may combine it with a third part of **silver** <note>original: "argento". The author uses both the word and the symbol ☽ interchangeably.</note>, but do so using a **cupellation fire** <term>cupellation: a refining process where ores or alloyed metals are treated under high heat to separate noble metals, like gold and silver, from base metals like lead or copper</term>.

To color it into **gold**, you will find the method in the other book.

## The Fixation of Silver <note>original: "☽". The symbol for the Moon, representing silver in alchemical tradition.</note>

Take as much **black salt** <note>likely common salt heated with organic matter or charcoal, used as a flux or reactive agent</note> as you wish and let it <unclear>soak in urine</unclear> <note>original: "pissare". While literally meaning "to urinate," in alchemical recipes it refers to the use of urine as a source of ammonia and salts.</note>; then mix it with an equal part of **common salt**. After this, soften it with a little **rainwater**, and let it sit as a **paste** for one night <gloss>24 hours</gloss>. 

Then, place it in a **Bassanello pot** <note>likely a ceramic vessel produced in the town of Bassano, known for its durable earthenware</note> with the lid **luted** <term>luted: sealed with "lute," a tough paste made of clay, sand, and sometimes hair or dung, to make a vessel airtight before heating</term> so that it cannot breathe [leak]. Give it fire for 6 hours until the pot is glowing red; then take it out and you will find the material has become hard. Crush it, and pour rainwater over it.

# Description of the Brief Work of the Stone

First, it must be known that the body <note>In alchemy, the "body" refers to the solid metallic substance that acts as the physical base for the work.</note> must be united in mercury with that very same mercury, and they will delight in the sulfur which will then be digested and cooked through the work of nature <note>Alchemists believed that metals grew in the earth through the "cooking" or "digestion" of two principles: sulfur (the active, masculine, combustible principle) and mercury (the passive, feminine, fluid principle). This recipe seeks to mimic that natural process in the laboratory.</note>.

This sulfur will be the seed, and the mercury will be the earth, but both must be prepared.

Take, therefore, <term>mineral gold</term> <note>original: "oro minerale". This refers to native gold found in nature that has not yet been subjected to the high heat of a furnace, which alchemists believed preserved its "vital spirit."</note> that has not been placed in the fire; and if you cannot obtain that, take the finest gold of the **<term>Zecchino</term>** <note>A Venetian gold coin (the Ducat) renowned for its extreme purity, often used as a standard for high-quality gold in technical recipes.</note> or something similar, for in this way it will not need further <term>preparation</term> <note>original: "preparat.ne". A common abbreviation for "preparation," the process of purifying or spiritually "opening" a metal for alchemical work.</note>.

In the same way, understand that concerning silver, if you cannot obtain it in such a pure state, take **<term>cupelled silver</term>** <note>original: "argento cupellato". Silver refined through cupellation, a process where the metal is heated in a shallow porous cup (a cupel) to oxidize and remove base metals like lead.</note>.

From these bodies, one shall make very thin foils.

Afterward, take mercury from a <unclear>mine</unclear>, or from mountain cinnabar <note>Cinnabar is the bright red ore (mercuric sulfide) from which mercury is most commonly extracted.</note>, or from marcasite <note>A brittle mineral often confused with pyrite; in this context, it refers to a source for extracting metallic or spiritual principles.</note>, and prepare it in this manner <insert>& prepared</insert>.

### The Assembly of the Philosophers
<note>original: "Turba philosophorum," one of the oldest and most influential alchemical texts, written as a record of a debate among Greek and pre-Socratic philosophers.</note>

#### Discourse 7.

...nor should the vapor of your <term>gourd</term> <note>original: "zucca," referring to the cucurbit or the bottom part of a distilling vessel, often shaped like a gourd.</note> ever be cooled down to the dregs.
Besides this: there is an immoderate heat <note>original: "calore disonesto," literally "dishonest heat," meaning heat that is inconsistent or too intense for the delicate process.</note> which is a most burning sign, of which it is said in the *Assembly*: "Finally,
> let the fire which is fire be made
> even more intensely burning."
<note>original Latin: "Denique ignis qui sit ignis licet fiat magis ardentissimus."</note>

After this, let it remain for the space of seven natural days. And then, furthermore, you will see formed within the vapor those things to which the names of the Heart, the plants, and the <term>vegetative soul</term> <note>In medieval philosophy, the "vegetative soul" was the most basic level of life responsible for growth and reproduction; in alchemy, it refers to the "life force" beginning to stir within the matter.</note> are given.

The signs by which you will understand these things will be these: a small disk [or wheel], which was almost black, will already become clearer, and the "little blackness" <note>likely a reference to the "nigredo" or black stage of the alchemical work.</note> will begin to move away; and furthermore, a little vapor will ascend from the "earth" into the "air." <note>The "earth" refers to the solid matter at the bottom of the vessel, and "air" to the space above it.</note>

Always remember <term>Our Art</term> <note>original: "Ar: nostra," short for *Ars Nostra*, the traditional way alchemists referred to their secret practice.</note>, observing always that its clouds must not run together into liquid water except when you see that they no longer evaporate from your earth, and those that have ascended do not descend. Then continue for more than two other days.

### Concerning the Matter in the Furnace

This shall be the method: Have a round and long earthen vessel, more than a year old <note>The age of the vessel ensures the clay is fully seasoned and less likely to crack</note>, filled with sifted and heated ash. In the middle, place the matter which contains the principal substance, so that the ash wraps and surrounds it. From the matter and within the ash on the said level, let it descend above the ash, so that they may better receive the heat; and place them around with <term>oltricari</term> <note>This term likely refers to small support bricks or spacers used to stabilize the vessel</note> so that they are low on the surface of the ash.

Once this is done, place a sheet of iron on top, which should be on a high iron tripod, and leave a space <note>original: "raggia," likely referring to a radius or clearance gap</note> of the required diameter. Place it in a vessel with other ash on top so that the bottom of the vessel is supported, ensuring that the smoke of the matter does not perish <note>i.e., is not lost or dissipated prematurely</note>.

Place the vessel with the matter upon this tripod, above the furnace and not below, so that the principal dryness is not lost, and so that it is not mixed with iron through my doing.

Then light the fire to begin; that is, let it be a fire that possesses continuous humidity and aridity, remaining permanent in its degree, so that it is pure, and does not extract from above, so that it can be increased or diminished.

### Concerning the Rights of the <term>Commune</term> <note>The local administrative body or municipality</note>

# Secrets of Morienus, the Roman Philosopher

->tested in the year 1118. hidden<-
->underground by the aforementioned in a stone of<-
->marble which said<-
->to my heirs.<-

<margin>Take 2 lbs of antimony and 2 lbs of sublimate <note>original: "subl^o^"</note> as [written] below</margin>
**First you will make a mercurial water in this way.**
Take antimony and <term>sublimate</term> <note>Likely mercuric chloride, a common alchemical reagent</note>, two pounds of each, and grind each thing separately; then join everything together and place it in a <term>retort</term> <note>A glass vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distillation</note>. Into the said retort you shall put two pounds of distilled urine; but before you distill it, place the urine in a small cauldron over the fire, let it boil, and skim off the foam. Note that the urine should be from a healthy youth, and then you shall distill the said urine. You will place the said urine in the said retort, which you will set upon the furnace to distill, joining the large receiver to the retort, giving it a slow fire at the beginning and a strong fire at the end. The water you have collected, distill it again. This water is celestial blue in color, and it is this mercurial water so celebrated by us philosophers. And when we have said that one touches the matter cast out into the streets, into the dung, which is of base price and available to both the poor and the rich, we have spoken then in <term>parabolic words</term> <note>The author admits to using "parables" or allegorical language, a standard practice in alchemy to hide secrets from the uninitiated</note>; and yet, we have spoken clearly.

# Regulus of Antimony

<margin>regulus of antimony</margin>
Take **antimony**, **saltpeter** <note>Potassium nitrate.</note>, and **crude tartar** <note>Potassium bitartrate, a byproduct of winemaking.</note> in equal parts <note>original: "ana parte."</note>. Grind everything together and place it all in a large <term>pila</term> <note>A mortar or deep, heat-resistant vessel.</note>, making a slow fire all around it until the fire reaches the inside. **Beware of breathing that smoke**, and stir it with a rod until it is well melted. Pour this into a vessel with a pointed bottom so that the dross <note>original: "fecce"; the impurities or waste material.</note> will rise to the top, while the <term>regulus</term> <note>The pure, metallic portion of a mineral that settles at the bottom of a crucible.</note> remains at the bottom in the manner of a metal.

# How the Calx of Bodies is Reduced into a Mass

<margin>reducing the calx into a mass.</margin>

Take the **calx** <note>The powdery residue or oxide of a metal remaining after it has been roasted or "calcined."</note> of any metal you wish and grind it very well upon the **porphyry** <note>A hard, purple-toned stone used by alchemists as a surface for grinding fine powders.</note> by washing it with distilled water two or three times. Pour away the turbid water and, by saving what settles, the water will eventually remain clear and the powder sufficiently washed. Then let it dry well, and soak it with **alum** water <note>original: "allume iameno," likely referring to rock alum or Yemen alum.</note> mixed with water of common salt. You shall dry it, soak it, and grind it many times until the calx becomes a "live" white, and almost shining in the fire. If you see that every part of it shines, grind it once more and soak it with **alkali salt** <note>Potassium or sodium carbonate.</note> water, trying to make it into a thick paste. Then place it in a vessel and seal it well, leaving a small hole on one side from which the **vapors** <note>original: "mofeta"; refers to the noxious or suffocating gases released during chemical heating.</note> may escape when it is set. Place said vessel in a <term>fusion fire</term> <note>A very high-heat fire designed to melt solids into a liquid state.</note>, blowing strongly with bellows so that it melts quickly. When the vapor escapes through the hole, and the material remains in an iron channel greased with **tallow** <note>Animal fat, used here to prevent the metal from sticking to the iron.</note>, you will receive the **white mass**, which you can consider extremely fine white, or even gold, because it is cleansed of all corruption <note>In alchemy, "corruption" refers to the base impurities that prevent a metal from being perfect or "noble."</note>.

But if you wish to work toward the **red**, soak the calx of the metals with red water made from **flowers of copper** <note>Likely copper oxide or verdigris.</note> or **Armenian bole** <note>original: "d'armenia," referring to a red medicinal earth or clay rich in iron oxide.</note>. Do everything exactly as was said above, and finally treat it with alkali salt water and melt it as described, and you will have the **red mass**.

Some dissolve **saltpeter** <note>original: "nitro."</note> and alum in vinegar, and in that, they wash away the blackness <note>The "blackness" or *nigredo* represents the initial, impure state of the material.</note> of the calx.

Others describe the treatment of **Copper** <note>original: "Venere" (Venus); the alchemical name for copper.</note> in this manner:

Then, take the said **precipitated arsenic** and soak it little by little with **water of egg whites** <note>Distilled egg whites were often used as a mild protein-based binder or solvent.</note> in which **sublimated sal ammoniac** <note>Ammonium chloride that has been purified through heating until it vaporizes and reforms as a solid.</note> has been placed. Put it in a damp place and it will turn into an oil, of which one portion is cast over ten portions of **White Angelic Water** <note>original: "b Angelo" accompanied by a downward triangle symbol (the symbol for water); this likely refers to a specific purified alchemical solvent.</note> and it becomes **fixed** <note>To "fix" a substance means to make it resistant to heat so that it no longer evaporates or changes when placed in a fire.</note>.

## How pearls are made

<margin>How pearls are made</margin>
Take 3 ounces of distilled **aqua vitae** <note>original: "acqua uita"; high-proof distilled alcohol.</note>, and one ounce of **aqua fortis** <note>original: "acqua forte"; nitric acid.</note> made from rock alum and saltpeter, using equal parts of each. Place inside it as much **fine silver leaf** as you wish. Keep it well-sealed in a small glass flask with the lid carefully secured so that it does not "breathe" <note>This means to create an airtight seal to prevent the escape of vapors.</note>. You shall place said vessel over **smoke** <note>Likely referring to a gentle, constant heat source or a fume-filled chamber.</note> for ten days, then you shall take it out.

# White Elixir

<margin>Take <unclear>and</unclear> <term>sal ammoniac</term> <note>original: "sal arm."; ammonium chloride, a salt used to clean metals and aid in the sublimation process.</note>.</margin>

Dissolve and distill this again seven times. If it does not do this, and still produces smoke, renew it again in **mercury** <note>alchemical symbol ☿</note>, imbibing it with the said oil until it behaves as described. Then, one part of this medicine is applied to 50 parts of purified and separated copper, and you will have the finest silver.

## Of the degrees of fire

<margin>degrees of fire</margin>

> *The first is fostered, as you feel by its mastery* <note>original Latin: "Primus fovetur, ut sentis di dominatu"</note>
> *Nature rejoices in the balanced second degree* <note>original Latin: "Extitit equato gaudet natura secundo"</note>
> *The third exceeds, but with happy tolerance* <note>original Latin: "Tertius excedit, sed cum tolerantia læti"</note>
> *You feel the destroyer; it knows not how to proceed to the fourth* <note>original Latin: "Destructor sentis nescit procedere quarti"</note>

The first degree contained in the first vessel was recognized in this manner: that by touching the ashes with your hand, or the cover of the furnace, or the lid of the vessel, you can keep your hand there without any injury. And in this degree, the <term>putrefaction</term> <note>the process of breaking down and decomposing the starting material, often associated with the color black</note> of our material takes place over 40 days; but he who performed the experiment completed the true putrefaction in 92 days, or at most 100, and this is the truth.

Note that although in the said putrefied material the <term>blackness</term> <note>original: "negretalla"; refers to the *nigredo* stage, the first main phase of the Great Work</note> does not appear to the sight, it does appear in the testing; indeed, that skin of blackness rarely appears, and yet the elements are already conjoined and united. Through the <term>application</term> <note>original: "devotione"; refers here to the steady, dedicated application of heat</note> of the fire, they are converted into other natures, and by the second degree of application, the hidden becomes manifest, and that which is now manifest becomes hidden.

<margin>Spirit and soul</margin>

## Oil of Vitriol

Take rectified **vitriol** <term>vitriol</term> <note>original: vitriolo; a sulfate mineral, most commonly iron or copper sulfate, used to produce sulfuric acid</note> and boil it in white wine, ensuring there is twice as much wine as vitriol. Let it boil until most of the moisture has been <unclear>lost</unclear> and the vitriol remains dry. Then, crush the dried vitriol, place it in a **retort** <term>retort</term> <note>original: storta; a glass vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distilling liquids or gases</note> and distill it. First, the **phlegm** <note>original: flemma; the watery, tasteless, and non-acidic portion of a substance that evaporates first during distillation</note> will come out; then, attach a large receiver vessel, well-sealed with **lute** <term>lute</term> <note>original: luto; a clay or paste used to seal the joints of chemical apparatus to prevent the escape of volatile vapors</note>, and distill in the usual manner. An oil will come out

# Solution

->Solution<-

Solution is the first part of chemistry <note>the alchemical art</note>.

Hence the Verse:

> If you dissolve the fixed, you make it fly <note>original: *volare*; meaning to volatilize or turn a solid into vapor</note>;
> If you make the dissolved fixed, you make it live again.
> In this way, you make the whole live again once more.

Solution is achieved by calcining <note>heating a substance to high temperatures to oxidize it or reduce it to powder</note>, which is done through fire by reducing a substance into powder. Through this process, unnecessary moisture is removed and the parts are fixed <unclear>or</unclear> joined together, <unclear>since</unclear> the parts of fire are not far removed from the state of fixation, and they more easily pass into a liquid state <note>original: *aquam*, literally "water"</note>.

Calcination is performed through an amalgam <note>a physical mixture of mercury and another metal</note> with **mercury** <term>mercurio</term>. If the metal to be calcined is soft, <unclear>four</unclear> <unclear>small</unclear> <unclear>parts</unclear> of mercury are sufficient; if it is hard, barely eight parts are needed. For iron, however, it is not calcined unless with sulfur, and with **gold** <term>sole</term> <note>literally "the sun," the alchemical symbol for gold</note> and **iron** <term>marte</term> <note>literally "Mars," the alchemical symbol for iron</note>.

<margin>Amalgam</margin> **Gold** <term>aurum</term>, **silver** <term>argentum</term>, <unclear>copper</unclear> <term>aes</term>, and **tin** <term>stannum</term> are reduced into an amalgam or powder if one part of the metal is mixed with them in either double or triple the amount of mercury.

## The Medicine of King Frederick of Naples
### For Copper, Lead, and Dissolved Mercury.

<margin>
White Stone <note>original: *Lap: Bianco*; the "White Work" or *Albedo*, a stage in alchemy that produces silver before gold</note>
</margin>

<margin>
Add the said salt; let it congeal for five years <note>The Roman numeral 'v' likely indicates five, though such long durations are symbolic in alchemical "maturation."</note> and cover the vein with the raw husk.
</margin>

**Take** <note>represented by the symbol **℞**</note> one ounce of refined gold <note>original: *oro di capella*; gold purified by cupellation</note> and 3 ounces of mercury. Make an amalgam, then take 4 ounces of the best sal ammoniac <term>sale ammoniaco</term> <note>ammonium chloride, used as a flux and for sublimation</note> and make it into a very fine powder. Put it into a vial <note>original: *boccia*</note> that is well-luted <note>sealed with "lute," a clay or paste used to make vessels airtight</note> up to the middle, with a "small fish" of mercury <note>likely a specific weight or a drop of mercury resembling a fish</note>. Once well-sealed, put it in a reverberatory furnace <note>a furnace that reflects heat onto the substance</note>. First, make a charcoal fire for six hours, and then raise the heat more strongly and maintain it for six days. Note that the fire must remain open just enough to let out all the humidity, which you should purge with an iron plate. Then, when you find the moistures of the air <note>likely the condensation or vapors</note>, stop the hole well with lute so that it does not breathe, and you will see it perform its work. When 24 hours have passed, let it cool.

Afterward, break the vial and take the sublimated <note>the portion that rose to the top as vapor and solidified</note> and the non-sublimated parts and mix them together. Grind them well until they are impalpable <note>a powder so fine it cannot be felt between the fingers</note>. Then, put them into another vial, well-luted as before, and set it to sublimate. Repeat this until the seventh time, until you see that it no longer sublimates. When the sublimations are finished, the matter will be entirely fixed at the bottom of the vessel.

Put this into a vial and cook the liquid in very warm horse dung <term>fimo di cavallo</term> <note>used by alchemists as a source of gentle, constant "natural" heat for digestion</note> for 30 days, and it will be converted into water. If you wish, you may put it in a water bath <term>balneo mariae</term> with one ounce of <unclear>demeritt</unclear>, and it will dissolve even faster. When this "Medicine" has been distilled and congealed, put the flask over very hot coals and use its receiver <note>a vessel to catch vapors</note> so it does not escape. When it becomes very clear, it will be like a most splendid crystalline stone.

Put one ounce of this stone upon a hundred ounces of raw mercury, or copper <note>original: *venere*; Venus</note>, or tin, and it will be converted into 24-carat gold. And the more you sublimate and combine this medicine, the more you will multiply your wealth, by the grace of God.

## From Giovanni Agostino Panteo
->The Venetian, in the book whose title is<-
->The Art and Theory of Metallic<-
->Transmutation<-

->From the exhortation of his entreaty.<-

He asserts that he has hidden the truth beneath a quite bitter husk <note>original: *amariori cortice*; a common alchemical metaphor for cryptic language that protects secrets from the unworthy</note> of words, so that it may be observed by no one who is ignorant or follows the rules of the barbarians.

->From the author's letter to Leo X.<-
<note>Pope Leo X (reigned 1513–1521), to whom Panteo dedicated his work to seek ecclesiastical approval for alchemy.</note>

He asserts that the sincere truth of the secret metamorphosis <term>metamorphoseos</term> <note>the transformation of base metals into noble ones</note> is contained in his little book, and that in certain places the deceptions and the "prostitution" of the work <note>original: *meretricitatem*; implying a cheapening or falsifying of the art</note> are removed. He claims this is easily done if one will examine the more secret meanings.

He says that in his writing he has deviated from the normal sequence so that the Stone <note>original: *lapis*; the Philosopher's Stone</note> might become known to the wise alone, while remaining hidden from those same ignorant people.

He argues that those who, beneath the husk of words, touch only their surface are in error, for beneath that husk are contained the secrets of the wise.

## How Nature Operates

->Putrefaction<-

## Let us look at putrefaction according to Bernard of Trevisan, the Chemist, in the second [book] of the Kingdom. <note>original: *Trevisanus Chimicus*; referring to Bernard of Trevisan (1406–1490), a famous Italian alchemist. The "Kingdom" refers to a division in his writings.</note>

Putrefaction is the corruption of the substance of a thing from which another thing is generated.
From this, it must be adapted so that the matter, having been placed in an impure state, cannot evaporate away.
And external heat <note>original: *calor alienus*; heat applied from the outside, rather than the "innate" heat of the substance itself</note> is the acting instrument of putrefaction: because it heats the thing placed upon it and causes the humidity to evaporate, for the heat still corrupts the thing itself, just as we see in wood; when it is placed by the fire, the fire causes the water and oil—with which it was previously connected—to evaporate, and once those are removed, ashes remain.
Hence, putrefaction was called "Ash" because of this similarity.

<insert>Observation</insert>

Because this putrefaction ought to be done with the fire of a lamp and ash, so that there is a moderate heat; for intense heat would dry it out rather than putrefy it. <note>Alchemists often used "lamp fire" (a steady flame from an oil lamp) or sand/ash baths to maintain the gentle, constant warmth required for the "slow digestion" of the material.</note>

### The Sign of Perfection for both the Oil and the Sublimate with Oil

This will be the sign: if you throw a small quantity onto a plate glowing white with fire, and it suddenly melts like wax without smoke, enters into its innermost parts, increases its color, and takes away <unclear>what had flowed in</unclear>; into that [plate], the best oil penetrates most quickly. "Quicksilver, since because of its coldness it is easily [lost] to inflammation, requires some medicine which, before its **flight** <note>original: *fugam*; refers to mercury's tendency to evaporate or "flee" when exposed to heat.</note>, may adhere to it in its depths, be joined to it through its smallest parts, thicken it, and by its own **fixation** <note>original: *fixione*; the process of making a volatile substance stable and resistant to fire.</note> preserve it in the fire until there comes to it a tolerance for a greater fire without loss of moisture. Through this benefit, the medicine converts it into a solid and most refined thing, that is, **gold**; where the medicine of the second order for silver has been prepared accordingly."

Indeed, this oil has all these properties and qualities. For what is more subtle and pure than oil? What adheres more to quicksilver than silver...

### 3. The Preparation.

<margin>Concerning the preparation</margin>

# Concerning the method and reasoning for raising this spirit of gold into the sublime.

Many have written much regarding the method and reasoning for raising this spirit of gold into the sublime <note>original: *in sublime*; refers to the upper part of the alchemical vessel where vapors condense during sublimation</note>. We shall briefly describe the method which is more efficient, easier, more consistent with reason, and born from experience.

Therefore, let gold be mixed with four ounces of quicksilver <term>quicksilver: the common name for mercury</term> on its own, through long grinding, until they are mixed into very tiny parts. Throw this mixture into a glass flask <note>original: *ampullam vitream*</note>. Having sealed the vessel <note>The OCR "destructo" likely refers to the closing or sealing of the vessel's neck</note> and while the mixture is still weak, first subject it to a low heat, then a violent and sudden heat for a space of twelve hours. When it has cooled, break the vessel and look in the upper part for the red sublimated quicksilver. 

For quicksilver is sublimated because of the similarity of the three substances, carrying with it <margin>Isepheus the Philosopher</margin> a small spirit of its gold, which they call Sulfur. Just like common sulfur, through coercion and sublimation, it shapes the quicksilver into a red color; and just as cinnabar <term>cinnabar: a bright red mineral, mercury sulfide, which alchemists believed held the secret to transforming metals</term> is made from both mercury and sulfur, so from this spirit of gold and the sublimated quicksilver, a red sublimate is produced.

But if not enough of the oil's spirit has ascended, mix what remains at the bottom again with new sublimated quicksilver and sublimate it once more. Repeat this same work until almost all the oil has been drawn into the spirit. I say "almost," for some things will settle at the bottom because of impurity, and these unclean remnants must be thrown away. This mixture of the spirit of gold and quicksilver is the true mixture for the Stone.

<meta>This page continues the technical and philosophical exploration of the alchemical process from page 236. But these are mere trifles, as is the view that the nature of what is metallic occurs through mere mixing into a single [substance], or by a simple change from one place to another, and that this same mixing can then dissolve it. However, since it occurs in various published modes, there are indeed things which cannot be opposed.

For every change of all things is either in **substance**—meaning the origin and death of its name, or "generation and corruption"—or it is in **quality**, which is called **alteration** <term>alteration: in Aristotelian physics, a change in properties (like color or hardness) that does not change the essential nature of the thing</term> by the ancients, which is properly defined as a change within the same matter.

Therefore, if a transformation of this kind takes place through some species of change, **quicksilver** <term>quicksilver: mercury; "argentum vivum"</term> and some other metal will become silver or gold; the method, however, is through mixing.

Furthermore, when we have said that gold was in the same place when mixed, and is able to return to gold, will the species of this change be "alteration"? 

However, because that **calx** <term>calx: the powdered remains of a metal after it has been heated or "calcined"; the fixed, earthy part of the substance</term> is increased by the addition of quicksilver, it will be an "increase" <note>original: *auctio*; an Aristotelian term for quantitative growth</note>.

Then, when gold in that same calx is turned into **salt**, the **Sun** <note>original: *sol*; the alchemical code name for gold</note> into **oil**, the oil into **spirit**, and again the spirit into calx, lest all these changes be said to be contained within the species of "generation and corruption"—if they can <unclear>be returned</unclear> through similar things—we respond according to **Aristotle** <note>Aristotle's *Physics* and *On Generation and Corruption* provided the scientific framework for medieval alchemists</note>, as with all other things and by the authority of the Philosopher, that "mixing" exists and is contained here within the genus of "change," and it differs from the other species.

So that this may be more clearly understood, let it be noticed—

<meta>This page continues the logical and physical defense of alchemical transformation. Having previously discussed "alteration" and "increase" in the Aristotelian sense, the author now defines the specific criteria required for a true "mixing" (mixtio) of metals, moving from abstract theory to specific proportions of gold and silver.</meta>

It is a matter of importance in mixtures and the act of mixing to agree—and to agree in such a way that all things in other mixtures of change might correspond, even when they do not seem to agree.

<margin>folio 438</margin>
First, those things which are being mixed must be distinct in actuality and separate by themselves before they are joined. Second, they must share a common **matter** <term>matter: "materia"; the underlying "stuff" that takes on different forms</term>. Then, while being mixed, they must touch one another and both act and be acted upon reciprocally through contrary primary qualities. Furthermore, in a true mixture, neither of the components should be corrupted or perish entirely; they should not destroy one another. Instead, the power, essence, and potential of both should be diminished from both sides and reduced to a certain **temperament** <term>temperament: "temperamentum"; a balanced state or "middle point" between two extremes</term>. Thus, a stable [mixture] of silver and gold is formed, where the **agent** <term>agent: the active substance that initiates change</term> completes the mass, while the **patient** <term>patient: the passive substance that receives the action</term> provides the underlying character. Finally, a body of a single form emerges from the two mixed things, reflecting the nature of both; yet, because it is neither perfectly the original agent nor the patient, you may define it as a "third something" in this way: 

**Mixing is the union of altered mixables.** <note>original: *Mistionem esse mistibilium alteratorum unionem*; this is a classic Aristotelian definition of a chemical compound.</note> See below for more on mixing.

<margin>folio 438 (3rd Proposition)</margin>
So that the cause may be the proportion of both the agent and patient subjects, let us suppose the acting mass—such as an ounce of **gold** <note>original: *auri*</note>—counts three degrees of heat, or **rarity** <term>rarity: "raritas"; the quality of being less dense or more "spiritual" and expanded</term>, and thinness. However, let the patient subject—such as an ounce of **silver** <note>original: *argenti*</note>—possess one degree of the contrary quality. In the mixing, there will be one ounce of **quicklime** <note>original: *calis vivi*; likely referring to the "living" powder or calx of the metal</note> and one of **quicksilver** <term>quicksilver: "argentum vivum"; mercury</term>.
