# The Stages of Stabilizing the Stone

The stages for stabilizing the **golden stone** <note>original: "lapidis aurei." The "Philosopher's Stone" in its final, perfected form.</note> are six in number:
**Digestion**, **Coagulation** or **Waxing**, the **First Fixation**, the **Second Fixation**, **Calcination**, and **Waxing** <note>original: "inceratio." A process of adding liquid to a hard substance until it reaches a soft, waxy consistency.</note>.

**Digestion** belongs to the **Sun** <note>original: "solis." As noted on the previous page, this refers to Gold or the masculine, "fixed" principle.</note>; for since I have defined perfection as the advancement of the <term>seed</term> <note>original: "seminis." The latent potential or "soul" within the raw matter that must be grown.</note> toward the perfection of its form, this process certainly completes it at once. The action of the **fixed** part, or its form, is preserved; for digestion is the proper treatment of the object, whereby its degree of perfection does not decrease, but its possession of that degree increases, as will be seen later in the operation. Thus, the fruit of the **olive**, and other things before they reach maturity, receive degrees of perfection; for in the intervening time, their initial fruitfulness develops from within until they have reached extreme ripeness.

But in our **golden seed**, the <term>fixation</term> <note>original: "fixio." The process of making a substance "fixed" so that it no longer evaporates or changes when exposed to intense heat.</note> must be indicated as it is achieved. When the external color has perfected that "efficient cause," and there are thus its stages, the first five are impressed by the five-fold path of color; the sixth stage, **waxing**, does not belong to those five degrees of color. However, while it is being perfected, the work must not be moved from its place, nor should anything be disturbed during the labors of digestion; these five degrees of color must be kept in mind.

->Stages of the Operation<-
->Sinolenis<-

**Sinolenis** <note>This appears to be a specialized or perhaps proprietary term used by the author to describe the first stage of the "golden heat." This is the reduction of the "living thing" <note>original: "vivi." Often a reference to *mercurius vivus* or "living mercury," the spirit of the matter.</note> from the earth, by the flow of light, into an **appension** <note>original: "appensionem." Likely referring to a state of suspension or the "weighing" of the spirit into the body.</note>. By this, the first degree of heat is produced, as well as five greater ones; through this union, a joining occurs in the **souls of light**, in which and before which they take...

## Epilogue

In mixtures [there is] the **stone** <note>original: *lapis*; referring to the Philosopher's Stone, the goal of the Great Work.</note>, a single material, which is at least the first preparation of all metals; you will have drawn it off with the unique **royal water** <note>original: *aqua Regis*; a highly corrosive mixture of nitric and hydrochloric acids, so named because it can dissolve "noble" metals like gold.</note>. Do not touch it thus; it knows how to be divided in these expositions. But it must be noted that this [is] ... entirely before the **fermentation** <note>original: *fermentacionem*; the stage where the alchemical agent is "multiplied" in power or brought to its final state.</note>.

For the rest, <unclear>unlvly</unclear> here, read most [of] this caliber <unclear>disi</unclear> <unclear>doz</unclear>.

# Some things taken from the Rosary
## Selected Philosophy

-> from the frontispiece <-

Our stone has spirit, <insert>body</insert>, and soul.
Turn our earth [around] and what you seek, you shall find.
Dissolve and coagulate <note>original: *solve et coagula*; the fundamental alchemical axiom meaning to break down substances to their essence before reuniting them in a purified state</note>.
Dissolve the bodies in water.

---

-> from the beginning <-

Living things themselves work by nature in a way that does not stray from the path, because from a human is born a human, and from an egg a chick, and every like produces its like.
We have need of two primary things, [yet] they are but one.
One is the stone, one the medicine, one the vessel, one the procedure <term>regimen; the specific method of managing the alchemical fire and stages of transformation</term>, and one the arrangement.
Our stone is from animal, vegetable, and mineral matter; although the names may be diverse, yet it is always only one single thing.
The active <term>agens; the masculine, transformative principle</term> and the passive <term>patiens; the feminine, receptive principle</term> are in genus one and the same, but in species they are distinct and diverse.
Matter longs for form just as a woman longs for a man, and the ugly for the beautiful.
The work <term>Opus; the "Great Work" of creating the Philosopher's Stone</term> is made from a natural root.
The stone is made from the four elements <note>earth, air, fire, and water</note>, and both the rich and the poor possess it; it is found everywhere and is likened to all things.
But it is composed of body, soul, and spirit, and is transformed from nature into nature.
The end of the mastery <term>magisterium; the successful completion of the alchemical process</term> occurs with our water, which is the seed <note>original: *sperma*</note> for all metals, and all metals are dissolved within it.
The salt of metals is our stone: water congealed in gold and silver.
The Sun <note>Sol, representing the masculine principle or gold</note> is the masculine of quicksilver <note>original: *argenti vivus*; mercury</note>.

<summary>This page features foundational maxims from the Rosarium Philosophorum, emphasizing the unity of the alchemical "Stone" and its derivation from nature. It outlines the core philosophy that the transformative process mirrors natural generation and requires a balance of masculine and feminine principles.</summary>
<keywords>Rosarium Philosophorum, alchemy, Philosopher's Stone, Solve et Coagula, Magisterium, four elements, Sol, Quicksilver, Hermetic philosophy</keywords>

<margin>From which the second is made.</margin>
Earth and water are the two passive elements in Mercury <note>original: ☿, the symbol for mercury or quicksilver</note>.
Air and fire are in it only in potential, which are the active elements; and these in pure Mercury are led from pure potential into actuality according to the proper guidance and proportion; from this, everything is made.

Here it helps greatly by providing the mercury with gold, especially that gold in which sulfur is most highly digested <term>digestum; the alchemical process of "cooking" or maturing a substance through gentle, sustained heat</term>.

> Take, take, it will cause; Take, take.
> This Stone exists at a meager and also cheap price.
> It is found again on the road.

The work and the mastery <term>magisterium; the highest level of alchemical skill or the completion of the process</term> is to cook the quicksilver <note>original: *argentum vivum*</note> and sulfur until they become one single quicksilver which protects the sulfur from burning, provided the vessel is well-sealed. This is done so that the quicksilver cannot evaporate, nor the sulfur be burned or blackened, because our quicksilver is our caustic water <term>aqua caustica; a corrosive or "sharp" liquid used to dissolve metals</term>.

<margin>gentle fire</margin>
Let the fire be gentle in the beginning until you see the water fixed <note>original: *fixam*; rendered solid or non-volatile so it no longer evaporates</note> without any rising; do not care what kind of fire it is, but govern it with patience until the spirit and the body become one. Cook this water systematically by putrefying <term>putrefactio; the stage of decomposition or "death" of the matter, usually marked by a black color</term> it until it changes from color to perfect color.

-> Thus the chapter on the mountains <-
-> (Question) <-

1. The Stone has a very soft and incombustible earth, fit for fixing that which is fixed with its own proper radical moisture <term>radical moisture; the innate, essential fluid believed to sustain the life and integrity of a substance</term>.
<margin>which are the active elements</margin>
2. ...airy and fiery moisture uniformly joined together.

Whoever has the true mercury has the elixir; and the elixir is mercury mortified <note>original: *mortificatus*; "killed" or deprived of its volatile, liquid nature</note> or fixed with the scent of the body, because the dragon does not die except with its brother and its sister <note>The dragon, brother, and sister are famous alchemical allegories representing the volatile and fixed principles that must be "slain" or united to reach the final goal</note>.

...let the fixed be made volatile with the volatile, that is with pure mercury <term>mercurio; the element mercury, often called quicksilver, viewed here as the 'spirit' that can dissolve solids</term>. **The First Matter** <term>Prima materia; the primordial, formless substance from which all metals originate</term> of bodies is something made from an oily and moist vapor; for from the moist part mineral water is made, and from the oily part the metallic body is made.

Common salt, as he says, increases the redness in gold and the whiteness in silver.

<page-num>221</page-num>

<margin>What the [matter] of the philosophers is.</margin>
Magnesia is the moon full of the mercury of the philosophers <term>mercurio phorum; the "mercury of the philosophers" is not common quicksilver, but a purified "spirit" extracted from metals</term>, the entire matter in which is contained the mercury of the philosophers, which nature has shown only a little, and though she has formed it into a metallic shape, she has nonetheless left it imperfect.

<margin>That the [matter] of the philosophers must be purified, which is done with saltpeter and tartar. That is, of silver.</margin>
And its purification—the removal of earthiness and wateriness through ingenuity—when made pure with white sulfur, will coagulate it into silver, and with red sulfur into gold.

<margin>Sulfur of the philosophers</margin>
This is our sulfur, and nothing from the outside is required except what is extracted from those bodies.

<margin>What the solution of gold ought to be. What kind of fire.</margin>
He who knows how to destroy gold so that it will no longer be gold <note>original: *destruere*; this refers to the alchemical "retrogradation" where a metal is broken back down into its formless primary matter</note>, he has reached the greatest secret <note>original: *arcanum*</note>. The fire in the solution should be temperate and gentle; in sublimation, moderate; in coagulation, temperate; in whitening, ordinary; in reddening, strong. Otherwise, you go astray and the labor fails.

<margin>What the Stone is</margin>
The Stone is from a living thing <note>original: *de re animata*; implying the source of the alchemical catalyst is organic or possesses a "life force"</note>. You will find it everywhere: in the plain, in the mountains, and in the waters; and both the rich and the poor possess it. It is vile, the most vile of things, and yet most precious; it grows from flesh and blood, and consists of them in body and soul. For the Ancients called the imperfect body "leaven" <term>fermentum; a substance that causes the "dough" of the metal to rise or transform</term>, the soul "soul," and the water "spirit."

<margin>What the soul of the stone is. That is, Sulfur or Salt. That is, Mercury. The soul is the pure movement in mercury.</margin>
The imperfect body is by itself an unclean body. The spirit is the water that cleanses, refines, and whitens the body. The soul is the leaven which the imperfect body drinks into itself.

# Concerning the salt of the philosophers <note>original: "phor," shorthand for *philosophorum*</note>

<margin>
Concerning salts.
</margin>
Sal ammoniac <term>Sal armoniacus; a volatile salt used as a flux to help dissolve metals</term> for the philosophers <note>original: "phis," shorthand for *philosophis*</note> is made from the Sun <note>The "Sun" is the standard alchemical symbol for Gold.</note>.

<margin>
common salt

<margin>
An explanation of the Stone through analogies.
</margin>
When the matter is dissolved, it is called sal ammoniac.
When it has been putrefied, they called it the "vile stone" and say it is found in the dungheap <note>original: "in sterquilinio inveniatur"; a recurring alchemical theme suggesting that the most precious substance has a humble, common origin.</note>.
When it has been converted into water, it possesses such power that it is called the "poor man's gem," and it is found in every thing.
When it has been whitened, it is called arsenic or Virgin’s Milk <term>lac Virginis; a term for a white liquid or precipitate in the flask</term>.
When it becomes red, it is called Jacob’s sulfur, or blood.
The Stone is called a "salt" because it is necessary to reduce it to the nature of a salt.
Salts and alums are the things by which our works are accomplished.
<margin>

Every salt, when well prepared, returns to the nature of sal ammoniac, and the same secret is found in common salt when it has been

### The Conjunction and Marriage
### between the Sun and the Moon

Join the son Ruessabium <note>Likely a variation of "Beya" or a similar name for the feminine principle in the *Rosarium Philosophorum*</note> with his daughter Scia <note>Likely "Gabricus," the masculine principle, though the genders/names are often swapped or corrupted in various manuscript traditions</note>, who is a shining girl—I speak through types <note>original: "per genera"</note>—who [Siph:] <note>Possibly a shorthand for a specific alchemical authority or "Siphara"</note> gives all that comes from her.

It ascended; thus they called it **water**, **soul**, and **spirit**, <note>In alchemy, these three terms often refer to the volatile components of a substance that vaporize when heated.</note> saying that their water was not the **common water** <note>original: "aqua vulgi"</note> nor **mercury**; and from this, the **earth** remained at the bottom. Wherefore, they would return that water back over the body, and again make it ascend by a mild fire, and again mix it with the earth until it carried all the earth with it in its belly. <note>This describes the process of "circulation" or "distillation," where a liquid is repeatedly evaporated and condensed back onto the solid matter to "purify" it.</note>
Wherefore it was necessary for them to have a great quantity of water, and by this means, the spirit was **fixed** <note>original: "fixus"; "fixing" refers to making a volatile substance solid and resistant to fire.</note> from the body.
They **putrefied** <note>Allowed the matter to decompose or break down.</note> it, therefore, until the **sublimation** <note>The process of a solid turning into vapor and then back to solid.</note> was complete; the whole remained fixed and unable to ascend. And thus the spirit was fixed in the body, and then it was incorporated into the **Sun** <note>original: "soli"; in alchemy, the Sun represents Gold.</note> and mixed into the smallest parts, and here the operation was completed.

# Of Sulphur and Quicksilver

<margin>
It is also said that Sulphur comes from the Sun and Moon, from which also [comes] what they do not say. Note well: the philosophers have their own sulphur.
</margin>

Quicksilver <note>original: "Argentum vivum"</note> is made when a body is liquefied, and such a sulphur exists in the Sun and Moon. <note>In alchemical symbolism, the "Sun" (Sol) refers to gold and the "Moon" (Luna) refers to silver.</note> In other things indeed it is what is told to no one, unless it be revealed by God. For they skillfully imagined how they might extract those sulphurs in these silver perfections, and purify its qualities through art, or how they might possess this beforehand through the mediation of nature—which did not appear in them before, although they possessed them fully and secretly earlier. They believed this could by no means be done without the resolution of the body and its reduction into the First Matter <note>original: "primam materia"; the foundational, undifferentiated substance from which all metals were thought to originate</note>, which is the quicksilver from which they were made from the beginning. This must be done without any mixing of foreign things, for foreign substances do not improve a stone of a different nature; nothing suits it except what is closely related to it. For example <note>original: "V.g." for "verbi gratia"</note>, if ice is placed in water, it is dissolved in it by heat and returns to its first substance; in the same way, by resolving the clean body into quicksilver <note>original: "☿ium"</note> with mercury, one can possess the hidden power

<margin>
That matter is called the "water" in which metals have been resolved and some spirit with which it agrees; it is said—which note well.
</margin>

from it in potential—namely, sulphur digested and ripened <note>original: "decoctum," literally "cooked down"</note> through the work of nature in the mine. For thus the stone is one, one medicine, which is called Rebis <note>original: "Rebis," from the Latin "res bina," meaning "double thing." This represents the union of opposites, such as spirit and body or male and female, into a single substance.</note> from a double thing—namely, from the body and the spirit, white or red—in which many craftsmen have erred.

<meta>This page continues the technical instructions for the "Great Work." While the previous page established gold as the essential "ferment" or yeast for the process, this page details the specific ratios and the chemical logic for transforming silver into gold, followed by instructions for a liquid dissolution.</meta>

Although this **stone** <term>Lapis: The Philosopher's Stone, the legendary substance capable of transmuting base metals into gold and conferring longevity.</term> already contains the end of the matter within itself—for it has been perfectly created as the **body of the mastery** <term>Magisterium: The 'Mastery' or the completed alchemical work.</term>—it nevertheless cannot move by itself unless it is perfected by art and labor.

Take one part of the **ferment** <term>Fermentum: A substance, often pure gold or silver, added to the base matter to 'leaven' it and direct its transformation.</term> and three parts of the **imperfect body** <note>In this context, the 'imperfect body' usually refers to a base metal like lead, tin, or unrefined silver.</note>. Dissolve the ferment in an equal amount of its own **mercurial water** <note>original: "aquae mercurij"; likely referring to a corrosive solvent or 'philosophical' mercury used to break down metals.</note>, and together with a very gentle fire, coagulate that ferment.

<margin>Note: Can gold be made?</margin>
It is possible for all silver to become gold, and no gold exists unless it was first silver. But silver contains within itself a certain undigested quality, which could be purged from it by art so that it remains fixed in **mercury**, and in the strength and soul of the nature of gold. Take Common Salt in whatever quantity you wish, and grind it into large pieces and put it under a clay lid <term>Lute: A paste or cement used to seal alchemical vessels to make them airtight.</term>, and put it to the blast furnace or bellows to fire it as if it were silver, until you have finished the crackling <note>original: "decrepitare"; the physical popping sound salt makes when heated as water trapped inside the crystals evaporates.</note>, and it begins to melt, until it is a dense mass, and make of it a single portion.

Then grind this salt and put it inside an ox bladder, and tie the neck with red string, and expose it to moisture. Pierce the bottom of the bladder with a needle with several holes, and receive the liquid below in a pan. When you have ten pounds of said water, pass it through a filter, and then through an alembic <term>Alembic: A classic alchemical distilling apparatus consisting of two vessels connected by a tube.</term>, so that you will find at the bottom of the glass a white mass like crystal; and this is the first operation.

Thus, step by step, distill, removing the water that comes out, and you shall repeat this so many times until the salt <insert>is fixed</insert> <note>original: "fissato"; in alchemy, to "fix" a substance means to make it resistant to fire so that it no longer evaporates or changes state.</note>... [until it] is so subtle and penetrating that upon a red-hot iron plate it flows like wax; and then you will have the fine oil and the wise salt. With the mercury of tin <note>original: "stagn"; possibly referring to a purified "spirit" extracted from tin.</note>, this salt dissolves metals and leads them into mercury, into the Moon <note>The Moon (Luna) is the alchemical symbol for Silver.</note> and into the Sun <note>The Sun (Sole) is the alchemical symbol for Gold.</note> if you apply it with skill, and with this secret the philosopher's stone is made.

## Realgar, Antimony, Zinc, Marcasite,

# Royal Gold Tincture.

Take 4 ounces of Roman vitriol <note>original: "vitriuolo rom:"; iron or copper sulfate, often used in dyeing and metallurgy.</note>, 2 ounces of rock alum, 2 ounces of verdigris <note>A green pigment/chemical formed by the action of acetic acid on copper.</note>, 1 ounce of sal ammoniac <note>Ammonium chloride, used as a flux in soldering and to purify metals.</note>, and 2 ounces of refined saltpeter. Grind all these into a powder together and place them in a <unclear>vessel with a spout</unclear> <note>original: "beco amesso"; likely a flask or retort with a delivery tube.</note>, and <unclear>take it</unclear> to be kept warm until they melt together. Re-heat it so that they can be ground finely, and with this, "cement" <note>The process of "cementation" involves heating a metal in contact with a powder (the cement) to change its surface properties or purify it.</note> white gold or a florin for three hours. For the first hour, the fire should be light; then for the 2nd and 3rd hours, maintain it with large coals and more [heat] as the <unclear>crucible</unclear> indicates, until you have gold of 24 carats.

## To make mercury of Antimony.

Take regulus of antimony <note>The metallic form of antimony, separated from its sulfide ore.</note> and sal ammoniac in equal parts. Grind them well together and <term>sublime</term> <note>Sublimation is the process where a solid turns directly into a gas and then back into a solid, used here to purify the substance.</note> them. Take that sublimate and grind it in a mortar, moistening it with oil of tartar <note>A saturated solution of potassium carbonate, made by letting cream of tartar absorb moisture from the air.</note>; then, [placed] upon a stone in a humid place, you will obtain the mercury.

## To extract mercury from Antimony.

Take 2 pounds each of calcined tartar and crude antimony; 1 pound of distilled vinegar. Place them in a glass retort and let them macerate for 5 to 7 days under dung <note>Fermenting manure was used as a consistent, low-heat source for laboratory "incubation."</note> or in a [water] bath. Then remove the glass and distill it, but ensure that the receiver contains <unclear>half-full</unclear> of water, so that you will see the mercury come out and settle in the receiver.

## Oil of Antimony.

Take stibium <note>Antimony sulfide, the most common ore of antimony.</note> and saltpeter in equal quantities. Grind them together and place them in a <unclear>pot</unclear> immersed in the fire. Let the fire ignite inside and burn it; and with fire—

You should have another very clean vessel which you must place among glowing coals; when it begins to glow white-hot, take it out from the fire and place it in a spot where you have enough room to work <note>original: "inter duos vel tres labores"; literally "between two or three tasks," likely meaning a workspace with sufficient clearance</note> so that you cannot easily step into it. ->The Good Stone of God<-

Take the sun <note>original: "sol"; in alchemy, the "Sun" represents gold or the masculine principle of sulfur.</note> which has no spots but more than one <unclear>change</unclear>, and has a core that has neither streaks, nor green, nor ruby, nor white.

Grind as much of it as you wish for a jug of <unclear>ground</unclear> powder and mix well together; afterwards, place it in a long-necked flask well-luted <term>luted: sealed with "philosophers' clay" or "lute" to make the vessel airtight</term> in a furnace in the sun. At the beginning of the motion from the top, let it <unclear>sit</unclear> for two hours; afterwards, strengthen the fire little by little with dregs <note>likely referring to "lees" or organic sediment used as fuel or to provide a steady, low heat</note>. After the spirit smokes the flame, it will run up the sides; once the flame has ceased, the sulfur will remain at the bottom of the vessel.

Break the vessel and grind what you find at the bottom, and take an equal amount of sal ammoniac <term>sal armoniaco: ammonium chloride, used by alchemists to cleanse metals and aid sublimation</term>, and incorporate them well together.

Afterwards, set it to sublimate <term>sublimation: the process of heating a solid until it becomes a vapor and then collects again as a solid in the cooler part of the vessel</term> in a vessel of earth or glass in this manner <insert>8</insert>. Take great care to seal the openings with the lute so that when you put it to the fire in the furnace, you give it only a little for two hours; and for another eight hours, strengthen the fire while the artifice <note>the "artifice" refers to the chemical reaction or the "work" itself</note> is being performed, until they <unclear>crack</unclear> at nine [hours], and finally one more hour of stronger heat.

Afterwards, open the vessel and take the sublimate along with what you find in the bottom of the vessel, and return to grinding once more and putting it back into the openings of the vessels; return to the fire, giving it the same heat. You shall do this three times, and if you reach nine times, you shall <unclear>have a better result</unclear>.

In the end, remix it and draw it out with the solar fire in reverse <note>likely referring to a "descensory" distillation where the heat is applied from above and the substance flows downward</note> so that it stays covered in the earthen vessel; and that which is rising again in the lower vessel is to be <unclear>preserved</unclear> for <unclear>use</unclear>.

# Manner of tempering the ferment
## for gold

If we wish to make **Gold** <note>original: "Sole" (the Sun); the alchemical name for gold.</note>, we put Gold into the ferment, and if we wish to make **Silver** <note>original: "luna" (the Moon); the alchemical name for silver.</note>, we put Silver into the ferment. If the ferment is not put inside, it does not take its color, and if you do not prepare the silver <note>The author likely refers here to the base metal or mercury being treated.</note>, it will not await the gold, and if you put in too little ferment, it will receive little **tincture** <note>The color-changing principle or "dye" that transforms a base metal into a precious one.</note>.

Take four parts of ferment (but the ferment must be such that we put gold and silver, then with the overturning and response <note>original: "ribalto et rispondi"; likely referring to a repetitive manual mixing or pouring technique.</note> until its <unclear>crude</unclear> moisture...) and one part of **mercury** <note>original: alchemical symbol ☿ (Mercury/Quicksilver).</note> purified and amalgamated in this manner: heat the ferment by itself, and heat the mercury in another vessel, and when the mercury begins to boil and the ferment begins to glow red <note>original: "infocarsi" (to catch fire or glow like a coal).</note>, cast the mercury over the ferment, and then mix with a small stick so that no more mercury is visible. Having done this, heat as much mercury as you did before, but do not reheat the ferment in such a way that it bubbles <note>original: "impolli."</note> to the point that the mercury would flee <note>Evaporate.</note>; rather, it is enough that the ferment be cooked. And while the mercury begins to boil, cast it over the ferment, mixing as before, and immediately it will be absorbed, and the matter will turn black and dry. The second time, heat one part of mercury and do as before, in such a way that there is as much mercury as ferment, and then put everything in the vessel, just as you did at the beginning, over a **slow fire** <term>foco lento</term> <note>A gentle, steady heat, often achieved using a sand bath or a lamp, essential for the long digestion periods in alchemy.</note>, and this for the space of two days.

## How the medicine is made infinite in its multiplication, and concerning its perfection.

<margin>
How it is made infinite in its multiplication, and concerning its perfection.
</margin>

Before anything else, the medicine possesses a perfect <term>liquation</term> <note>The ability of a solid substance to melt or flow like a liquid when heated, essential for it to penetrate other metals.</note> and can be multiplied infinitely in a certain way; there are three ways to multiply it.

The first [way] is by dissolving the same medicine by itself and congealing it many times. This dissolution is performed with nothing other than fire, because after the medicine has reached the point of resisting the fire, the longer it stays in the fire, the more its goodness will increase.

Dissolution is a liquefaction of the <term>aforementioned</term> <note>Original: "d.ta," an abbreviation for "detta."</note> medicine in the manner of oil, and because the medicine has been congealed—one and the other together—it manifests the quality of the <term>aforementioned</term> thing. Since it has reached its perfection by liquefying and congealing again, it <term>therefore</term> <note>Original: "dunq.," an abbreviation for "dunque."</note> must be dissolved and congealed several more times for the same reason, and it will become more perfect. This is what Rosinus <note>Rosinus is the Latinized name often associated with Zosimos of Panopolis, a foundational alchemist from the 3rd or 4th century.</note> says: the more times the medicine is dissolved, sublimated, and restricted, the better and more abundantly it works. This <term>dissolution</term> <note>Original: "solut.ne," an abbreviation for "soluzione."</note> is not understood to be in rain water <note>Original: "acqua di nuvola," literally "water of the clouds."</note> as the ignorant think, but rather that the dry substance is converted into a moisture of such a useful degree. One should <unclear>increase</unclear> [the heat] as much as possible so that the work of dissolution is attributed to nothing other than refining the substance. This is the intention of **Geber** <note>Geber is the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, an 8th-century polymath; his works were central to medieval and Renaissance alchemy.</note> the philosopher, who taught how to make the fixed stone fly through the methods of sublimation, and to fix it an equal number of times.

# True Nature, True Art
## The Craftsman Does Not Come <note>original: *Artifex non venit*</note>
### Concerning the Medicine of Metals

From the beginnings, there were the four elements: Earth, Water, Air, and Fire; and from all of these come the mixed bodies. The four elements have four qualities: Dry, Cold, Moist, and Hot. And from these four qualities is born a fifth, which is neither fire nor air, nor water, nor earth; and it is neither hot, nor moist, nor cold, nor dry. It is the Essence <note>The "Quintessence," a refined substance that transcends the physical elements</note>, and from it the Suns <note>Referring to gold or perfected substances</note> are made.

In the inferior bodies <note>Physical matter on Earth</note> sits corruption, but in the superior ones <note>The celestial spheres</note> resides the influence, which is more noble. Of the elements, two are active—which are Air and Fire—and two are passive—which are Water and Earth.

The Earth has creatures that only have being, such as stones; others that have being and life, such as plants and minerals; others that have being, life, and feeling, such as the brute animals; and others that have being, life, feeling, and understanding, such as men.

The minerals <note>Specifically the metallic ores</note> are therefore seven, the harmonizable ones, and they are of seven kinds: namely Gold, Silver, Iron, Tin, Copper, Lead, and Quicksilver.

Gold is perfect, and Nature strives to make all the others the same, but for lack of means <note>Such as insufficient heat or purity in the earth</note>, they do not all reach perfection.

Mercury is the primary matter of all metals; it is born in the earth of the mine and is water united by the continuous decoction <term>decoction</term> <note>A process of concentrated heating or "ripening" by subterranean heat</note> of the mineral's virtue within the gold mine, and it settles in such a way that in time it becomes quicksilver.

Metals are generated from quicksilver and sulfur. Sulfur is generated by its continuous decoction in the mine from the fatness of the earth <note>The "sulfurous fatness" was thought to be an oily, combustible principle that gave metals their substance and color</note>, and it becomes either white or red.

It explains the "Mercury-Sulfur theory," asserting that all seven metals are composed of these two principles and that Nature inherently strives to refine all metals into perfect gold.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the theoretical discussion from the previous page, moving from the definition of the four elements to the practical philosophy of "metallic generation." According to whether it has more or less decoction <note>original: *decoctione*; the process of slow, steady heating used to mature a substance</note>, because through decoction is the soul, and in the end, it is gold.

First, therefore, Nature makes quicksilver <note>original: *argento uiuo*; literally "living silver," the common term for mercury</note>, and then the white sun <note>silver</note> or gold. But it makes silver almost perfect, and gold which is perfect. And the metals that are drawn from the white sun have more proximity to silver, and those from the [red] sun to gold.

It is necessary, therefore, that the artist <note>The alchemist</note> imitates Nature in the virtues of the earth. And just as man generates man, silver generates silver, and gold generates gold.

Where Nature finishes, the artist begins. Nature finishes in silver and in gold, and the artist begins either from silver or from gold, according to whether he wishes to work toward the white <note>the *albedo* stage, producing silver</note> or toward the red <note>the *rubedo* stage, producing gold</note>.

The seed of gold <note>original: *seme d'oro*</note> putrefies in our "earth" and bears fruit. Wherefore, if one wishes to sow gold or silver in their earth, it is necessary not to take them in their hard and solid body, but to reduce them to their first matter <note>original: *prima materia*; the primordial substance from which all metals originate</note>, which is their quicksilver. This is because every thing comes from that, and belongs to that, into which it is resolved—just as frost resolves into water, because it was originally made from water.

If, then, these metals are resolved into quicksilver, it is certain that they can generate and multiply <note>increase in quality or quantity</note>. And the said virtue is sown in its earth, which shall be prepared. This earth is properly the "water" of all metals, in which no other matter must be mixed; let it be pure and clean, and therefore it must be assisted with its own smoke <note>vapors or spirits</note>. Let him take the moisture of its seeds and bring it to her [the earth].

Through decoction, the silver or gold becomes one thing with that [earth], and thus it is reduced into its first substance, which is quicksilver. In this way, the words of the philosophers are made clear when they say: "Our gold and our mercury are not common mercury" <note>original: *mercurio uolgare*; alchemists claimed their starting materials were refined versions of everyday chemicals</note>.

# Practice of the Philosophical Antimony <note>symbol: ♁</note>

Take common purified antimony. If it is good, take it with a piece of silver and temper it multiple times, putting a piece of it in the crucible. Therefore, lift it with tongs and [if] the quicksilver <note>symbol: ☿</note> vanishes in smoke, there remains a turquoise or black color, beautiful and stable, which is true and good antimony. If a white color remains, it is a sign that it is from a mine where its [virtues] have vanished; but if the other remains white-gold in color, it is the best, which is a sign of its devotion and it yields the finest gold.

This antimony should be obtained, if possible, either black from the mine or at least from <unclear>Schito</unclear> <note>possibly a reference to a specific mining locality or a type of schist</note>, and of the grain of the iron mine that is extracted as antimony. [It is] like a <unclear>raven</unclear> and like <unclear>joy</unclear> of the <unclear>arm</unclear> and it will be renewed when seen to work. It is carried as grain in a goat skin, sealed with the black seal of Bragaria <note>likely a specific merchant mark or regional seal to guarantee purity</note> so that it is not sophisticated with lead or tin or with iron; and that needle-like variety that comes from the East is good—the "needle of God" <note>a reference to the long, needle-like crystals found in high-quality stibnite/antimony ore</note>.

<margin>Preparation</margin> Purify the antimony by grinding it with salt in a glass bowl, or a glass vessel, or a marble mortar with a wooden or glass pestle. Always grind in one direction for one hour, tempering it with water until it becomes extremely soft. Then, wash it well in boiling water and finish until it is turned; then wash it with strong vinegar so that the vinegar becomes clear and can be dried with a fine silk cloth; if the dregs are <unclear>desired</unclear>, it is not good.

If, in the "cooking" of the silver, a black, gray, or turquoise color <unclear>appears</unclear>, it is good and well-purified, or [perhaps] tin.

Quicksilver is purified by mixing it with a mixture of marble—either black or gray—or sand among other things, and the appearance will be renewed clearly.

It is cooked, and the process described continues until a poison is purged, and afterward, to the praise of God and for the benefit of the soul alone, maintaining abstinence at the beginning.

## True and Proven Gold of Salt
### A perfect medicine to cure
### every infirmity.

Take one part of prepared gold in a flask and take four parts of rose water that has been distilled ten times. Set it to distill and remove the water, drying the substance. Then, soak <note>original: "imbevite"; to saturate or "imbibe" the solid matter with liquid</note> it with new rose water in the same manner as before. Do this nine times, and thus your gold will remain at the bottom as an impalpable powder <note>a powder so fine it cannot be felt between the fingers</note>.

Afterward, take eight ounces of honey and enough <term>Aqua vitae: "Water of life," a high-proof distilled spirit used as a solvent</term> to knead the <note>original: "cenere"; literally "ash," referring to the calcined remains of the gold</note> of your gold in a glass vessel. Place this in <term>Duck dung: Used by alchemists as a source of gentle, consistent heat for "digestion"</term> like an ointment, and then place it in a well-washed bottle and keep it in the open air <note>original: "sereno"; literally the "serene" night air, believed to have cooling and purifying properties</note> for eight days. 

Then, put warm water in the flask and mix it very well, stirring it back and forth. Leave the glass vessel near another glass and let it settle <note>original: "cedenza"; the process of sediment falling to the bottom</note>. Pour off the water from the top and discard it. Distill the sediment seven times. Regarding the <term>Calx: The powdery metallic oxide remaining after heating</term> of your gold, it will be discarded; compose it again with raw gold <note>original: "oro male"; likely referring to unrefined or base gold</note> and repeat the process as above nine times, and nine times again. 

In this way, your gold is prepared to resolve itself into water. Once it is so prepared, wash it with common warm water until the water comes out "clear of sin" <note>original: "chiara di peccato"; an alchemical expression meaning the water remains perfectly clear and free of impurities</note>. Afterward, you will have your dissolved gold in a bottle. Pour our homemade rose water over the calx of your gold, enough to cover the gold by the width of one finger. Close the flask so it cannot "breathe" <note>making it hermetically sealed</note> and place it in manure for eight or ten days. By itself, this water will become clear; you shall then extract it by distillation. Keep it diligently and well-sealed, because in that water is your gold dissolved.

<margin>
The Stone and extraction with signs

Our Stone is made of a single Thing, because our whole **mastery** <term>Magisterio: The entire alchemical process or "work" required to create the Philosopher's Stone</term> is performed with our water; for it is the seed <note>original: "sperma"; here used in the biological sense of generative fluid or the essential "life-force" of minerals</note> of all metals, and in it all metals are dissolved. # Seven stages of this magistery.

<margin>
Note well these stages. They are understood by the effects that the soul <note>In this context, the "soul" refers to the volatile essence or spirit being worked upon.</note> [of] the <unclear>... [likely "body"]</unclear> in its furnace. Virtue of the philosophers and water.
</margin>

1st: <term>Purification<note>original: "purificatio"</note></term>, which is to draw the pure matter from the stone.
2nd: Or, to cleanse the pure from the impure.
3rd: <term>Sublimation<note>original: "sublimatio"; the process of heating a substance until it turns to vapor and then collects as a solid again, used to refine the material.</note></term>, which is to separate the coarse parts from the subtle.
4th: <term>Putrefaction<note>original: "putrefattione"; the symbolic "death" and breakdown of the matter.</note></term>, which is to dissolve the bodies and turn them into <term>quicksilver<note>original: "argento vivo"; literally "living silver." In alchemy, this usually refers to a state of liquidity and spiritual potential rather than just the metal mercury.</note></term>, that is, into our water.
5th: <term>Mortification<note>original: "mortificatione"</note></term>, which is to cleanse the body from the little blackness.
6th: <term>Congelation<note>original: "congelatione"</note></term>, which is to congeal; therefore, when you see the water congealed, you will be certain that the art is true.
7th: <term>Calcination<note>original: "calcinatione"</note></term>, which is to dissolve and convert into ash, and this serves to facilitate the dissolving.
7th: And <term>Fixation<note>original: "fixatione"; the final stabilization of the substance so it can withstand heat without vaporizing.</note></term>, which is to whiten or to redden. <note>The colors white and red refer to the two final stages of the Stone: the White Work (making silver) and the Red Work (making gold).</note>

->End<-

In the book of Master Giacomo Cornaboni <note>possibly a reference to a local practitioner or a specific manuscript owner</note> were written the following words from the *Book of Truth*.
The most certain and the best thing in the art is natural gold, and mercurial water; these two, similarly mixed, change all metals into the finest gold.

That which is called mercurial water is made through the sublimation <term>sublimation: the process of heating a substance until it turns into vapor and then solidifies again, used to purify chemicals</term> of the Quintessence of vitriol <term>vitriol: a historical term for sulfate minerals, often used to create powerful acidic "spirits" or solvents in alchemy</term>.

## Common Operations in the Art.

To putrefy, that is, to dissolve. To distill, that is, to wash. To circulate <note>Usually refers to a process of continuous distillation in a closed vessel, though glossed here as "macinare" (to grind)</note>, that is, to grind. To filter, which is to purify with its own water, and to decant, that is, to evacuate. To decant, which is to separate the pure from the impure, that is, the corruption of the Moon <note>original: "Luna," the alchemical name for silver</note> or Earth; to nourish and to multiply are the proper operations.

<margin>Close this <note>likely an instruction to seal the vessel</note></margin>
Refine the earth by preserving its form, so that there is no melting of its 
<margin>own water</margin>
moisture unless it is with its own water: to flow and congeal, and to separate and dissolve, and to continue such that it is no longer dry; that is, to congeal, dissolve, and separate until it becomes white and no longer produces smoke; but remains like sal ammoniac <term>sal armoniaco: ammonium chloride, a volatile salt used to clean metals and in various chemical reactions</term>, and 
<margin>our earth</margin>
our purified earth is refreshed and made fit to receive its spirit and its soul, as is taught in the first work.

Let it undergo a putrefaction for one month, but a philosophical one <note>Philosophical putrefaction refers to a slow, gentle heating process intended to break down the material symbolically and physically without destroying its "spirit" through excessive heat.</note>; take and weigh this black material thus putrefied, and place it upon your shining white [substance], from which our mercury—which is called our head and the tail of the dragon <term>Head and Tail of the Dragon: An alchemical symbol for the cyclical nature of the work, often referring to the beginning and end of a specific chemical reaction or the union of opposites</term>—comes when it is half of a black body, so that the body might be diminished; and this will happen quickly, since every dry thing causes it to drink its own moisture. Then place it in the same heat, well-sealed, and in the space of about ten days it will congeal and dry out. Beneath, it is a marvelous thing, as no other liquid congeals over such a long duration.

After you have performed this congealing, weigh this matter again and add to it a fourth part of its weight of the said mercury, or rather crude and pure white oil. Again, weigh the congealed mass and mix with it a fourth part of the aforementioned oil, always fresh, and cook it with a similar degree of fire until it congeals. And you shall do the same for the third and fourth times, always with a fourth part of the oil. In the third composition, you will produce a green color mixed with black, but in the fourth time, an azure color will appear, a color that tends toward white.

Once this fourth imbibing <note>original: "imbitione," referring to the process of a solid absorbing a liquid until saturated</note> is done, always with a fourth part of the white oil or the mercury itself, then you come to dissolve your congealed earth; if you add moisture to it, let it remain alone. Afterward, so that it might congeal—which it will not do without its own moisture—add a seventh part of its own weight of the same fresh mercury. You will see it in the same heat, but let it be a little cooler; it will be a very white color like pearls, and then it is a perfect medicine for the white work <note>The "white work" or *albedo* is the second major stage of alchemy, representing purification and the creation of the "White Stone" capable of transmuting metals into silver.</note>, which the philosophers call Ribar <note>original: "Ribar," likely a corruption or specific variant of an Arabic-derived alchemical term for the white elixir or mercury.</note>.

## The procedure for the red is this

<margin>to ferment</margin>
You shall dissolve the white medicine by itself, either in a [water] bath or by keeping it at a temperate heat in a closed vessel, which will be achieved in a few days. Once this is done, it must be congealed with heat: red, or blackened rubification <note>rubification: the process of turning a substance red, symbolizing the final stage of the alchemical process</note>, which rubification <gloss>rubification</gloss> is performed through the extraction of the red tincture—or rather, red gold—from our dregs, which are called Cenon <note>original: "Cenon"; likely referring to the "empty" or exhausted matter remains</note>, the vital essence. Place this over the rectified white mercury, or rather dissolved white oil, and place it in a [water] bath in a closed vessel to ferment until you see that the said mercury is well-reddened. You must then gently <gloss>gently</gloss> pour it off by inclination <note>inclination: the act of tilting a vessel to pour off liquid without disturbing the sediment at the bottom</note> and once again place new white mercury <gloss>mercury</gloss> over the same <gloss>same</gloss> dregs, fermenting as before until it turns a red color. You shall continue this until the dregs no longer yield anything. At that point, you shall throw away those dregs that remain. And this mercury of yours, 

<margin>mercury now animated like salt.</margin>
thus reddened, will congeal by itself with the tincture like salt; and this is our mercury, animated with our salt, which has entered into it. Take, therefore, that part of the medicine that pleases you...

Take one ounce of this salt, and one ounce of Gold <note>original: "Sole" (Sun); the alchemical symbol for Gold</note>, and two ounces of Silver <note>original: "Luna" (Moon); the alchemical symbol for Silver</note>, and one ounce of the said oil, and put them in two separate vessels in a water bath <note>original: "bagno maria"; a method of gentle heating using a vessel placed in boiling water</note> for natural hours until the Gold and the Silver are converted into a substance like gum. Whoever teaches that the **perfect bodies** <term>corpora perfecta</term> <note>In alchemy, gold and silver are the "perfect" metals because they do not corrode or rust; all other metals were considered "imperfect" or "diseased" versions of them.</note> of **gold** and **silver** must be liquified and dissolved from silver into **mercury**, and that mercury, no matter how much it prepares itself by purifying through **distillation**; it does nothing more; it does not lose that humidity or become altered through such rectifications like **common sublimation** <term>vulgaris sublimatio</term> <note>Sublimation is the process of heating a substance until it turns to vapor and then solidifies again. <meta>This page continues the alchemical theme from the previous entry by Andreas Thincendry, moving from the philosophical "Stone" to a specific practical recipe for a "Universal Medicine" capable of transmuting metals into both silver and gold through repeated sublimation and deliquescence.</meta>

# Universal medicine both 
## for Silver <note>represented by the Moon symbol ☽</note> and for Gold <note>represented by the Sun symbol ☉</note>.

->White and red<-

Recipe: Refined silver <gloss>living</gloss> filed, ten ounces; well-purified mercury, 4 ounces; sal ammoniac, one pound and a half.
Divide the sal ammoniac into three equal parts, ground into powder—that is, six ounces per part—and set it aside. Afterward, incorporate the silver well with the mercury in a marble mortar, grinding it until it is well crushed and incorporated. Then take six ounces of sal ammoniac and incorporate it well with the said silver and mercury, and grind until the mercury is no longer visible. After this, put this material in a crucible <term>sagiuolo</term> <note>A heat-resistant vessel used for melting or high-temperature reactions.</note>, seal it well, and then place it in a furnace to sublimate with a slow fire <note>original: "fuoco sordo," referring to a low, steady heat</note> according to the art; the sublimation is completed in 12 hours. Then break the vessel, take the material, and grind it well. Add another six ounces of sal ammoniac and sublimate again according to the art. Then break it and add the remaining six ounces of sal ammoniac as before, and sublimate for the third time. After the third time, take the material, grind it well, and sublimate as many times as necessary until it no longer sublimates, breaking the vessel after every sublimation. Then take the said material, reduced to a fine powder, and place it in a cellar upon a marble slab; in three days it will dissolve <note>The process of deliquescence, where a substance absorbs moisture from the air to become liquid oil.</note>. If you place a drop of this oil upon a sheet of copper, it will become white; and if the copper is red-hot, the oil will penetrate it from side to side; this serves to know if you have operated correctly.
<margin>Red</margin> Place this oil inside a small flask <term>capirolo</term> to congeal over a slow ash fire. One part of this substance is used upon one hundred parts of purified copper and converts it into fine silver.
If you wish to work for the red <note>The "Red Work" or Rubedo, the final stage of alchemy aimed at creating gold.</note>, in place of the silver mass you shall use filed gold, and operate in the same manner. One part of this will convert one hundred parts of refined silver into fine gold.

This work will be described with succinct words and in a manner that is neither entirely hidden nor entirely revealed; not through dense enigmas or figures, but through brevity of words, yet in such a way that it may be manifest to the wise, profound to the mediocre, and to the ignorant, wretched and blind.

The craftsman must be of keen intelligence; the coarse man is excluded from this work, as is the greedy, the fickle, the hasty, the insane, the lazy, the poor, the impatient, and the intemperate who is <unclear>without composure</unclear> <note>original: "senza flemma." This science is not <unclear>learned</unclear> in books, because they speak through figures and metaphors.

You will find it not by doctrine but through the experience of nature and with great, studied labor, through which you will discover the kindness of nature itself.

The principles of this famous **art** <note>The "Art" refers to Alchemy.</note> are the same as those that occur naturally within metals.

These are the principles of metals upon which the art of forming them is founded.

The sole principal matter of all metals in their mines, from which they are generated, is a rich water that they call living water or quicksilver <term>argento vivo</term>, and a stinking spirit, which they call sulfur <term>zolfo</term>; however, this is not in the form it takes when created in its mines. For in the veins where they are generated, no metal is found, but rather this matter is a <unclear>doughy</unclear> substance created by containing within itself the substance of these two; and from this matter and substance—

### The Matter

From the aforementioned matter, you will distill a clear water. The first waters, up to the tenth part, are of no value and you shall not collect them. Then, place the receiving vessel and **lute** <term>lute: a paste used to seal the joints of alchemical apparatus to prevent vapors from escaping</term> it well and seal it tightly. To know when the "good water" begins to emerge, take a knife and let a drop fall upon it; if it boils and turns black, then it is time to collect it. When you handle the receiver, do so with a dry linen cloth and not with wet **lute** <note>Wet sealing paste on a hot glass vessel would cause it to crack due to the temperature difference.</note>, because the vessels would break.

Continue this gentle fire for 20 hours or slightly more, and then gradually light it further, increasing it until it is double or more than what was necessary at first. This increase must continue until the vessel appears to "freeze" <note>likely referring to a white sublimation or a specific state of crystallization inside the glass</note>, and then you shall increase <gloss>of</gloss> the fire, which shall be a **reverberatory fire** <term>reverberatory fire: a furnace design where the heat is reflected or "reverberated" from the roof onto the material</term>, so that the sharpest and strongest part is reserved. <margin>In winter</margin> This third order of fire you shall continue for six hours, until all the **strong water** <note>original: "acqua forte"</note> has come out, leaving the earth arid and dry, without any moisture.

Then follows the composition <gloss>joining</gloss> of this water with the earth, <margin>marriage</margin> which is called **marriage** <term>marriage: the chemical union of the volatile "spirit" (the water) with the "fixed" body (the earth)</term>. This is done immediately once the water is made; one must not wait to do this for more than two hours, because the power <unclear>perio</unclear> of this spirit quickly vanishes if it is not understood through its composition <gloss>joining</gloss> with the body. Therefore, it is necessary <margin>Autumn</margin> to do it immediately. And this is called **Autumn** <term>Autumn: the stage of the alchemical process where the "fruits" of the labor ripen and reach perfection</term>, because that is when the fruits reach perfection, and this water brings perfection to this operation or marriage.

This is what the **Philosopher** <note>Usually a reference to Hermes Trismegistus or the author of the *Emerald Tablet*.</note> said: "The wind—that is, the water—carried that—that is, that spirit of the **quintessence** <term>quintessence: the "fifth element," the purest and most medicinal essence of a substance</term>—in its belly." ## Chapter 4.

The first part of the elixir is white, which is made from white earth; the second part is red, which is made from red earth. Thus, the one is called the White Elixir, and the second the Red Elixir. Although it appears that there are two elixirs, these two are but one alone, which serves for both—that is, the first for the white, and the same [process] with the other [material] is used in the same way for the red. 

But the red **stone** <term>lapis: Latin for "stone," referring here to the Philosopher's Stone</term>, that is, the part of the red elixir, extends to both. For in this art [certain] things are possible: those that whiten <note>imbiancano: refers to the albedo or "whitening" stage of the alchemical work</note>, and those that redden <note>rubificano: refers to the rubedo or "reddening," the final stage of the Great Work</note>. Therefore, for the composition of the red elixir, the same species and materials mentioned above are required, but with different weights. 

That is: take one pound <term>lib: i.: one pound (libra)</term> of green copper <note>rame verde: likely verdigris or copper acetate, used as a base for the red stage</note>, six ounces <term>℥ vi: six ounces</term> of white sulfur, and six ounces of heavy red tartar. You shall then proceed with these materials in every way just as was said for the white elixir; however, in the conjunction, or "marriage" <note>matrimonio: a common alchemical metaphor for the chemical union of substances</note>, instead of the white earth, one places the red earth. 

In the conjunction of this earth with the spirit of the stone, it must be further purged of its earthy dregs and superfluous fluid. This is because, before it is placed in the said water, it must be purged in its proper manner; once purged and clean, it must be [formed] into very thin sheets, coiled, or reduced to powder or filings. Then it must be placed in the aforementioned water as described. 

However, when it is placed in said water, it will not dissolve like the white earth—though the white **quicksilver** <term>argent’viva: "living silver," the alchemical name for mercury</term> acts upon it—but it will only take on color, reducing itself to an impalpable powder. Once this is done, remove the other <unclear>vinegar</unclear>, <unclear>changing</unclear> the water.

<margin>Note</margin>
If you place a greater quantity of water upon the said body,

<margin>Useful errors.</margin>

<margin>Note on the solution.</margin>
Note that the solution of the stone which we mentioned 
above must be made in a viscous state. Some dissolve it 
by itself in the air, some under **dung** <term>fimo: horse dung was used in laboratories as a source of gentle, constant "natural" heat for digestion.</term>, and then congeal it

by itself just once and dried it as described,

small amount—that is, the sixth part of its weight—of

out of it and not from another. If it is made in this way, 
it must be simple and not impregnated with <unclear>arsenic</unclear> 
or spirit, and then they set it to dissolve in the air 
according to how you will be instructed in this place.

Warning that the solutions made under dung or by fire 
are not true solutions, but rather fusions or liquefactions. 
Look well to what the true solution must be, 
because upon this depends great loss or great gain; 
therefore, pay close attention.

already very well cleaned) until it is thoroughly dry and parched.

# The Sublimation of fixed Mercury marked by the lime of Gold

<margin>Sublimation of Mercury <note>original symbol: ☿</note></margin>
Take **strong water** <term>aqua fortis: nitric acid, a powerful corrosive used to dissolve metals</term> made from Roman vitriol, saltpeter, and green calamine, of each [an equal amount] distilled and well-purified with vinegar and salt, just as one does with the water of **Gold** <note>original symbol: ☉</note> or with **strong water**, in which [specific] pound there are as many pounds as required. Distill the water from it, and pour it over again; do this four times and you will have recovered a better water, and it will be **precipitated Mercury**. If you have 1 pound, mix it with 1 pound of prepared common salt and with half a pound of Roman vitriol; pour it over again and add the total of the prepared salt, then it will be reduced to powder by precipitation, better and better, and repeat such moistenings until neither <unclear>vixi</unclear> remains. When it is nearly [dry], put it in a glass vessel well-sealed with **lute** <term>lute: a clay or paste used to seal laboratory glass airtight</term> to sublimate for 24 days. Afterward, the sublimated material will be found at the top; sublimate it three times in this way, then with double its weight of red glass [powder], sublimate the **sublimated Mercury** again. It will emerge with a quality near that of sublimated talc and will be prepared so that with this substance, one can "hide" or fix **live Mercury** with **Gold** just like water.

# To calcine Mercury, Copper, and Tin

<margin>Lime of Mercury, Copper, and Tin <note>original symbols: ☿ ♀ ♃</note></margin>
Take that nitrate material from where you distilled the prepared common salt; afterward let it be well powdered. Place it in a fixed pot, cover it and seal it well with lute, place it in the furnace for days and nights and you will find the **lime** <term>calx: the powdery metallic oxide remaining after a metal has been roasted or burned</term>. Likewise, you can pour and sublimate as above until the whole process is finished in such a furnace with the **Mercury** within.

# The Soul of Gold

<margin>The soul</margin>

Then let the distillation occur by the **water bath**, and there will remain "wool" <note>a fluffy, fibrous precipitate often seen in alchemical mineral work</note> from the superfluous waters. Afterward, pour one part of the product into <gloss>cleared</gloss> water <note>original: "aqua picolatuna"; possibly a corruption of a term for filtered or pitch-purified water</note> and distill it through an **alembic** <term>alembic: a hooded distilling apparatus used to cool vapors into liquid</term>. It will then be better for all uses. After this, filter it and distill through the **water bath** as you did with the liquids, and on the fifth time, the "earth" <note>the solid residue</note> will remain converted into a very white salt, like snow. When you reach this fifth time, do not delay, until you reach this point and it well-fills the middle part of the long neck.

In time, let the distillation occur by the **Hermetic seal** <term>sigilla hermetis: an airtight glass seal made by melting the neck of the flask shut</term>, or rather, to ensure strength, pour the sealing over the neck and let the joint be well-luted <note>sealed with clay or paste</note> so it does not breathe. Thus, for 15 days, let it be buried in warm **horse dung** <term>fimo equino: decomposing manure, used by alchemists as a source of steady, gentle "digestion" heat</term>. Let it be heated by the sun and the **water bath**, and the **Silver** <note>original: "luna" (the Moon), the alchemical symbol for silver</note> will remain like very bright Gold. Through the night, [expose it] strongly to the sun <note>likely referring to "starlight" or the cooling cycle</note> then going outside and giving it "the wheel" <note>original: "rota"; a term for completing a circular process or a specific stage of high-heat circulation</note>. O medicine! Everything descends into the receiver, for it is said that this is the best medicine for the human body. In a similar way, **potable water** <note>original: "aqua potabile"; likely "Potable Gold" or a medicinal spirit</note> is made, which has been in the dung until now; it is a medicament for the human body and ought to be produced through the furnace. Bind it in a smooth linen cloth and set it to be fixed in the distillation, and you will arrive at a wine similar to that used by the healers of the body.

# Work of gold and copper

Take oil of antimony <note>original: "olio d'antim."</note>, oil of burnt leather <note>original: "scordename"; referencing the "burnt leather" mentioned on the previous page</note>, crocus of copper <note>original: "croci di rami"; red copper oxide</note>, iron, and oil of sulfur, 3 ounces of each. -> Oil of iron like copper <-
-> Oil of Antimony <-

<margin>of crocus of copper</margin>
Take 1 pound of copper <note>original: "ramamine"</note>, 1 pound of saltpeter, and 1 pound of tartar. Place it in a damp place <note>original: "al humido"; to allow it to deliquesce into a liquid state</note> upon a copper plate, and you will make the oil you seek.

-> Oil of crocus of Mars <-
<margin>water of crocus of Mars</margin>
Make the crocus of Mars <note>Mars is the alchemical symbol for iron; crocus of Mars is iron oxide</note> with aqua fortis <note>nitric acid</note>, dry it with the gold, and then sublimate it with an equal amount of sal ammoniac <note>ammonium chloride</note> three times, separating the sublimate from the dregs. Then place those dregs in a damp place upon a piece of marble, and you shall have the oil of Mars and of gold.

-> Oil of verdigris <-
<margin>Oil of verdigris</margin>
Take verdigris <note>original: "verde rame"; copper acetate</note> and burnt copper, 3 ounces of each. Boil in strong vinegar, stirring until it is purified. Powder it well, then dry it with fire; make [a paste] of the aforementioned and then place it on the marble in a damp place, and you shall have the oil of verdigris.

-> Other <-
<margin>other</margin>
Take the burnt red [powder], well-pulverized, with the urine of a young boy <note>a common source of ammonia and phosphates in early chemistry</note>; rub it for 24 hours and soak it in very strong vinegar, adding the copper as it is consumed. Put the burnt [material] in a flask at the bottom of the embers; once it is formed into the aforementioned light and distilled as many times as needed until it remains as a pure leaf of gold, you will have completed your works by *dyphatione* <note>original: "dyphatione"; likely a corruption of "defectione" (purification) or a specific term for the final clarification of the metal</note>.

The Rule of Picanus

->Rules of Picanus<-

Take the <term>regulus</term> <note>A pure metallic mass that settles at the bottom of a crucible during smelting; original: "regulum"</note> of Picanus with mercury as is described below, and place it upon purified silver, and in a <term>luted</term> <note>Sealed with a protective clay paste</note> pot, as is said below. For example, if one pound in four of the regulus requires 36 hours of high fire, if there were two pounds of [itacoro?] of the regulus, you must give fire for 48 hours.

# To fix Sal Ammoniac:

<margin>Fixed sal ammoniac</margin>
Take two parts of quicklime <note>calcium oxide</note> and one part of **sal ammoniac** <term>Sal Ammoniac</term><note>original: "sale arm."; ammonium chloride, a salt used to help dissolve metals</note>, ground together. # Purification of Lead

<margin>To purge lead</margin>
Melt the lead and quench it ten times in vinegar in which prepared sal ammoniac has been dissolved. Do this during thorough calcination <note>heating to a high temperature to remove volatile substances</note> and it will lose its blackness and softness (unless it was already <unclear>pure</unclear>). Place it in a well-luted <note>sealed with alchemist's clay</note> vessel in a bread oven for one day and one night, and you will find it much changed in color, hanging like gold. <note>original Latin: "Funde plumbum et estingue decem vicibus..."</note>

<margin>medicine for Gold <note>original: $\odot$</note></margin>
<margin>iron distilled with aqua fortis</margin>
Take as much iron filings as needed and dissolve them in "strong water" <term>aquafort</term> <note>nitric acid</note> made from purified saltpeter, Roman vitriol, and rock alum in equal parts <term>anā</term>. Afterward, distill the liquid to capture that iron calx <term>calina</term> <note>the powdery residue left after a metal is burned or dissolved in acid</note>. Mix this with an equal amount of sulfur and place it over lit coals so that all the sulfur evaporates, leaving the iron calx as a reddish powder. Sublimate <note>a process of heating a substance until it turns to vapor and then solidifies again</note> this with an equal amount of sal ammoniac several times. Expose it to the air five times, so that in each sublimation the iron calx is broken down. In the final sublimation, separate the salts from the calx and place it upon a stone in a humid place. It will transform into a film <term>ostia</term> and resolve into a blue oil <term>oglio cerulo</term> without any dross.

<margin>calx of copper</margin>
Take copper sheets and place them in a vessel <term>testa</term>. Moisten them with vinegar and "sulfur of Venus" <note>an alchemical term for a preparation of copper sulfur</note> until it becomes brittle. Grind this and sublimate it with an equal amount of sal ammoniac. Place it upon a stone in a humid place to distill into an oil, and preserve it.

## Another [method] for extracting **Mercury** <note>original: "🜔"</note> from **Gold** <note>original: "☉"</note> or **Lead** <note>original: "♄"</note>

Wash with hot water until the salt completely <unclear>separates</unclear>. From this, take Gold <note>original: ☉</note>, Tin <note>original: ♃</note>, and Copper <note>original: ♀</note>, and make filings, filing them finely, or use thin sheets of Tin <note>original: ♃</note> and Copper <note>original: ♀</note>. Then <unclear>maintain the balance</unclear> well so that the <term>body</term> <note>original: corpus; the solid metallic matter</note> does not breathe [leak]: place it in dung for ten days and afterward distill with a dry fire in the manner of strong water until you see that the good part, which is pure Gold <note>original: ☉</note>, rises in two parts. Distill it gradually until the impure part remains at the bottom as a black matter that is worth nothing. When the distillation is finished, re-distill it using a <term>water bath</term> <note>original: balneum mariæ; a vessel of water used to heat another container gently</note>; the water will rise into the <term>receiving vessel</term> <note>original: targa; a shield-shaped or specific collection vessel</note> and will no longer be good, but the remainder at the bottom will be clear and fragrant.

And now, concerning this oil of Tin <note>original: ♃</note> and of Gold <note>original: ☉</note> mixed together: put them in a long-necked vessel, tightly closed with another vessel on top, in dung for 15 days. Afterward, place it over a gentle fire, and within ten days it should congeal into a stone as clear as <term>crystal</term>. From then on, give it a more subtle fire continuously for 27 [days] so that all of it flows very easily into a clear and shining oil without thickening; keep it in a clean vessel. Sprinkle one part of this over 10 parts of <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: ☿ vivi</note>, and it will become a medicine, one part of which [placed] over another part of quicksilver—and subsequently any other imperfect body—will reduce it into the finest gold. # First operation for prepared Mercury <note>original: ☿</note>

Grind together one pound <note>original: lib: i.</note> of pure salt <note>original: ⊖</note> and 6 ounces <note>original: ℥ 6.</note> of such prepared Mercury <note>original: ☿</note>. Pound them so that the Mercury does not appear but instead becomes a powder; then perform a strong <term>sublimation</term> <note>the process of heating a substance into a vapor so it collects as a solid on a cooler surface</note> in a receiving vessel. You will then have prepared Mercury, which you should wash with lukewarm water and dry with a linen cloth.

# Second operation: Amalgamation

[Take] 1 ounce <note>original: ℥ i.</note> of cemented and filed Gold <note>original: ☉</note> mixed in salt <note>original: ⊖</note> <unclear>as below</unclear> and <unclear>hammered</unclear>. Put in 4 ounces <note>original: ℥ 4.</note> of purified Mercury <note>original: ☿</note> as described above; when the Mercury begins to boil, remove it from the fire and immediately place the gold upon it. Mix it well and it will be <term>amalgamated</term> <note>blended into a soft, silvery paste of mercury and another metal</note>. Throw it into a dish filled with water, moving it with your finger until you feel the Gold <note>original: ☉</note> is well incorporated with the Mercury <note>original: ☿</note>. Pour out the water and dry it with a cloth.

# Third operation: Sublimation of the amalgam

Take the amalgam mixed with common salt in a polished bowl, and place another bowl on top of it. Set it to sublimate, and the Mercury <note>original: ☿</note> will rise <unclear>again</unclear> and adhere to the upper bowl; collect that and save it for many stages of the work. What remained in the lower bowl should be put into hot water; the salt will dissolve, and the Gold <note>original: ☉</note> will remain at the bottom. Empty the water and dry the "sun" <note>original: solem; the alchemical name for gold</note>.

# Fourth operation: Washing the amalgam

Amalgamate the dried Gold <note>original: solem</note> with purified Mercury <note>original: ☿</note> as described above, and sublimate it again as above. Do this four times, always setting aside the mercury or whatever has sublimated to one side. In this manner, you will now have prepared gold that is most excellently <term>calcined</term> <note>original: calcinatum; reduced to a fine, pure powder through heat and chemical action</note>. In all sublimations performed during calcination, take the Mercury that was sublimated with salt and add new Mercury, collecting it in each sublimation. <unclear>Calcine</unclear> them together in one dish separately.

# 6th operation: sublimating the amalgam

# Some Notable Remarks

## 1st: Regarding fixed Gold <note>original: ☉ (the Sun/Gold)</note> when it is not as it should be

<margin>Note</margin>
How the volatile is placed with the fixed should be noted in paragraph 7 of the first [part]; namely, that it must be inside so that you know it ought to exhibit it. The fire appropriates through its motion the salt that it wishes to have, and [the point] up to which it is placed.
<margin>In the <term>athanor</term> <note>original: "alm. M."; likely referring to the *athanor* or "pigeon-house" furnace</note> and cooked for three [days/periods]</margin>
Let the mass be placed to break down its qualities in the vessel <note>original: ♁ (the symbol for the Earth or a crucible; here likely the reaction vessel)</note>. The vessel is full of water, because that which is more fluid contains, like pleasing forces, its own mobility; and it is properly said that we have been close to the secret, and it must be held for 40 days.

<margin>putrefaction <note>the alchemical stage of decomposition and blackening</note></margin>
## Concerning Putrefaction

Let the dissolved compound be placed in dung <note>original: *fimo*; horse manure was frequently used in laboratories to provide a gentle, constant heat</note>, which you previously placed together in a certain glass vessel through the top and high up. Let it be ensured that it is kept continually within the stench <note>the vapors produced by the decaying organic matter or the chemical reaction</note>, and let the "water of Silver" <note>original: ☾ (the Moon/Silver)</note> have its own nearby furnace, and it ought to last for 40 days.

<margin>the stone</margin>
## Concerning the Oils of Silver <note>original: ☾</note> or Gold <note>original: ☉</note>

In whatever way the oil of Silver or Gold is made, the Stone <note>the Philosopher's Stone</note> is obtained, because [the substance] is retained within the waters. Let the composition be made with or without Gold, and the medicine [is multiplied] infinitely by the power of Iron <note>original: ♂ (Mars/Iron)</note>, that is, it is made upon Iron itself. It is said that by digesting it with four parts of glass <unclear>heruỹ</unclear> and the salt of the elixir, it is called "permanent water" <note>original: *aqua permanens*; a solvent that does not evaporate</note>. This water, according to our [masters], has no end regarding its multiplication because it is fixed and acts upon Silver and Tin <note>original: ♃ (Jupiter/Tin)</note>; it congeals that which is not fixed into a powder.
