## First operation

Take <note>original: "R"; the standard alchemical and medical abbreviation for 'Recipe,' meaning 'Take.'</note> 2 pounds of Roman <term>Vitriol<gloss>a sulfate of iron or copper, used here as a primary reagent</gloss></term>, 2 pounds of saltpeter, 2 pounds of rock alum, 6 pounds of <term>Cinnabar<gloss>mercury sulfide, typically used to provide mercury or for its red color</gloss></term>, and 3 pounds of <term>Verdigris<gloss>a green pigment or crust formed on copper, often used as a source of acetic acid or copper</gloss></term>. Having crushed these in a <term>retort<gloss>a glass vessel with a long neck used for distillation</gloss></term>, distill them by fire. This water is called "Magisterial Water," but it must be distilled twice so that it remains clear.

Take 1 pound of quicksilver <note>original: "q: arg.to" for 'quinto argento' or 'quicksilver'</note> and 4 pounds of that water. Put the quicksilver in small grains into the mouth of the flask and once it has dissolved, let it boil with the mouth open for the space of an hour or thereabouts. Then distill all that water into another flask, and continue distilling until the whole mixture goes to powder at the bottom. Remove it from the fire and put into the said flask a good glassful of cistern water <note>original: "acqua di cisterna"; usually rainwater, considered purer for chemical processes</note> after it has become cold. Let it rest for one night. In the morning it will be very clear, and the black dregs will be at the bottom. Distill what remains so that it does not become fouled, putting it to distill in a <term>urinal<gloss>a specific type of rounded glass vessel used in laboratories</gloss></term>. Be advised that the water that distills then is not good, because it is cistern water. At the bottom there will remain <margin>Silver salt.</margin> the silver salt like a red flame; let this be dissolved at a rate of about an ounce per hour. This is the first operation.

According to the daily astronomical records of the Lower Worlds, folios 41 and 49.

Mars [iron] essentially joins with Venus [copper], and because their houses are equidistant, he overcomes her by gazing upon her and fixing her. Likewise, melt Mars ♂ by means of arsenic <term>mercury<gloss>here referring to the volatile "spirit" of the arsenic rather than quicksilver</gloss></term>; afterward, place it in the fire in a **reverberatory furnace** <term>reverberii<gloss>a furnace that reflects the flame down onto the material</gloss></term> until it becomes malleable and is joined to the Sun ☉ [gold]. It shall not be separated from it for eternity, and this is truer than all other experiments.

Jupiter [tin] gazes in **sextile** <term>sextile<gloss>an astrological aspect where planets are 60 degrees apart, usually signaling a harmonious or productive combination</gloss></term>, through Aquarius by way of Capricorn from a fiery sign; therefore, Jupiter calcines, and is absorbed by Saturn ♄ [lead], and <unclear>of which</unclear> you lose much of the moisture <note>original: "humoribus," referring to the liquid or volatile parts of the metal</note>.

The **powder of reduction** <term>pulvis reductionis<gloss>a substance used to return a "calcined" or oxidized metal back to its metallic state</gloss></term> is prepared in this way: **Take** <note>original: "℞," the standard abbreviation for "Recipe"</note> one part of this kind, two parts of common salt; cook it in a pot with <unclear>urine</unclear> <note>original: "te," possibly a shorthand for an earthen pot "terre," though the text immediately clarifies it as "id est urina"</note>—that is, as much urine as there is bile; add to it one part saltpetre and one part **calcined tartar** <term>tartari calcinati<gloss>potassium carbonate, used as a flux to help metals melt</gloss></term>; grind them together. Likewise **take** <note>original: "℞"</note> <unclear>two</unclear> parts of the other part of the body to be reduced. The superior always overcomes the inferior; thus, in this way, one removes the **cry of Jupiter** <term>stridorem Jovis<gloss>the distinctive crackling sound made when pure tin is bent, which alchemists sought to "cure"</gloss></term>. Jupiter ♃ melts Mars ♂; Mars ♂ calcines the Sun ☉ [gold]; the Sun ☉ perfects Venus ♀ [copper]; Venus ♀ perfects Mercury ☿; and Mercury ☿ perfects the Moon ☽ [silver].

Let Venus ♀ [copper], having been calcined, reduced, and purified by means of arsenic, be soaked with Jupiter ♃ [tin], which has been distilled through an **alembic** <term>alembicum<gloss>a specialized glass or ceramic still used for distillation</gloss></term> until it is **fixed** <term>figatur<gloss>stabilized so it no longer evaporates or changes when heated</gloss></term> and reduced into true Moon ☽ [silver].

**The Moon** [silver], but **Jupiter** [tin] hates the **Moon** and is friendly to the **Sun** [gold]: therefore it also dissolves the **Sun**. # Unique and Tinging Water

Take 4 pounds each of reddened Roman vitriol <note>original: *Vitrioli Romi rubificati*; iron sulfate heated until it turns red</note> and saltpeter <note>potassium nitrate</note>, and 1 pound each of lead alum and rock alum. Take 6 ounces each of common antimony <unclear>vulgare</unclear> and cinnabar <note>mercury sulfide</note>, 1 ounce of orpiment <note>original: *auripigmentum*; arsenic trisulfide</note>, and 1 ounce of saffron of Mars <note>original: *crocus Martis*; iron oxide</note>. Grind all these things well: place them in retorts and pour the aforementioned water over them. Add as much <margin>quicksilver in <unclear>linca</unclear></margin> quicksilver <note>original: *☿ vivus* (mercury)</note> as the liquid is able to dissolve; and set it to circulate <note>a process of continuous distillation and condensation in a closed vessel</note> for 40 days with a lamp of five wicks <note>original: *lucerna quinque filorum*; a lamp with five threads to provide a constant, moderate heat</note>, and you will have 3 ounces of gold for every pound [of the mixture].

---

## Oil of Copper <note>original: *Oleum ♀* (Venus)</note>

Grind the calcined <note>heated to a powder</note> and washed flower of Venus <note>likely copper acetate or copper oxide</note>, and grind it well upon a porphyry stone with refined burning water <note>original: *aqua ardenti finissa*; strong distilled alcohol or brandy</note>. Set fire to it, then grind it again with burning water and ignite it again; do this until the entire powder is converted into a green oil. Let the labor not weary you until the whole is turned into oil.

## Fixation of Tin <note>original: *Fixatio ♃* (Jupiter)</note>

Boil the tin, ground very finely, in common oil for one hour. Afterward, pour in <margin>... [marginal note: threads/lines ... properly/legitimately]</margin> vinegar, and the oil will come to the top. Drain it off with the vinegar and do the same to the quicksilver <note>original: *☿* (mercury)</note> after the final boiling. Separate the oil.

# The Fixation of Arsenic

Take 1 pound <note>original symbol: ℔</note> of raw arsenic and 1 pound of saltpeter <note>potassium nitrate</note>, <term>equal parts</term> <note>original: "ana"</note>; and 3 ounces of tartar. Mix the ground ingredients and place them bit by bit into a crucible over a fire so that they melt and the smoke ceases. In this process, take care that when the end is reached, you let it cool; it will be a red mass. Grind this and mix it with an equal part of saltpeter. Proceed as above for 6 hours in the fire, then let it cool; it will be a white mass. Grind it and separate the tartar and saltpeter by washing with hot water. The <term>fixed arsenic</term> <note>Arsenic that has been rendered non-volatile by chemical reaction, often used in alchemical "whitening" of copper</note> will remain at the bottom, without poison. Note: also congeal the water that contains the saltpeter and tartar, which can be used again another time.

# Antimony in True Vitriol
<margin>Starry Regulus of Mars</margin>

### Augmentation of Gold

Take <term>silver</term> filings and <term>lead</term> <note>original symbol: ♄</note> filings in equal parts <note>original: "ana"</note>. Place them in a glass vessel that has a small hole like a needle. Mix well and amalgamate them. Place it in a furnace for 20 days and it will be <term>fixed</term> <note>rendered stable and non-volatile under heat</note>. In place of the silver, you may put gold, and it will be fixed into gold.

## ## O. Oil of Saffron of Mars <note>original: "oglio di Croco ♂". In alchemy, Mars represents iron. "Saffron of Mars" refers to iron oxide (rust) prepared in a specific way.</note>

## ## Oil of Venus <note>original: "oleum ♀". Venus is the alchemical symbol for copper.</note>

## ## Oil of Sulfur <note>original: "oleum 🜍"</note>

Take 1 pound of sulfur and incorporate it with 1 pound of <term>soda ash</term> <note>original: "alume catino"; an alkaline salt derived from the ashes of saltwort plants, used in glassmaking.</note>. Place 3 ounces of <term>sal ammoniac</term> <note>original symbol: ✶</note> inside a pot, then light a fire within and let it burn for the duration of two "Miserere" prayers <note>A common way to measure time in early modern recipes by reciting Psalm 51 ("Miserere mei, Deus") at a steady pace.</note>. 

Then cover the pot with a cloth to extinguish the fire. Afterward, the moist powder will turn into an oil of a golden color. If you wish to work more quickly, treat the sulfur with sal ammoniac and tartar; the "water" will come out. Place the dregs in a moist place and it will become oil. Of these oils, take 1 ounce of each. Take <term>hematite stone</term> <note>An iron oxide mineral.</note>, <term>revivified swans</term> <note>original: "vivificata di cigni". In alchemical allegory, the "swan" often represents the white stage of the work or purified mercury.</note>, and <term>Alexandrian tutty</term> <note>Zinc oxide collected from the flues of furnaces.</note>, 2 ounces of each. Grind them into a powder and soak them.

### Prepared Common Salt
Dissolve common salt in urine that has been mixed with an equal amount of <term>quicklime</term> <note>original: "calce viva"; calcium oxide, a caustic chemical.</note> and then strained. In this liquid, dissolve the common salt and let it congeal. Dissolve it again by moisture, dry it, and congeal it 3 times; and it will be prepared.

### For the Red, True and Proven <note>original: "Ad Rubeum Vero e prouato"; the "Red" refers to the *Rubedo*, the final stage of the alchemical "Great Work" intended to produce gold or the Philosopher's Stone.</note>

**Recipe:** <note>original: "℞."; the traditional symbol for a medical or alchemical recipe, shorthand for the Latin *Recipe* ("Take").</note> Take five ounces of very well purified **mercury** <note>original symbol: "☿"</note> and one ounce of **fine gold leaf**; you shall amalgamate them together. You shall place said amalgam in a flask that has a round body and a neck about three palms <note>Approximately 24–30 centimeters.</note> long, and then you will place four ounces of **blood of Antimony** <note>A red oil or tincture derived from antimony, considered a powerful solvent and transmuting agent in early chemistry.</note> over it. Afterward, you shall seal it hermetically. The flask must be luted <note>Luting involved coating glass vessels with a protective layer of clay, sand, and sometimes dung to protect them from the direct heat of the furnace.</note> very well to the thickness of a <term>testone</term> <note>A large silver coin used in 16th-century Italy, here serving as a reference for the thickness of the clay coating.</note>, and once dry, you shall place it upon the furnace. Beneath it, you shall place a lamp with four wicks as thick as a goose quill, leaving the flame beneath the flask for three natural days <note>A "natural day" refers to a full 24-hour cycle.</note>.

Then, you shall break it once it has cooled, and inside you will find a substance that is a **medicine**. Of this medicine, you shall take one part, and seven parts of **cupelled silver** <term>copella</term> <note>Silver refined through cupellation, a process of heating the metal in a shallow porous bowl to remove impurities like lead.</note>. You shall melt the silver, and once it is molten, you will **feed** <note>original: "cibarai"; an alchemical term for adding a "potent" or "noble" substance to a molten base metal to transform its nature.</note> it with one part of this medicine, and you will keep stirring it with a small stick until it is well incorporated with the silver. Cast it into a rod, and you will have **gold of 22 and a half carats**, permanent against every test <note>Meaning the gold is of high purity and will pass the traditional tests of the touchstone or acid.</note>.

# Method for Making the Blood of Antimony

<margin>Blood of Antimony:</margin>
Take <note>original: "℞"; the traditional symbol for a medical or alchemical recipe, shorthand for the Latin *Recipe* ("Take").</note> raw **Antimony**, that is, from the mine, which has not been melted; you shall crush it and pass it through a sieve. Then put it into a flask, and over one pound of the said antimony, you will place 2 pounds of **aqua vitae** <note>literally "water of life," a term used for concentrated alcohol or distilled spirits used as a solvent.</note> drawn through a <term>water bath</term> <note>original: "p: b:"; an abbreviation for *per balneum* (or *balneum Mariae*), a method of gentle heating by placing the vessel in warm water.</note>. Then seal the flask well and place it under **dung** <note>original: "fimo"; fermenting animal dung was used in early chemistry to provide a steady, low, and natural heat for incubation.</note> for 3 days. Then remove it and filter the aqua vitae, and you shall continue doing this—putting in new aqua vitae—until it no longer becomes colored.

Gather all the colored aqua vitae that you have drawn and put it in a flask on the furnace; distill it over a fire of ashes <note>A "fire of ashes" or "ash heat" involved placing the vessel in a bed of hot ashes to distribute heat more evenly than a direct flame.</note> until the aqua vitae has come out. There will remain in the bottom of the flask a red matter like blood.

Note that in the same flask you will find a **golden matter** <note>Refers to a sublimated byproduct, likely crystalline, that gathered in the neck of the vessel during the heating process.</note> sublimated, which you shall take and place in a glass jar, set aside and well sealed.

Infuse new aqua vitae into the <term>matter</term> <gloss>matter</gloss> that remained in the bottom of the vessel, and continue in this way until that golden-colored matter no longer sublimates. That which remains at the bottom will be like red blood.

<summary>This page details the extraction process for "blood of antimony," a red tincture produced by incubating raw antimony in alcohol using the gentle heat of a water bath and fermenting dung. This substance was a key ingredient in the alchemical pursuit of creating gold as described on the preceding page.</summary>
<keywords>Antimony, aqua vitae, distillation, alchemical extraction, blood of antimony, golden matter, laboratory methods</keywords>

## Of the line of the heart and of the head

The line of the heart, near its beginning, signifies <unclear>death</unclear>, and near the **rosette** <note>original: "rosetta." This refers to the "bracelets" or horizontal lines found at the base of the palm where it meets the wrist.</note> of the hand, it signifies detriment and misfortune.

The line of the head signifies all things that are in the **outflow** <note>original: "escapo." In this context, it likely refers to the external expression of thoughts or the sensory output of the mind.</note>, and the points made like the letter O signify the eyes. Thus, when such points are in the **descent** of the hand <note>original: "desensio." This refers to the lower or downward-sloping portion of the palm.</note>, they signify detriment and the loss of the eyes, and that location is a place of damage. It is a sign, then, that the power of the eyes is not ready to produce black marks except in a useful place and the brain, and it signifies in this a grave case.

The **ascent** of the hand in the **mount of the thumb** <note>original: "monte del pollice." In chiromancy, this area—often called the Mount of Venus—is traditionally associated with vitality, willpower, and passion.</note> signifies virtue and honor, and the descent of the hand toward the rosette signifies the contrary. Therefore, when lines depart from the line of the heart, if they are ascending, they signify a good <term>complexion</term> <note>original: "complissione." A person's unique physical and mental constitution determined by the balance of bodily fluids (humors).</note> and that nature will help the person to learn and to fulfill whatever they desire; but if they descend, they signify the contrary.

A heart line that is well-proportioned and well-formed is a sign of long life. If the **circle line** <note>original: "linea del cerchio." An archaic term likely referring to a curved line such as the Girdle of Venus or a line associated with the spirit.</note> is thin and short, the power of the circle is weak, and it causes **folly** <note>original: "stoltitia." A lack of wisdom, stupidity, or common sense.</note> and little intellect.

## Of the liver line

### Concerning the Table Line.

The <term>Table Line</term> <note>original: "linea mensale"; in Renaissance chiromancy, this is the uppermost horizontal line of the palm, known today as the Heart Line. It was called "mensal" because it forms the boundary of the "Table of the Hand."</note>, when it is straight, thin, and long, signifies good <term>virtue</term> <note>In this context, "virtue" (uirtù) refers to the body's innate vital power and health.</note> and a healthy disposition of the body, or the contrary when it is poorly formed; this is because this line proceeds from the vital force of the entire body.

The <term>mounts</term> <note>The fleshy cushions at the base of the fingers, believed by chiromancers to correspond to planetary influences and specific parts of the body.</note> of the middle finger and the index finger signify what is "above the head." The descent of the hand <note>The area leading down toward the wrist or the outer edge of the palm.</note> signifies the part pertaining to enemies. Just as those mounts are located in the upper part of the hand, so the head is in the upper part of the body; and enemies are contrary to the honor and exaltation of man, and the descent of the hand or the downward part at the <unclear>base</unclear> <note>original: "asento"; likely referring to the bottom or seat of the palm.</note>—and therefore enemies are read from the lower part of the Table Line where the hand descends.

When, therefore, the Table Line proceeds from the descent of the hand up to the mount of the index finger, placing itself between that and the middle finger, it signifies that enemies will oppose the "head" and the honor of such a man. And just as the mount of the index is divided by such a line, so it signifies that the head will be "divided" and wounded. Wherefore, men who have such a mark must beware of every one of their enemies, because it is very likely that they will be killed and slain by them.

->The Calcination of Silver<-

Take one pound of filed cupelled silver <note>Silver purified in a cupel, a small porous bowl, and then filed into shavings.</note> and three pounds of Spanish mercury <note>Mercury from Spain, particularly from the Almadén mines, was highly valued for its purity in early modern chemistry.</note>. Heat the mercury in a crucible and throw the silver into it, stirring it constantly with a small rod. Once it is well incorporated, throw the whole mixture into a basin of lukewarm water; wash the said amalgam <note>A mixture of mercury with another metal.</note> well with fresh water until the amalgam no longer gives off any blackness <note>This refers to washing away the oxidized impurities that color the water dark.</note>. Afterward, place the amalgam in a cloth and wring it out for the following operation.

Take three parts of prepared common salt and one part of the aforementioned amalgam; incorporate everything well by pulverizing it and grinding it upon a porphyry stone <note>A hard, reddish-purple stone used as a slab for grinding substances into fine powders.</note>. Then, drive off the mercury with flame; if you do not wish to lose the mercury, collect it using a small retort <term>stortina</term> <note>A glass vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distillation and capturing vapors.</note>. Once this is done, let it cool, and throw the silver into a basin of lukewarm water so that the salt is washed away and the clean silver remains at the bottom of the vessel. After drying this silver, you shall amalgamate it once more with mercury as described above, and you shall perform the other operations just as before, up to a total of eight times. By doing this, you will have the said silver calcined <note>Reduced to a fine powder through repeated chemical processing.</note>, and it will have turned into "grass" <note>original: "tornerà per erba"; this likely refers to the silver taking on a fine, perhaps crystalline or filamentous structure, or a specific stage of chemical "growth."</note>. You shall use this silver to convert it into gold as mentioned above.

## Refreshing the liver

Take long corals <note>original: "coralbe," likely referring to white coral, which was ground and used in early modern medicine to treat various ailments.</note>, make a fine paste of them, and lay them out on a plate, and sprinkle sugar <note>original: "succaro"</note> over them, and then leave them in the open air <note>original: "al sereno"; specifically the cool, damp night air.</note> for one night; in the morning you will find that a liquid has formed. ## from the same Geber

It is suitable in many of the modes of preparation; one through calcination <note>The process of heating a substance to high temperatures in air to cause thermal decomposition or oxidation.</note>, another through the ends [purposes] by which it is perfected. From here, the sublimated [substance] is prepared for the cleanest gold through its own making, either in its skin or in its body, such as salts, and alums, or through a bath of <term>quicksilver</term> <note>Mercury; "argentum vivum" in Latin.</note>, whose method of calcination, or through calcinations of reduction, these things are narrated elsewhere, or through solutions and the reductions of that which has been dissolved back to the matter of the body, or it is purified through baths of quicksilver, just as the remaining bodies <note>In alchemy, metals were often referred to as "bodies."</note> diminished from perfection are purified.

The cleansing of Copper <note>original: "Veneris"</note> is twofold: one indeed toward the white [work], the other toward the red. # On the medicine of the sun of the 3rd order.

The medicine of the sun, however, is made from gold that has been dissolved and prepared in the manner of the moon <term>moon: the alchemical name for silver</term>. To this solar material, join 3 parts; of arsenic <term>arsenic: in alchemy, this usually refers to arsenic sulfide, used to "whiten" or "fix" metals</term>, add one and a half parts. Let them be ground with oil of vitriol <term>oil of vitriol: sulfuric acid, a powerful corrosive agent</term> which has been salted with sal ammoniac <term>sal ammoniac: ammonium chloride, used to make metals volatile or to "spirit" them</term>. In the end, add [these] to make everything into a lunar chapter <note>original: "lunari capitulo"; this likely refers to a specific vessel or a final stage in the silver-making process</note>, and it will be a medicine that cures every body <note>the "body" refers to base metals; "curing" them means transmuting them into the "healthy" state of gold</note> and it fixes mercury <note>original: "mercurium"; quicksilver</note> into true gold. Use one part upon six or more, according to the method already described. Read and read again the *Summa of our Perfection* <note>original: "summa perfectionis nostre"; a reference to the *Summa perfectionis magisterii*, the most famous alchemical handbook of the Middle Ages</note> and you will find the method of governance ordained for you, so that you may remain infinitely vigilant if you possess a sharp wit. Do not wander here and there among the various ambiguous sayings of the philosophers, for they all tend toward one perfection; you can experience that which has been sufficiently handed down by us, if you are wise. Farewell; but if you are not [wise], withdraw, because you will only incur loss and emptiness.

# Chapter on Sublimation <note>original: "capitulo sublimationis"</note>

...[the substance's] impression remains in a similar way unless it is fixed <term>fixed: "fixation" is the process of making a volatile substance stable so it no longer evaporates or changes when heated</term>; nor does it shine <note>original: "illustrat"</note> unless the most foul substance is drawn out from it by skillful means, and it is constrained by such heat during its operation. So it stands—or rather, persists—yet in its fixation, caution must be used to soften hard things and harden soft things with this [substance]. It must be known, however, that moisture should be gently balanced with cooling agents, according to the requirements of the fixation being sought.

Through this, it is clear that such a preparation <term>preparation: the initial purification and treatment of a raw alchemical material</term> must be administered, by which the foulest and most impure substance is drawn out of it. Then, let it truly be fixed and caution be applied to them, so that the craftsman may be skilled in managing the fire <term>fire: the primary tool of the alchemist, categorized by intensity (slow, moderate, or intense)</term> during the process of fixation. By this, he can dry out only as much moisture as is necessary to achieve a perfect fixation. Specifically, if any hard bodies are to be softened through this fixation, a gentle fire should be applied at the beginning of their creation. For a slow fire preserves moisture and brings the action to perfection; but if the goal is to harden soft things, the <unclear>opposite</unclear> of it...

### On the purification of quicksilver

<margin>purification of quicksilver</margin>
Quicksilver <term>quicksilver: mercury (argentum vivum). It was considered a "prime matter" of all metals due to its liquid, metallic nature</term> is purified in two ways: either by sublimation or by washing. # On the Calcination <note>original: "calinatione", a variation of *calcinatio*. This refers to heating a substance to high temperatures in the presence of air to transform it into a brittle powder or oxide.</note> of both
## Bodies <note>In alchemy, "bodies" typically refers to the solid metals.</note> and Spirits <note>"Spirits" refers to volatile substances like mercury, sulfur, or arsenic that can "fly" from the fire.</note> with
### their causes and methods.

<margin>Calcination and its cause</margin>
Calcination is the **pulverization** <unclear>puluerizatio</unclear> of a thing by fire through the <unclear>removal</unclear> of humidity and the easy <unclear>consumption</unclear> of moisture. The cause of its invention is so that the burning sulfurousness <term>sulphureitas adustiua: the "combustible sulfur" believed to cause impurities and corrosion in metals</term> may be removed and subsequently destroyed by the fire. It is varied, however, according to the diversity of the things to be calcined. The discovery is that <unclear>in this way</unclear> <note>original: "nemo", likely a transcription error for "modo"</note> one calcines bodies through fire, and they are cleansed for **reduction** <term>reduction: the process of restoring a calcined powder back into its metallic form</term>.

The special calcination of soft bodies <note>This likely refers to metals with low melting points, such as lead or tin.</note> is such that when they are prepared by it and ignited, we find that they <unclear>change</unclear> <note>original: "mouent", literally "move"</note> better.

The cause for the calcination of spirits, however, is so that the **fear** <note>original: "metus". In alchemical literature, the "fear" of a substance often refers to its volatility or its tendency to escape the vessel when heated.</note> of the substances may be broken, and they may be more easily dissolved into water. For every calcined type is more **fixed** <term>fixed: "fixation" is the process of making a volatile substance stable under heat so that it no longer evaporates.</term> than one that is <unclear>un-calcined</unclear>, and it is more easily **dissolved**, because the parts made subtle through fire are more easily <unclear>mixed</unclear> with waters and converted into water.

Calcination of other things serves to prepare them for <unclear>requirements</unclear>; for instance, even **silver** is calcined. However, silver is calcined differently than other bodies, and different bodies are similarly calcined by one another in various ways. **Saturn** <term>Saturn: the alchemical name for lead</term> and **Jupiter** <term>Jupiter: the alchemical name for tin</term> are calcined with fire by removing the <unclear>impurity</unclear>, specifically by a black film being created on the surface until...

# On Dissolution

<margin>
Dissolution, the reason for which
</margin>
Dissolution is the reducing of a dry substance into water. Every dissolution should be performed by its own means using apportioned waters, and especially with those that are sharp and piercing <note>original: "acutis", referring to acidic or corrosive liquids like "strong waters" or vinegar</note>. Because previously no [substance] feels the sharpness of dissolution, I distill [them]; and one is bitter, such as that which often happens from a much-distilled pomegranate <note>original: "mola granata", likely referring to the fruit, often used in alchemical metaphors for its seeds/red juice</note>, and similarly from distilled substances and things similar to these.

<margin>
The reason for its discovery
</margin>
The reason for the discovery <unclear>of this process</unclear> was the refinement <term>subtiliatio: the alchemical process of making a substance thinner, purer, or more "spirit-like"</term> of those things which can neither be melted nor ground, but for which a great dissolution kindly allows the spirit to be unburdened from the constraints of their own nature. For everything that is dissolved must necessarily have the nature of either a salt, an alum <term>alum: a mineral salt used as a reagent and for its astringent properties</term>, or even of animal substances.

However, so that the natures of those things which are to be dissolved may be <unclear>prepared</unclear>,

Therefore, when many substances have lost their own nature but have instead combined with one another, it is necessary that bodies be <unclear>generated</unclear> from that [mixture] and be <unclear>regenerated</unclear> by <unclear>penetration</unclear>.

But this is not achieved except through perfection and brittleness <term>fragilitatem: here referring to a state where the material is purged of its "oily" metallic bonds and is ready to be broken down</term>. 705 Species

<margin>
The method of purification
</margin>
Provided that it can be purified, that which is able to be purified does not necessarily need to be admitted or mixed in order to be calcined <term>calcination: heating a substance to high temperatures to reduce it to a powder</term> or dissolved. For a good result arises from these actions, and once the substances have entered and are fixed <note>original: "fixis", referring to substances that can withstand fire without evaporating</note>, they remain stable.

But what is the method? It is twofold in its form, and this is done with rare, "groaning" water <note>original: "raris gemente aquam"; "groaning" likely refers to the hissing or bubbling sound of the chemical reaction or steam</note>.

The first method is that the calcined material is placed in a glass flask <note>original: "ampulla"</note>, and over it is poured a quantity of distilled vinegar or a sharp, acidic liquid <note>original: "acrimonię"</note>. It should sit in this, and the opening of the flask must be well-sealed, so that the spirit from this hot smoke stays inside and is not released. Afterwards, it must be entirely dissolved through distillation. Let the calcined remains stay at the bottom; let the rest be filtered and flow again in a similar manner until the whole amount has flowed.

But the method by boiling in water is better. It is performed so that the calcined material in the flask is cooked together with vinegar with the opening closed so that it does not escape. For this purpose, the vessels are lowered into a cauldron full of water and cloth <note>original: "stamine"; rags were often used to pad glass vessels in a water bath to prevent breakage</note> <unclear>to be submerged</unclear>, just as we have described in similar methods for boiling. Afterwards, a fire should be lit beneath it until the water has worked through this; then all of it should be distilled, and the calcined material should be boiled in this again and again, and the substance will flow from this sequence.

### On Fixation

<margin>What fixation is</margin>
Fixation is the adaptation of a thing fleeing from the fire <note>referring to volatile substances that evaporate easily</note> to endure its violence. The reason for its invention is so that every tincture <term>tincture: a substance that can infuse or "dye" a base metal with the properties of a noble metal</term> and every alteration may be made permanent in <unclear>whitening</unclear> <note>original: "albatum"; likely referring to 'albedo,' the white stage of the Great Work representing purification</note> and not be changed. These processes are diversified according to the nature of the things to be fixed.

### On Ceration.

<margin>Ceration</margin>
Ceration <term>ceration: from the Latin "cera" (wax); a process of softening a hard substance until it has a wax-like consistency and can melt or flow easily</term> is the softening of a hard thing toward a fusible state for melting.

The reason for its invention was so that what does not receive an impression, nor has liquefaction in the fire <unclear>in amissi</unclear> compared to <unclear>other</unclear> things, might be softened so that it might flow and receive an impression. But some have found that Ceration <insert>by</insert> ought to be done through liquid waters. And that is erroneous.

We, imitating the works of nature, must necessarily proceed in this way. For nature itself "waxes" <note>the text uses "cerat," meaning to treat with wax or make wax-like</note> at the root; it softens the fusible thing with a humidity which, above all other humidities, withstands the heat of the fire; thus it is necessary for us to "wax" with a humidity.

### On the calcination of Mars <note>Mars is the alchemical name for Iron.</note>

### On the calcination of middle minerals

<margin>calcination of middle m[inerals].</margin> All clay vessels, and only three types of minerals, and various other things are calcined with a moderate fire, or by this experimental method of calcining as it appears in the book *On the Magisteries* <note>original: "De Magisterijs"; a common title for alchemical instructional manuals detailing the "mastery" of substances.</note> where it is made manifest; however, the calcination of silver is not done in this same manner.

### On the washings of the calcination of burnt silver

<margin>Washings of the lime of burnt silver.</margin>
Place the material in a large glazed earthen vessel filled with warm fresh water, with which you should wash any <term>lime</term> <note>The powder remaining after a substance is burnt or calcined.</note> of calcined silver by rubbing it with your hand along with salt and <term>alum</term> <note>A mineral salt, usually potassium aluminum sulfate, used as a reagent.</note> and more salt. Then, when the residue has settled, pour off the water carefully so that no silver is lost during the washing. Place the calcined material back into hot water and repeat the process as before until it is thoroughly and perfectly washed and smooth.

## On the reduction of the calx of Mars into a mass.

### ->Concerning the Regimen of This<-

## Concerning the ferment of silver from the pure state.

<margin>ferment of silver to the pure state</margin>
When the silver <note>original: "luna"; literally "the moon," the alchemical name for silver</note> has been dissolved in corrosive aqua regia <note>original: "aqua regia"; "royal water," a powerful acid mixture capable of dissolving noble metals</note> made from vitriol <note>sulfuric acid or sulfates</note> and saltpeter, let the silver be fermented to its pure state <note>original: "azimu"; likely referring to an unleavened or "pure" state</note>. Through this water, let it be dispersed until for a third of the time in the air, or for several days, crystalline stones descend. If you dissolve these again by themselves in the athanor or in the furnace for several days, it will be the oil of silver and the true ferment which serves the white work <note>the "albedo," the second stage of the Great Work producing silver</note>.

## Concerning the ferment of gold for the red work.

<margin>ferment for the red work</margin>
The ferment of gold <note>original: "solis"; literally "the sun," the alchemical name for gold</note> is made thus: when the gold has been dissolved in aqua regia and dried, let the prepared water of the ferment be taken just as with the ferment of silver, and it will be the ferment of gold for the red work <note>original: "ruben"; the "rubedo," the final stage of the Great Work producing the Philosopher's Stone</note>, just as described above.

## Concerning the regimen of Venus and Saturn.

<margin>regimen of ♀ and ♄</margin>
Take three parts of Venus <note>copper, represented by the symbol ♀</note>, two pounds of Saturn <note>lead, represented by the symbol ♄</note>, and one pound of Red Armenian <note>likely Armenian bole, a reddish clay used as a base or catalyst</note>. Let these be optimally distributed and finely ground.

## On the operation of the elements
## Vessels prepared by distillation
### Know this rule regarding the invention of descension.

<margin>Descension <note>original: Descentio; a method of distillation where the vapor or liquid is forced downward rather than upward.</note></margin>
It is one [method] when some <unclear>matter</unclear> has been <unclear>introduced</unclear> into that vessel which we call a <term>descensorium</term> <note>A specialized vessel used for distillation by descent, allowing the refined substance to flow into a receiver placed below the heat source.</note>, then it may descend from the top of the vessels through a <unclear>flame</unclear>, and through its descent, the end of this pure <unclear>work</unclear> may be achieved.

Regarding the bodies of these things, through them—both in those present at the <unclear>opening</unclear> <note>original: hostium; likely 'ostium' meaning a door or opening.</note> and afterward <unclear>moved</unclear> by its <unclear>heat</unclear>—for when we attempt to lead back the bodies from their <unclear>places</unclear> by <unclear>heat</unclear>, we always desire to lead back all that part of the water and that very <unclear>moisture</unclear> which <unclear>was</unclear> first in the natural <unclear>body</unclear>, until it might be <unclear>overcome</unclear>; [otherwise] the greater part of it would vanish through the fire. It becomes necessary for you to invert the <unclear>vessel</unclear> alone when the portion is to be led back, and the <term>dezonated fire</term> <note>original: ignis dezonatus; a technical term likely referring to a fire that is not concentrated in one 'zone' or a fire applied from above rather than below.</note>; this, however, is done by descension.

The reason for its invention is the preservation of the <unclear>parts</unclear> from every foreign thing; for the water descends alone, pure, and leaves every foreign thing behind in those <unclear>vessels</unclear>.

Its form is usually made such that—<unclear>namely</unclear>—the <unclear>rim</unclear> and its walls are equal, standing out with a cavity in the bottom, so that each part might be free.

<margin>13. The operation</margin>
<margin>How many things stand equal in the breadth of the stone</margin>
<margin>The accumulation of stones</margin>
I say, as the Philosopher <note>likely referring to Hermes Trismegistus or Aristotle, the traditional authorities in alchemy</note> is said to say, that our **stone** is composed of three things: from **water**, **spirit**, and **soul**. The **body** is the **white foliated fermented earth** <note>original: "terra alba foliata fermentata"; the purified solid matter processed into thin layers</note> and the **soul**, which nourishes life. It restores [the matter] by the mediation of water, which is called the **spirit**. Therefore, join these three parts together in one, like a **marriage** <note>original: "matrimonialiter"; a "chemical wedding" or union of opposites</note>, upon the stone, keeping the purified substance well and improving it in its nourishment through the smallest parts into a single **confused chaos** <note>original: "chaos confusum"; here meaning a primal, undifferentiated mass where the ingredients are perfectly mixed</note>, so that all things may return as one inseparable body.

Afterward, you should wisely place this into a suitable **flask** <note>original: "phialam"</note>, and return it to its **warm bed** <note>original: "thorum suum calidum"; likely a sand bath or a furnace that provides gentle, steady heat</note>, so that they may <term>coagulate</term> <note>the process of a liquid thickening into a solid</note> and be <term>fixed</term> <note>rendering a substance stable so it does not evaporate or change when exposed to heat</note>, and it may become one **white body**, by which you may most easily produce the **bright stone**.

<margin>Devotion of the stone</margin>
Let us bless <note>original: "Benedicamus"; the author uses religious terminology to describe the ritualistic care given to the chemical process</note> this also more gently in the most pure stone; and likewise, with a third part of its own **water**, you should soak it again and again by <term>imbibing</term> <note>the process of a solid gradually absorbing a liquid</note>, and let it wash all the parts. Again, place it in a well-cleaned, closed vessel in its **tempered place** <note>a place of moderate, regulated heat</note>, and let it settle, and let it begin to dry again. Once the water is drawn off, allow it to be dried immediately in its own **vapors** <unclear>vapors</unclear>, and thus you multiply the free cycles until [you achieve] the most excellent stone.

<meta>This page continues the technical instructions for the final stages of the "White Work." While the previous page described the union of the water, spirit, and soul into a "confused chaos" within a flask, this page explains how to "fix" that substance and then "multiply" its power through repeated cycles of feeding and soaking. This is the transition from the theoretical preparation to the practical application of transmuting base metals into silver.</meta>

<margin>the quality of the stone</margin>
Once you have prepared the **white stone** <note>original: "Lapidem album"; the intermediate goal of the Great Work, used for making silver rather than gold</note> into a fixed state through these repeated steps, it will at last wonderfully enter into other bodies with great speed. It flows like a "fixed water" over the fire, and it overcomes the "Silver of Mercury" <note>original: "Argentum mercurii"; likely referring to quicksilver or a refined metallic base</note> and all other bodies that have strayed from perfection, transforming them into **true silver**.

<margin>repetition of the great work</margin>
And take note: the more quickly and fully this process is repeated—dissolving, enlivening, adhering, and fixing—the more the **medicine** <note>the alchemical elixir or the Stone itself</note> is strengthened and increased through this very repetition.

<margin>multiplication of the medicine</margin>
Its power grows more and more. For every time we pour its own inherent "goodness" back onto the stone through **feeding** <note>original: "cibationem"; the rhythmic process of adding liquid "nourishment" to the dry matter to increase its potency</note>, you will multiply its strength. This is seen when you perform **projection** <note>original: "proiectione"; the final act of casting a small amount of the Stone onto a molten base metal</note> upon bodies that lack perfection. If one part of the medicine is cast in its first stage, it converts ten parts of any metal into **Silver** <note>original: "Luna"; the alchemical name for silver, associated with the Moon</note>. In the second repetition, it converts a thousand parts; in the third, ten thousand; in the fourth, one hundred thousand; in the fifth, a million; and in the sixth, infinite thousands.

Therefore, **repetition** is the great secret of the philosophers. A single **soaking** <note>original: "imbibitio"</note> would be sufficient <unclear>if</unclear> they did not repeat the work until its power reached its peak.

<margin>17. operation for the red [work]</margin>
If, therefore, you wish to convert this glorious **White Kingly Stone** <note>original: "lapidem regem album"; the result of the previous stage of the Great Work, capable of making silver</note>—which transforms and tinges <note>original: "tingit"; colors or permeates through its essence</note> mercury and all imperfect bodies into true **silver** <note>original: "lunificam"; silver-making</note>—into the **Red Stone**, so that it may become an **elixir** and a **tincture of redness**, which transforms and tinges mercury, silver, and every metal into the truest **gold** <note>original: "solem"; literally the sun</note>, proceed as follows.

<margin>the stone for redness</margin>
Take the white stone itself and divide it into two parts. You shall increase one part into the **white elixir** as was previously described, using the regenerated **white living water** <note>original: "aqua viua regenerata alba"; a purified alchemical solvent or spirit</note> which never leaves its side. But place the other part into a new **prophetic throne** <note>original: "thronum prophoticum"; a symbolic term for a clean, clear, and round glass alchemical vessel</note> that is clean, sound, bright, and round. Place it thus into the **furnace of divine digestion** <note>original: "furnum diuinae digestionis"; a kiln or heat source used for slow, steady ripening of the matter</note> and increase the heat of the fire gradually. Continue until, by the force and power of the fire of digestion, it is converted into a most rich **Red Stone**. Among the <margin>digestion</margin> **philosophers** <note>historical alchemists</note>, this stone is called "bloody," the "purple dawn," "red coral," and **red sulfur**.

Then take this **Joyful and Fervent King** <note>original: "Regem gaudentem et feruentem"; an allegorical name for the Stone in its active, high-heat state</note> carefully and pulverize it so that it becomes a red powder of redness, transforming and tinging <term>mercury</term> <note>quicksilver</note>, <term>silver</term> <note>original: "luna"; the moon</note>, and every body into the truest **Gold** <note>original: "Solem"; the sun</note>. From this point, it is necessary to **ferment** <note>original: "fermentare"; the final stage where the stone is stabilized and "ennobled" by being joined with a small amount of the actual metal it is intended to create</note> three parts of this substance with one and a half parts of the purest gold.

...of the purest substance let it be prepared, so that here, by the most subtle and sharpest spirit <note>original: "acerrissima"; likely referring to a strong corrosive or a highly active "mercurial" fire</note>, with two portions of water artificially "solified" <note>original: "aquae solificatae"; water that has been endowed with the qualities of the Sun or gold</note>, it is reduced into a single **chaos** <note>the "chaos" refers to the prime matter in a state of dissolution, where its old forms are broken down to be reborn</note> by a thorough mixing of the smallest parts until the fourth burning. <margin>And mercury dissolved by the sun and from gold.</margin>

—cleanses one hundred parts of mercury. When placed with salt, as you know, in a crucible over a small fire, the red stone or silver <note>original: "lune"; literally the moon</note> may be immediately tinged into the most true gold <note>original: "solem"; literally the sun</note>, better than any natural gold. And thus you shall persist in the repetition of the Stone, discovering how mercury and silver themselves are declared to be turned into gold <note>original: "solificari"</note> infinitely.

# At Padua, a wonder, a marvelous discovery of the alchemical art
<note>original: "Patavij"; the Latin name for the city of Padua, a major center of learning and site of this famous legend.</note>

A clay urn was here, decorated with verses.

> Thieves, do not touch this gift sacred to Pluto; <note>The Roman god of the underworld, associated by alchemists with the treasures and secret fires hidden within the earth.</note>
> That which lies hidden in this urn is unknown to you.
> For the great Olibius enclosed the elements, arranged with heavy labor,
> Within these modest vessels. <note>original: "Vasa sub hoc modico"; referring to the containers holding the secret alchemical substances.</note>
> May Abundance herself be present as a guardian with a fruitful horn,
> Lest the value of such a great treasure be lost.

Inside this large urn was another smaller one; when it was opened, two vials were found, skillfully crafted—one of silver, the other of purest gold—filled with a certain liquid, by which it is thought a lamp was preserved, still burning while <unclear>enclosed</unclear>. Inscribed upon them were these verses:

> Depart from here, you wicked thieves!
> What do you want with your prying eyes?
> Depart from here with your mercury; <note>A double meaning: Mercury was the god of thieves, but also the primary substance alchemists sought to "fix" into a solid, non-volatile state.</note> go about your business.
> Maximus makes this sacred gift to the greatest Pluto.

## The True Practice of Ortulanus
<note>original: "Practica vera Ortulani"; Ortulanus, or "The Gardener," was a famous pseudonym for a 14th-century alchemist credited with explaining the Emerald Tablet. His "practice" focuses on the physical laboratory work required to produce the Stone.</note>

<margin>Vitriol, saltpeter, and cinnabar in the preparation of the stone.</margin>
<note>Vitriol (sulfates), saltpeter (potassium nitrate), and cinnabar (mercury sulfide) were the foundational "spirits" of the laboratory, used to create the acidic waters needed for transmutation.</note>

Take 12 ounces of chosen vitriol, and of rock salt and cinnabar **three parts of each**; let them all be ground together intimately <unclear>non ronae</unclear>. Let them be ground as finely as possible and then placed in a urinal <note>A common glass vessel named for its shape, used for observation and distillation.</note> or a glass cucurbit <term>cucurbit: the lower, gourd-shaped part of a still where the matter is heated.</term> well-sealed with lute. Let the alembic <term>alembic: the "head" or cap of the still that collects and cools the vapors.</term> be placed on top and well-sealed around the joints, so that no breath of the matter itself may evaporate. Let the cucurbit be placed among the ashes to the thickness of one finger on all sides. 

Let a slow fire be made <unclear>lepay</unclear> for 6 or 8 hours, so that the phlegmatic water <note>original: "aqua flegmatica"; the first, weak, watery liquid that boils off before the potent acids appear.</note> may come out, and let it remain there until it begins to drop before it is collected. There is a certain sign to know when the phlegmatic water has finished exiting: a man should place a slightly heated knife under the nose of the alembic and wait until a single drop falls upon the knife. If the drop boils and turns black, then the phlegmatic water has departed and its stage is ended, and the water that follows is to be collected. 

But if this does not happen yet, one must wait until it reaches that state; and afterward, all this pure water is to be received in a clean receiver <note>original: "receptaculum"; the vessel at the end of the still that catches the distillate.</note>. Take great care that the receiver is well-fitted to the nose of the alembic and sealed, and then strengthen the fire moderately and properly until the alembic...

### Regulus of antimony
<note>A "regulus" (meaning "little king") is the pure metallic mass found at the bottom of a crucible after a mineral ore has been smelted. In this period, the regulus of antimony was highly prized for its star-like crystalline pattern.</note>

<margin>Composition of antimony</margin>
Take crude antimony and <term>tartar</term> <note>Tartar is the potassium-rich crust found in wine barrels, used here as a flux to help the metal melt and separate from impurities.</note>—one pound of each. In a new crucible on the first furnace, let them be incorporated. When the crucible is glowing red-hot, throw the aforementioned substances in powder form inside, a little at a time, into the charcoal. Place an iron rod inside—that is, after it has all joined together with the smoke in such a <unclear>way</unclear>—and when the smoke coming out of it <unclear>ceases</unclear>, you will see the black [surface]. Then you shall remove the molten material—may it be <unclear>molten</unclear>—and you will find the regulus at the bottom.

### To make oil of tartar

<margin>How oil of tartar is made.</margin>
Take the whitest <term>tartar of wine</term>. Let it be <term>calcined</term> <note>To calcine is to heat a substance to high temperatures until it reduces to a dry powder or ash.</note> in a sack in a <term>reverberatory furnace</term> <note>A furnace that reflects heat from the roof onto the material, preventing direct contact with the fuel.</note> for ten hours. Afterward, let it be pulverized and placed upon a marble slab to dissolve in a cold and humid place. <note>"Oil of tartar" is not actually an oil, but a concentrated liquid formed when the dry salt (potassium carbonate) absorbs enough moisture from the air to turn into a liquid—a process called deliquescence.</note>

# Concerning the Heart Line <note>original: "Della linea mensale." In traditional palmistry, this is the "mensal" or "table" line, known today as the Heart Line.</note>

This is because Mars governs the gall and the choleric humor within the human body. When the extension of the **Heart Line** is moderate and average, it signifies that it was formed by a natural and balanced heat. However, when the extension of the said line is excessive and ends where it should not, it signifies that it was produced by a surplus of heat. The Heart Line should begin beneath the **mount of the index finger** and encircle all the mounts of the fingers; but it must begin so that it falls upon the **Mount of Jupiter** <term>Jupiter: in chiromancy, the Mount of Jupiter is the fleshy area at the base of the index finger, representing authority and benevolence</term> if the line is delicate. When the lines of the hand are not well-proportioned according to natural measure, it is a sign of weakness and an inability of natural heat, as well as an abundance of preternatural heat. When the **Heart Line** ends and then departs from its conclusion to extend toward the **Head Line** <note>original: "linea del capo." ## There are eight operations

1st. is sublimation <term>sublimation: an alchemical process where a solid substance is heated until it turns into vapor and then solidifies again, used to purify the material.</term>
2nd. is distillation <term>distillation: the process of heating a liquid to create vapor and then cooling that vapor to collect it in a purified liquid form.</term>
3rd. is calcination <term>calcination: the application of high heat to a substance to reduce it to a dry powder or "calx."</term>
4th. is solution <term>solution: the process of dissolving a solid substance into a liquid solvent.</term>
5th. is coagulation <note>This entry is obscured by a large ink blot; coagulation refers to the thickening or solidifying of a liquid.</note>
6th. is <unclear>fixation</unclear> <note>original: "fixio"; the process by which a volatile substance is made stable and resistant to heat.</note>
7. Ceration <term>ceration: the process of adding a liquid to a hard substance to soften it until it reaches a consistency like wax.</term>
8. Reduction <term>reduction: the process of restoring a substance (often a metal) to its original state or form.</term>

<gloss>There are eight operations: sublimation, distillation, calcination, solution, coagulation, fixation, ceration, and reduction.</gloss>

<margin>Preparation of silver <note>The text here refers to the preparation of base metals in general, though the margin notes silver specifically.</note></margin> Imperfect bodies <note>In alchemy, metals like lead, tin, or copper were considered "imperfect" versions of gold.</note> possess such a superfluous mass that it does not allow for their entry into the process of mixing within themselves for the generation of gold itself—they retain a corruptible end that hinders both their inward movement and their action.

Because of this, the superfluity must be removed by these arts that find them in their roots. Because the defect is accidental <term>accidental: in alchemical philosophy, a quality that is not part of the essential nature of a metal (like tarnish) and can therefore be removed</term>, it is possible for us, and necessary, to remove this with fire. By cleansing the superfluities, we strip away these accidental qualities so that only the substance of the quicksilver <term>quicksilver: original "argenti vivi"; mercury, considered one of the two primary roots of all metals</term> and the sulfur of the root remain.

And this is the complete preparation for the imperfect [bodies] and their perfect purification.

Sublimation, it must be noted, should be performed with the <term>flowers of metals <note>original: "floribus metallorum"; the fine, powdery substance—often an oxide—that rises and collects at the top of a vessel during heating.</note></term> and their <term>calxes <note>original: "calcibus"; the dry, crumbly powder left after a metal has been thoroughly burnt or oxidized.</note></term>, since the operation of sublimation is easy in those things. That which is indeed sublimated without flowers or without the calxes of the bodies occurs in great quantity. That which is indeed done with flowers works a <unclear>union</unclear> through <unclear>sublimation</unclear> without powder, so that it may show the whole substance ignited without any <term>soul <note>original: "anima"; the vital or volatile principle that alchemists believed could be separated from the "body" of a mineral.</note></term> remaining, yet [joined] with the whole substance.

<summary>This page explains the chemical affinity between substances during sublimation, specifically comparing sulfur and arsenic. It emphasizes that for a successful alchemical union, one should use the "flowers" and "calxes" of metals rather than the raw bodies.</summary>

<page-num>831</page-num>
<page-type>text</page-type>
<warning>Institutional stamps from the Biblioteca Apostolica Vaticana and a "RESERVED" mark are present on the page, occasionally overlaying the text on the left margin.</warning>

The fire should not drive everything out from the spirit so that all escapes, but it should prepare it, and [maintain] its <gloss>continuity in the matter</gloss>. This is our [fire] of resolution—for it was possible, because the spirit must be preserved from them. They foster the <term>sublimation <note>The process of heating a solid substance until it turns into vapor and then cooling it back into a purified solid, leaving impurities behind.</note></term> gradually throughout the whole process, which must be observed in many other matters.

The established proportion is such that it follows the quantity of things to be sublimated. However, the practice of the craft can act upon even the smallest things. For the smaller the things are in quantity, the greater and swifter the sublimation will be. In the world, and according to the various examinations, this rule of proportion is established there for <term>distillation <note>The process of purifying a liquid by heating it into vapor and then condensing it back into a liquid.</note></term>. For in a small quantity, a small fire is drawn forth for perfection; in a large quantity, a large fire; and in a greater quantity, a greater fire.

<margin>moderate fire</margin>
But because fire cannot be [precisely] measured, even wise men happen to err in this when they have little experience with them.
<margin>moderate fire</margin>
And the common rule is that in the beginning there should be a small fire, expressing only the wateriness; because once the water that ascends by that fire is removed, the fire should not be increased from the start. Through the weakest fire, the weakest part <unclear>prevails</unclear> and is placed above, which is the cause of adaptation. However, when nothing or very little ascends, the fire should be increased <unclear>over the white</unclear> and a red fire will be seen, just as <term>Geber <note>original: "Geber"; the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, a 13th-century author (or group of authors) whose works were the most influential alchemical texts in Europe.</note></term> says in Book 4, Chapter 42 of the <unclear>Summa Perfectionis</unclear> <note>original: "summa perfecti"; referring to the "Summa perfectionis magisterii" (The Height of the Perfection of Mastery), a foundational medieval alchemical textbook.</note>.

Indeed, the better method of fire is like the breath of iron or its <unclear>combustion</unclear>, and this is easy to complete, and its essence may be <unclear>changed</unclear>.

If **gold** <note>original: ☉</note> and **silver** <note>original: ☽</note> are melted together and remain, add to them earth, and as much **sublimate** <note>original: Solimato; corrosive sublimate or mercuric chloride, used as a powerful reagent</note> as the three weigh together. <meta>This page shifts from the practical laboratory refining of the previous page to the theoretical and ethical foundations of the 'Hermetic' art. # On the Hermetic Secret of Philosophy.

->Canon 1<-

1. The beginning of this art is the fear of the Lord; its end is charity toward one’s neighbor. <note>A classic alchemical framing where the pursuit of the 'Great Work' is presented as a spiritual journey requiring divine favor and ethical purpose.</note>
2. Love for the supreme Lord is the leader of the **tincture** <note>original: tincturae; the transformative substance or elixir</note>.
3. The most profound knowledge of the art is divine nature, which concerns itself with the kingdom of metals.
<margin>Note whether the principle of metals must know perfection.</margin>
Let its practice shine in the principles of metals, or let them be engaged in works far more perfect than those performed before.
4. This art requires a skillful man, free from any other business whatsoever.
5. Let the student of this art be solitary, calm, and humble.
6. Sublimations, distillations, solutions, congelations, exhalations, and concoctions—the **operations of the spirits** <note>original: Operationes spirituum; likely referring to volatile substances like mercury or sulfur, though the author suggests these common chemical processes are "to be rejected" in favor of a deeper philosophy</note>—are to be rejected.
7. Let him reflect on the **cardinal arts** in the choir of philosophers. F.
<margin>† This shows in what way they all mostly agree.</margin>
8. Let him beware the reading of false philosophers.
9. Let him study a few but learned authors. Let him hold easily understood things in suspense, for truth lies hidden in obscure things. Whence **Geber** <note>A foundational 8th-century chemist/alchemist</note> says: "Where we speak more openly to the chemists, there we have hidden the art." Nor is it true how obscurely the philosophers write. <note>The author suggests that when alchemical writers seem clear, they are being deceptive, and when they are obscure, they are being honest.</note>
10. For us, the primary authors should all be **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary father of alchemy</note> and **Morienus** <note>A legendary 7th-century hermit and alchemical teacher</note>.
<margin>† Likewise, from which [work] of the philosophers.</margin>
11. **Count Trevisan** <note>Bernard Trevisan, a 15th-century seeker</note> and **Ramon Lull** <note>A 13th-century philosopher to whom many alchemical works were attributed</note> published his transition just as those who lead the way, who wrote of the **first water of the philosophers**, about which the noble Pole **Dionysius** <note>Michael Sendivogius, author of "A New Chemical Light" (1604)</note> wrote in his *New Chemical Light*, and also for us in his *Treatise on Sulfur*.
12. They express their philosophy better through icons and enigmatic figures, as in the table of **Senior** <note>The Arabic alchemist Zadith ben Hamuel</note>, the allegorical pictures of the *Rosarium*, the riddle of Aristotle in the diagrams of **Flamel** <note>Nicolas Flamel</note>, and the emblem of **Michael Maier** <note>Author of "Atalanta Fugiens," famous for its alchemical illustrations</note>.
13. That the **philosophers' stone** is one.
15. <note>The source skips number 14</note> One must beware lest force be applied to things in a manifold way. And the philosophers hide their mysteries there. He who has done everything, let him always praise [them] obscurely, as if in shadows.
16. From metals, metallic things proceed, just as human seed proceeds from a human.
17. Metals are not multiplied by the instinct and labor of nature alone; but by the help of the art, the power of multiplying, hidden in the depths, is manifested.

### Sulfur
What it is, is well known to the novice: for it is hot and dry, containing natural fire within itself, and this is called the heat of fire. When from here the Sun <unclear>reaches</unclear> the degree of **Cancer**, it emits much vapor, for it is seen in its "tender limbs"—as the saying goes—but then, behold, a **snowy light** <note>this signifies the *albedo* or whitening stage</note> appears, while the **Moon** sits and reigns in the glory of her own house <note>In astrology, the Moon "rules" or has her "house" in the sign of Cancer</note>.

In **Leo**, where the Sun reigns, through the Sun—which ends in **Libra**—a **red color** <note>the *rubedo*, the final stage of the alchemical process</note> mixed in appearance is determined through the degrees which represent the two signs of **Scorpio** and **Sagittarius**, marking the completion of the **elixir** <term>Elixir: Here refers to the "Red Elixir" or "Philosopher's Stone" in its final, most potent state</term>. And so, O friend, while **Jupiter** is reigning—truly under Jupiter’s reign—it reaches its end and total conclusion through the Sun, which they call **Chrysocolla** <note>original: *Chrysocolam*; literally "gold-glue," used here to describe a substance that "fixes" or perfects the gold</note>. <unclear>See below, etc.</unclear>

# How metals are reduced into water.

Take **Lime of the Sun** <note>original: *Calce di sole*; refers to Gold that has been chemically reduced to a powder (calx)</note> or indeed **Lime of the Moon** <note>original: *Calce di luna*; refers to Silver powder</note> and **sal ammoniac** <note>original: *sale armoniaco*; ammonium chloride, a vital salt in alchemy used for sublimation and dissolving metals</note> sublimated, in equal parts. Grind everything together upon a **porphyry** <note>original: *porfido*; a hard igneous stone used as a flat slab for grinding medicinal or alchemical substances</note> stone; then you shall sublimate the sal ammoniac from the lime of the bodies <note>alchemical "bodies" are the solid metals</note>, repeating the sublimation seven times. Once sublimated <unclear>which</unclear>, you shall then place it upon the stone to dissolve. Some note that they sublimate the matter together, <unclear>sprinkling it</unclear> with **borax water** <unclear>distilled</unclear> seven times.

->Likewise<-

Take the calcined bodies with an equal weight of sal ammoniac and **lime of eggshell** <note>original: *calce di uivo d'ouo*; likely quicklime made from burned eggshells, used as a caustic or drying agent</note>, and place them in a glass vessel over a slow fire until the whole makes a mass. Let it cool, and break <unclear>the egg-shaped vessel</unclear>, and reduce the matter to powder in a place of <term>resolution</term> <note>the process of dissolving a solid into a liquid state</note>.

With "cotton water" <note>original: *acqua di cottone*; identity uncertain, possibly a specific distilled vinegar or herbal water</note> dissolve the sublimated spirits into water. **Water of marble** <unclear>overwrites</unclear> the smoke, but when you wish to reduce them into a body <note>to return the liquid back into a solid metal</note>, **evaporate** that water over a slow fire, or melt it with <term>tartruca</term> <note>original: *tartruca*; likely a derivative of "tartar" (potassium bitartrate) used as a flux in melting</note>. Gold calcined with salt, with <term>aqua fortis</term> <note>Nitric acid; literally "strong water"</note>, dissolves into <unclear>red</unclear> water.

## Transmuting Silver (☽) into Gold (☉)

Take calcined Sun [gold] <unclear>2 grains</unclear>, roasted copper, and <term>crocus</term> of iron <note>original: *croco di ferro*; iron oxide or rust, used for its red pigment and perceived solar qualities</note>, 1 grain each; calcined sal ammoniac, 3 grains; sublimated <unclear>vitriol</unclear> <note>OCR: *nitriolo*; almost certainly *vitriolo* or vitriol (sulfates)</note>, 1 grain. Powder them in such a manner, and when <unclear>oil/air</unclear> is dissolved in it, mix the said powders upon the porphyry. And when the said powders have soaked up all the water of the salt, place the whole in a glass vessel that has a long neck under the smoke <note>likely referring to a heat source or a furnace's vapor</note> for 24 days, renewing the smoke every day.

# Quince Paste in the Portuguese Style.

They should be gathered when well-matured without bruising them; once they are well-cleaned and prepared, they are put to boil with the peel without cutting them until they are cooked, which is known by touch and by the cracking of the skin.

Afterwards, they are taken out and the skin is removed instead, and they are left upon a cloth to cool.

This done, the seeds <note>original: *ossi*; literally "bones," referring to the pips or core</note> and the tough parts are removed, and one takes that pulp which is cooked, working it until it becomes like an ointment <note>meaning a smooth, uniform paste</note>, and of this, one shall take ten pounds.

It is necessary to take ten pounds of sugar and put it to boil, and skim it, and boil it until it acquires a consistency as if one were making <term>marzapane</term> <note>marzipan; here referring to the "hard ball" or "crack" stage of sugar syrup used for almond pastes</note>.

Then <unclear>one must</unclear> throw into it the above-mentioned mass of quinces, and with a ladle or a spatula, keep it moving so that it combines and does not burn at the bottom of the pot or pan.

When <unclear>it nears</unclear> taking the form <unclear>of a hard paste</unclear>, then it is removed from the fire and it will be done.

# Cinnabar

To make white common salt, take as much anobbi <note>an alchemical term, possibly referring to a purified mineral or a specific form of antimony</note>: or for two pounds of *p d'arco* <note>possibly litharge or a specific crystalline form</note>: boil the vinegar, and when the process is finished, the whole is well-incorporated and placed in a vessel; let the vinegar be distilled off by a <term>water bath</term> <note>original: *bagnam:* abbreviated for *balneum mariae*</note>. You shall do this for one or three days—every day if you wish to do it three times—for excellence: the one that is better, and this is returned as "made water" <note>original: *aqua factosa*</note> which has been collected. This is placed in a rich vessel and washed; then take an ounce of anobbi in an ounce of *amine* <note>potentially a chemical amine or a specific spirit</note> and as much starch as there is anobbi, which is placed upon marble, heating it with water. Do this four times to turn it into powder; place it in a flask, and over it put enough water so that it rises by two fingers. Place it on a stove and give it the flame of a lamp with two wicks, from six in the morning until the excess is driven out. Then put it in a flask with its water that covers it; let it be served for one day so that nothing remains; put it back in a hot furnace for two days, or one day, or nine in this manner, until the water is filled so that the water remains very white. This is to be distilled for the vinegar <note>original: *acco*, abbreviation for *aceto*</note> once, then having made two or three waters, this results in the most excellent shiny white powder. Dry it, and you will have an excellent white like snow. One way for two ounces of purified gold; you will have made it with every judgment, and of this for the life of Antuono <note>possibly a reference to a specific practitioner or patron</note>.

# Fixation D.

Fixation D. Take ground <term>vine-cuttings</term> <note>original: "sarmenti," the slender branches of a grapevine</note>, and wood from the <term>canopy</term> <note>original: "capellonata," likely referring to the overgrown or "hairy" branches of the vine</note>; place them over the fire in a clean vessel. Add a little <term>lime</term> <note>quicklime</note> that is very strong for one hour, and let it settle, so that the <term>lye</term> is always at the top. After an hour has passed, take that <unclear>lye</unclear>, and join it to the powder for another hour, and so on until the third time. Let the substance <note>The letter "D" likely serves as a shorthand for the substance being treated</note> cool, and the <term>result</term> <note>original: "rispondenza," the chemical reaction or yield</note> will be achieved.

---

# Fixation 4

Fixation 4. Take the juice of honey, <unclear>pennacer</unclear> of herbs, or of wood; put inside crushed <unclear>zagme</unclear>. This removes the <term>stench</term> <note>original: "thidore," a dialect variant of "fetore," referring to the foul smell of alchemical ingredients like sulfur</note>, and with <term>saffron</term> <note>original: "saprana," a corruption of "zafferano"</note> the <unclear>color</unclear> is given to it, and the stench is removed if it is thrown inside several times.

# How to make strong vinegar

Take <term>ashes of lees</term> <note>original: "cener di fecie," the burnt sediment of wine, rich in potassium carbonate</note>, and boil a little strong vinegar. Put those ashes of lees into a small bag shaped like the <term>pointed foot of a jar</term> <note>original: "piede d'olla fitta," a conical filter bag</note>, and pour that hot water <note>or hot vinegar</note> over it. Let it strain, and put the strained liquid into the vinegar, which will then become extremely strong.

## Preparation of the Master Powder

Let these things be reduced to a very fine powder, each one individually; then, pass them all together through a <unclear>fine</unclear> sieve, and keep this powder for this master work.

Take a <unclear>glazed</unclear> <note>original: "vernata"; referring to a ceramic glaze used to prevent the porous clay vessel from absorbing the chemical materials.</note> earthenware pan, or one of other well-fired clay, not very large and about a finger-breadth high around the edges. Place it upon a low tripod over well-lit coals. Spread all the aforementioned powder within it, and when it begins to smoke, keep turning it here and there, always spreading it out. In this way, continue stirring it until no smoke of any kind is seen rising from it. When this is <unclear>seen</unclear>, remove it from the fire and let the whole thing cool well, taking care to provide a moderate fire so that the materials do not <unclear>clump together</unclear> <note>original: "rupinare"; likely meaning to fuse, scorch, or cake into a hard mass rather than remaining a dry powder.</note>, but rather to dry it out thoroughly.

<margin>Continue in a similar fashion.</margin>

Take silver of the kind that is purified on a copper plate <note>original: "ramina"; a copper vessel or tool used in the refining process.</note>; set it to be drawn out <note>likely referring to "drawing" the metal into wire or thin strips to increase its surface area.</note>, and after this, let it be cut into small pieces. With <unclear>rough</unclear> pincers, secure the pieces and arrange everything **SSS** <note>An abbreviation for the Latin *stratum super stratum*, meaning "layer upon layer." This is a standard alchemical and metallurgical technique where metal sheets or pieces are layered alternately with powdered chemical reagents to ensure an even reaction.</note> as is customary in a clean **crucible** <term>A vessel made of ceramic or graphite that can withstand very high temperatures, used for melting metals or performing chemical reactions.</term> which has been sealed with luting <note>original: "luti"; a clay-based paste used to seal the joints of vessels to make them airtight or protect them from direct flame.</note> on the outside. Let it remain for some time in the midst of a moderate charcoal fire, and let it be tied or sealed across the top, ensuring it is done well; then remove it and let the whole thing cool.
