## Sublimation of the first Saffron

Take our first **Saffron** and an equal weight of salt, first prepared, which is to be ground with our **Saffron**. Place its body in a flask <note>original: "boccia." A round-bottomed glass vessel used for heating and distilling.</note> to be sublimated <note>Sublimation is the process where a solid turns into vapor when heated and then solidifies again on a cooler surface, used here to purify the substance.</note>. When the sublimation is finished, it should be removed from the fire and allowed to cool; then grind the sublimated body again, and afterward the **dead head** <note>original: "capo morte." Also known as *caput mortuum*, this is the useless residue or dregs left at the bottom of a flask after distillation or sublimation.</note>—or let us say the residue—since they mix together. Return it to the same flask to sublimate again, and this order shall be followed 4 times. The last time, set aside the sublimate in clean paper, keeping the flask in a safe place with the **dead head**.

## Sublimation of the second Saffron

Take our second **Saffron** and **equal parts** <note>original: "ana." A traditional medical and alchemical term indicating equal quantities of each ingredient.</note> of **common sublimate** <note>original: "sublimato comune." Usually refers to corrosive sublimate (mercury chloride), a frequent reagent in alchemical processes.</note> of the beautiful and shiny kind. Grind them together upon the porphyry <note>A hard igneous rock used as a slab for grinding chemicals and pigments.</note>, then in a flask that is not very large and has a long neck, its sublimation shall be performed. When completed, grind it every time, and put it back to sublimate again; this order shall be followed six times.

## How to extract the salts from the said Saffrons.

Take the aforesaid **Saffrons** <note>original: "crochi." Fine metallic powders, usually oxides, named for their saffron-like color.</note> and grind them upon the **porphyry** <note>original: "porfido." A hard stone slab used by alchemists and painters to grind materials into an extremely fine powder.</note> little by little together until they become almost impalpable to the touch. Afterward, take a clean glass **vessel** <note>original: "urinale." While the word literally means "urinal," in an alchemical context it refers to a rounded glass vessel with a wide neck used for digestion and extraction.</note> and place them inside. Pour over them enough **distilled vinegar** so that it stands a finger’s width above the powder. Then, with a clean white rod, stir everything well for some time. Afterward, let it all rest, covered with white paper, throughout the following day and night. The next morning, take the vessel again and gently decant <note>To "decant" means to pour off the top liquid while leaving the sediment at the bottom undisturbed.</note> all the colored vinegar into another similar clean vessel, covering it with white paper and setting it aside. Over the first vessel, where the Saffrons remained, pour more distilled vinegar, but much less—it is enough that it stands three fingers above—and stir once again

### To fix sulfur.

Take three ounces of <term>flowers of sulfur</term> <note>fine powder produced by heating sulfur until it becomes a vapor and then solidifies</note>, nine ounces of <term>salt of tartar</term> <note>potassium carbonate, a common alchemical salt</note>; put it all into a <term>glass urinal</term> <note>a round-bottomed glass flask with a long neck, named for its resemblance to a medical vessel</note>, pour in enough water so that it rises a palm's width above the contents; place the vessel over a <term>sand fire</term> <note>a sand bath, which provides gentle, even heat</note> for 24 hours. The water will become red; cause everything to <unclear>evaporate</unclear> <note>original: svaporare</note> <unclear>until</unclear> <note>original: finché</note> it is dry, then pour fresh water over it; the water will dissolve the salt of tartar; decant the water, and you will find the fixed sulfur at the bottom of the vessel; dry it over a slow fire, and you will have <term>fixed sulfur</term> <note>sulfur that has been chemically altered so it no longer evaporates or "flies" when heated</note>.

---

### Fixation of <term>mercury</term> <note>represented by the symbol ☿</note>, which does not <unclear>sublime</unclear> <note>original: muove; likely referring to the "movement" or volatility of the metal during heating</note>

Place the <term>mercury</term> <note>☿</note> into <term>aqua forte</term> <note>nitric acid, a powerful solvent</note> so that it dissolves; then evaporate the liquid, and a <term>precipitate</term> <note>a solid residue left after a chemical reaction</note> will remain at the bottom; then place a little <term>oil of tartar</term> <note>a concentrated, oily solution of potassium carbonate</note> over it until it becomes like <term>lime</term> <note>original: calce; meaning a metallic oxide or "calx"</note>, and it will <unclear>never</unclear> <note>original: mai</note> sublime again.

# Easy rule for tuning
## a harpsichord by means
## of the guitar

First tune the middle of the <term>harpsichord</term> <note>original: cimbalo; a general term for a harpsichord or similar plucked keyboard instrument</note> and then tune the rest as follows. That is:

1st. <unclear>the bottom of the key is tuned with</unclear> that is the harpsichord to the first <unclear>bass of the harpsichord with the first string</unclear> <note>presumably the first string of the guitar</note>.
2. with the 2nd string of the guitar <term>fretted</term> <note>original: tastata; pressing the string down against a fret to change its pitch</note> at the 2nd fret.
3. the bass of the harpsichord with the 3rd string of the guitar.
4. the fourth [note] with the first [string] <term>unfretted</term> <note>original: non tastata; an "open" string played without pressing down on any frets</note>.
5. the fifth [note] with the first [string] fretted at the 2nd fret.
6. with the first string fretted at the 3rd bass <note>this may refer to the third bass note of the harpsichord sequence or a specific position</note> that is with the <term>treble string</term> <note>original: cantino; the highest-pitched string of the guitar</note> which corresponds to the first [string] unfretted with [at] the fret.
7. with the 2nd [note], the 2nd string unfretted.
8. with the same [string] fretted at the 2nd fret.

Afterwards, the ninth bass is tuned, which should be tuned with the 8th <term>octave</term> below, and so on step-by-step until the end.

The <term>black keys</term> <note>original: neri; the sharps and flats of the keyboard</note> remain: the 1st is tuned with the 7th, but with the bass of the 7th; the 2nd with the 8th; the 3rd...

# Elixir of the Moons which
->one part goes over 3 ounces<-
->of silver and remains pure<-

## Take 3 ounces of calcinated silver, which will be calcinated by remaining
<margin>calcinated in several ways</margin>
The way to prepare it for that most noble tincture of gold is this, namely: **1st method**
The ounce is calcinated by rolling it into thin sheets and cutting it into small pieces; and one should make <term>sss.</term> <note>original: stratum super stratum; a Latin phrase meaning "layer upon layer"</note> with such a prepared composition in a small pan, and in the middle making a small hole, putting it all in the <term>cementation fire</term> <note>a process of heating a metal with other substances to purify or change it</note> to temper for 12 hours.

## 2nd method
It is done by taking <term>aqua forte</term> <note>original: acqua forte; literally "strong water," the historical name for nitric acid</note>, that is 3 ounces for every 1 ounce [of silver]. Cast it into a basin and cut it [the silver] minutely, and let it be "eaten" <note>an alchemical term for dissolution in acid</note> by the said water; and putting the vial in the chimney, the <term>calx</term> <note>original: calce; the powdery metallic residue or oxide left after heating or acid treatment</note> will go to the bottom; and seeing that the <term>effervescence</term> <note>original: frigidezze; literally "coldnesses," referring here to the bubbling reaction of the acid</note> ceases, immediately give it a glass of fresh water, and you will see all the calcinated silver fall to the bottom.

## 3rd method
It is calcinated with the smoke of <term>antimony</term> <note>original symbol: ♁</note> or of quicklime. It is placed in a <unclear>crucible</unclear> over the lit ashes and the silver is given [to the mixture] to be "eaten," and after the process for calcinating it, the <unclear>rest</unclear> of the silver will remain in the calcination.

The said calx should be washed with distilled well water, and let it be added [dried] in the sun or on hot ashes.

# The Soul of Venus for the work.

Take several pounds of **copper**, beaten fresh into **thin sheets**; for every pound of copper, take an equal weight of **steel** in sheets, and cut that into small pieces. Combine this with raw **vitriol** <note>original: "vitriolo"; a sulfate mineral, likely copper or iron sulfate</note> and **salt of tartar** <note>original: "sale di tartaro"; potassium carbonate, used as a flux</note> <term>ana</term> <note>Latin term meaning "of each" or "in equal parts"</note> 1 lb. Grind these together very well into a solid mass. Then, draw this into a body using a furnace with a **lively fire**, <margin>reduce in vinegar with tartar</margin> packing the materials with raw tartar, saltpeter, and **black zaffre** <note>original: "zaffera nero"; a cobalt oxide pigment, here likely used as a flux or to affect the color of the metal</note>. By standing a short while with said soap <note>Likely a reference to a fluxing mixture that "cleans" the metal like soap</note> and adding a quarter at a time, everything will **melt with ease** and flow like water into the casting channel.

Take one and a half ounces of this calcined earth from the total result. Take some <term>aqua forte</term> <note>original: "acqua forte"; literally "strong water," usually nitric acid</note> made from refined **vitriol** without sulfur and **Roman vitriol** <note>original: "vitriolo romano"; blue copper sulfate</note> <term>ana</term>. In this liquid, dissolve and let fall a quarter-ounce of the aforementioned **cemented copper**. Once it has fallen in, place the **castle** <note>original: "castello"; a piece of distilling apparatus, likely the head of an alembic</note> upon it. Using an **ash bath**, draw off half of the water from the copper, <margin><unclear>distilled</unclear></margin> putting it into a well-glazed earthenware vessel until it is time to use it.

## Projection of our Fixed Elixir.

Take 40 parts of our prepared <term>body</term> <note>in alchemy, the "body" is the base metal intended for transformation</note> and heat it; when it is glowing brightly, give it a little powdered <term>borax</term> <note>used as a flux to help the metal melt and to remove impurities</note> to soften it. Finally, pour it into a casting channel <note>a mold</note>; once it has cooled, you will immediately find the whole transformed into excellent silver.

<meta>This page continues the alchemical instructions from the previous leaf, shifting from the production of silver-like metals to the preparation of a potent "ruby" tincture. <margin>2</margin>Take 2 pounds of selected and very clean <term>sal ammoniac</term> <note>original: "sale amm:o"; ammonium chloride, a salt used in alchemy to help dissolve or volatilize metals</note> and one pound of raw common salt, or edible table salt. Grind them well and place them in a <term>flask</term> <note>original: "boccia"; a round glass vessel with a neck</note>, and sublimate the salt now as best as you can according to the usual rules of fire. Let the weight of the sublimate be nine parts to the said salt, and let it be re-sublimated; this shall be done three times, always throwing away the <term>caput mortuum</term> <note>original: "capo morto"; literally "dead head," the useless chemical dregs or residue remaining after a distillation or sublimation</note>.

Of this sublimate, take 1 pound and grind it with two other pounds of excellent <term>Roman vitriol</term> <note>original: "vitriolo romano"; a historical name for copper sulfate, often used as a source of "spirit" or acid in alchemical reactions</note>. Then, once joined together, let them be placed in a flask to sublimate. When the sublimation is complete, the <term>caput mortuum</term> shall be ground and put back with the sublimate to be sublimated again. Once these two sublimations are finished, the <term>caput mortuum</term> shall be thrown away, taking two other pounds of new vitriol. It shall be made to re-sublimate again for two more times just like the first two. This sequence shall be followed nine times, renewing the "new body" <note>the fresh supply of vitriol</note> every two sublimations according to the measure stated above. In this way, it will be charged with a most beautiful <term>tincture</term> <note>original: "tintura"; in alchemy, a concentrated essence or coloring agent capable of "tinging" or transforming other substances</note>, more brilliant than a ruby, which shall be purified in its own water, which is made in this manner:

To test it, take a clean glass <term>jug</term> <note>original: "boccale"</note> and plug the <term>hole</term> <note>original: "busio," likely a dialectal variant of *buco*</note> of the jug with your finger, and put the water and the oil of antimony inside—both together—and after everything has settled and descended to the bottom, the water is dried away. When only the oil of antimony has come out, then it is kept, for [the impurities] will have gone away with the water, and only the [essential] antimony will remain.

->The Fixation of Silver <unclear>Luna...</unclear><-

Take 3 ounces of prepared **Silver** <term>Luna</term> <note>The text uses the alchemical name for silver, associated with the Moon</note>
1 ounce of **Saffron of Mars** <term>Croco di marte</term> <note>A red iron oxide powder produced by heating iron</note>
3 ounces of **sublimated salt** <note>likely common salt purified through sublimation</note>
3 ounces of **sublimated mercury** <note>mercuric chloride, a potent chemical agent in alchemical reactions</note>

One must grind <unclear>together</unclear> these substances into a powder
and pour over <strike>with aqua forte</strike> **aqua fortis** <term>aqua forte</term> <note>literally "strong water," which is nitric acid</note>
made from **saltpeter** <term>salnitro</term>, **vitriol** <term>vitriolo</term>, and **alum** <term>allume</term>,
one pound, and it is collected by means of a **retort** <term>storta</term> <note>a glass vessel with a long neck used for distillation</note>.
With this water, one **calcines** <term>calcina</term> the Silver, and it is 
reduced to a powder <term>calce</term> <note>referred to as a "calx," the residue left after a metal is treated with acid or heat</note>, noting that one ounce
of Silver requires three ounces of the <gloss>said</gloss> water.
Afterward, the <gloss>said</gloss> powder is **cupelled** <term>cupella</term> <note>refined by heating in a porous cup to remove base metals</note>; afterward, it is again
reduced to powder with the <gloss>said</gloss> aqua fortis.
But one must not use that [acid] which 
has already worked, but specifically that [fresh acid]
which remained passed over
the powders, and again the <gloss>said</gloss> powder is **cupelled** <term>cupella</term>.
And this order is maintained three times,
and the Silver will become "fixed" <note>meaning it has become stable and resistant to change by fire</note>, and will fall in
**flakes** <unclear>pagliola</unclear> <note>small grains or scales of metal</note>, and by adding a <unclear>portion</unclear>
of <unclear>Zanino</unclear> <note>potentially a specific catalyst or reagent</note>, <unclear>it remains</unclear> <unclear>entirely</unclear> as **Zecchino gold** <term>Zecchini</term> <note>gold of the purity used in Venetian sequins (zecchini), which were the gold standard of the time</note>.

<header>Purification of Mercury <note>original: "Purgatio ☿"</note></header>

### Purification of Mercury <note>original: "Purgatio ☿"</note>

Scrape the <term>cyclamen</term> <note>original: "pan porcino," literally "pig's bread"; the tuberous roots of this plant were used in alchemical cleaning processes.</note>, and with that
handle the <term>mercury</term> <note>represented by the symbol ☿</note> well and then go
and wash it well with vinegar, then wash it first
with water, so that it will all unite together,
decant the water, and use it; this is how it is done.

---

### Congelation of Mercury <note>original: "Congelatio ☿"; refers to the process of "fixing" or solidifying liquid mercury.</note>

In an iron <term>helmet</term> <note>original: "celata"; a light Renaissance-era helmet, here used as a sturdy iron vessel for heating.</note> place very strong vinegar
or else <term>chalybeate water</term> <note>original: "acqua ferrata de fenari"; water from a blacksmith's trough where iron was quenched, thought to be infused with the "virtue" of iron.</note> from the blacksmiths, and 
heat the <term>mercury</term> and when the whole thing begins to boil
you shall put inside half a pound of <term>vitriol</term> <note>A sulfate of iron or copper, used as a powerful reagent.</note>
and half a pound of <term>verdigris</term> <note>original: "verde rame"; the green patina formed on copper, often used in recipes to provide "acidity" or metallic spirit.</note> and then
one pound or as much as you wish of <term>mercury</term> and make
a wood fire, ensuring that it never ceases
to boil for the space of three,
or six hours until the water has dried up,
turning it somewhat with a small stick, but
often when the mixture pops, cover it;
outside, watch with the <term>bellows</term> <note>original: "soffietto"</note> so that
it does not escape, for the <term>mercury</term> would be lost.
And when the water is dried so that
only earth remains, draw from it, put the gold
back on top while it is boiling, keeping the fire 
gentle in a <term>pyre</term> <note>original: "pira"; referring to the arrangement of the fire or furnace.</note>.

### Copper for Fixation and Congelation

Take an ounce of **cupelled silver** <note>original: "argento di capella," silver that has been purified in a cupel furnace to remove base metals.</note> in an **iron vessel** <note>original: "ferraccia," likely a low-quality or scrap iron pot.</note> and throw it into 4 ounces of **aqua forte** <note>original: "acqua forte," the historical name for nitric acid, used here to dissolve the silver.</note>, so that it consumes it all. # From Arnald of Villanova
## On the Mastery, addressed to the King
### of Aragon: The Flower of Flowers

**Quicksilver** <note>original: *argentum vivum*, literally "living silver"</note> is the mother of metals. It is the blood to my head, a single <unclear>mixture</unclear> by way of example, because from it, it is clear that metal is generated; metal is not reduced to anything except from the primary **mercury**.

Therefore, the unrefined and the ignorant are deceived when they attempt [to make metals] by taking <term>arsenic</term>, **sulfur**, **quicksilver**, and <term>sal ammoniac</term> <note>a salt used in alchemy, specifically ammonium chloride</note>, because metals are not generated except from this **seed** <note>original: *spermate*; in alchemy, the "seed" is the foundational substance or essence of a material</note>. Indeed, outside of this metallic seed, no genus [of metal] exists; therefore, nothing can be generated in those metals from such substances. Just as in the generation of a human or an animal, there is no mixing of different [species], so too metal does not require a mixing of divine essence.

Neither in salts nor in alums is this knowledge found, nor in prepared bodies and souls alone, whether dissolved or coagulated. This is because the seed is extracted from the <unclear>depths</unclear> in which the body is augmented, just as it is in its own nature.

And because **quicksilver** is the principle of metals, some have prepared it by **sublimating** <note>a process of heating a substance until it turns to vapor and then becomes solid again</note> and **fixing** it, yet they achieved nothing. For just as the seed of a man is useless unless it is cast into the **womb** of a woman, so also mercury is of no use unless it is cast into the womb of the body <note>in alchemy, the "body" usually refers to a base metal like lead or copper that "receives" the mercury</note>.

<margin>#</margin> Some have mixed **quicksilver** with a "body" by amalgamating it, and they <unclear>labored</unclear> and fixed it, believing that through this it might be mixed with another body; yet they found nothing except a clean, perfect body. The cause of this error is that the seed is not joined with the body except by the mediation of the **moon** <note>the Moon is the alchemical symbol for Silver</note>, since the **soul** <note>original: *anima*</note> is the medium between the **spirit** <note>the spirit usually refers to the volatile mercury</note> of the silver, joining them to one another. The soul, however...

### Tobacco

Place the stalks one above the other on the drying rack <note>original: *serabone*; likely a regional term for a specific frame or structure used for air-drying plants</note> and when they are sufficiently dry, place them on a cloth. Position the cloth over a support made of half-canes in the middle of the fire <note>this suggests a gentle, indirect heat from a hearth</note> so that in a short time they will be very dry.

Then, place them in a mortar and, with alternating scraping along the edges using the pestle, turn all the leaves into powder. The stalks should also be added, but they should be removed quickly, and the leaf powder will remain. The leaf powder will be improved the more it is passed through and separated by a sieve, because the stalks are separated at the bottom; or you can mix them together if it seems right to you.

Then proceed in this way: take as much water as seems sufficient to make a sauce <note>original: *salsa*; in the context of historical tobacco production, this refers to a "casing" or a flavored liquid used to cure and aromaticize the tobacco</note> for that tobacco. Once the tobacco is put into a clean and prepared jar <note>original: *caraella*; likely a vessel similar to a carafe or small jar</note>, you will place it in a heating chamber <note>original: *era*; likely referring to a warm area near a hearth or a controlled heat source</note>. Inside it, for every pound <term>libra; a local unit of weight, roughly 339 grams</term> of tobacco, you will add an ounce <term>oncia; roughly 28 grams</term> of dried roses—of the grated variety—into the glass bell-jar <note>original: *campana di uetro*; a bell-shaped vessel used in distillation and infusions</note>, along with two ounces of <unclear>prodipinelamente</unclear> of healthy water in the bell of <unclear>srodipinelamente</unclear>, whether it be hard or soft. Let it boil in the heating chamber until the water reduces by four pounds. Then, pour it through a strainer over the tobacco; and when it has cooled slightly so that it can be handled, work it and squeeze it well with your hands for a bit. After it is prepared to make pastes, you must cover the jar.

<note>The vocabulary list below clarifies the technical terms used in the processing of tobacco and the aromatic infusion.</note>

*   **Tobacco:** The plant leaves being processed
*   **Stalks:** The woody stems of the plant
*   **Mortar:** A bowl for grinding
*   **Pestle:** The tool used for crushing in the mortar
*   **Sieve:** A tool for sifting powder
*   **Pound:** A unit of weight (libra)
*   **Ounce:** A unit of weight (oncia)
*   **Dried roses:** Used for flavoring the tobacco
*   **Glass bell-jar:** A vessel for infusion or distillation
*   **Sauce:** The flavored liquid casing
*   **Jar/Carafe:** The storage and processing vessel
*   **Cooled/Lukewarm:** The state required for manual handling

## To make strong vinegar

Take the **stems** <note>original: *raspi*; the woody stalks of the grape bunches</note> removed from the **pomace** <note>original: *vinaccie*; the skins, seeds, and stems remaining after grapes are pressed</note>, <unclear>placing them</unclear> in a <unclear>vessel</unclear> and wetting them well with strong vinegar until they are thoroughly soaked; and the following day, wet them again as before. 

Then place them ~~in a small cask~~ in two **small casks** <term>small casks</term> <note>original: *caratelli*; specifically small barrels used for aging or fermenting liquids</note>, or barrels, in which you will first make a base of stems, and ~~then~~ throw over that <unclear>side</unclear> powder made of dried and crushed **vine leaves** <note>original: *pampini*</note>; then make another layer of vinegared stems, and then powder, and then stems, and then powder until they are full, but do not press them down so much that <unclear>the stems are crushed</unclear>.

Afterwards, pour wine over them, or **stalk-wine** <term>stalk-wine</term> <note>original: *raspato*; a thin, inferior wine made by pouring water over the grape stalks and pomace</note>, or even water, into just one of those small casks or barrels, and then let it sit for 4 or 5 days. Then draw out all the vinegar from the **spigot** <term>spigot</term> <note>original: *canula*; a small tube or tap at the base of the barrel</note> and place it into the other cask of stems. 

Refill the one you have emptied with new wine, or watered-down wine, or water; and after another 4 or 5 days have passed, proceed by drawing the vinegar that was placed in the second cask. As it empties, refill it with the liquid vinegar from the first cask; proceed doing this step by step so that you will never lack vinegar. And if you wish to give it a pleasing flavor, throw in a little powder of **summer savory** <term>summer savory</term> <note>original: *savorelle*; an aromatic herb often used in vinegars and seasonings</note>.

Take a jug of the dregs of <unclear>foul</unclear> water that remains at the bottom of the **distillation boiler** <term>distillation boiler</term> <note>original: *tamburlano*; a technical term for a component of a still or a large heating vessel</note>, and pour it over a barrel of watered-down wine, or water, and it will become strong vinegar.

<summary>This page outlines a traditional method for creating a perpetual supply of strong vinegar using layered grape stems and vine leaves in a two-cask system. It also includes a "shortcut" method using the acidic residues from distillation equipment.</summary>

## ->Proven remedy for gout<-

Take a bunch of **nettles** <note>original: *ortica*; specifically the stinging nettle (*Urtica dioica*)</note> that have sharp leaves and sting intensely, and with them, thoroughly beat the foot afflicted by **gout** <term>gout</term> <note>original: *podagra*; a painful form of arthritis traditionally associated with "rich" diets and treated in the early modern period by attempting to draw out "bad humors"</note>. This will cause several blisters to form, which will eventually burst. By keeping the foot warm, these blisters will discharge a great deal of fluid for three days. Afterwards, the foot should be anointed with **cooling ointments** <note>In the humoral theory of medicine, gout was often seen as a "hot" inflammation, requiring "cold" remedies to restore balance</note> mixed with the juice of **mercury** <note>original: *cicigna*; likely referring to *Mercurialis annua* (annual mercury) or possibly *Stellaria media* (chickweed), both used in folk medicine for their cooling and emollient properties</note> until it is healed. The gout will then not only cease to cause trouble, but it will never return.

To perform this experiment, use 1 part Gold and the fixed substance in the form of Antimony for testing, and thus in whatever way you proceed, <term>Silver</term> <note>original symbol: ☽</note> is also approached.

And this by way of 10 parts <term>quicksilver</term> <note>liquid mercury</note>; nothing ends this, and this to 12 parts. Let the mass overcome the mass, almost in the waters mentioned, before the foil is used, for 12 hours; through 12 "dews" <note>distillations or washings</note> it finishes, and it will be until it is cured, and it will be as the <term>Sun</term> <note>Gold</note>.
